modules.title: Expressing intentions in Vietnamese
modules.description: In Vietnamese, expressing intentions is essential for discussing plans, goals, and desires. Key expressions such as định (intend), lên kế hoạch (making plans), and sẽ (will) allow speakers to communicate their intentions with clarity and nuance.

faqs.question: How to use Định in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: “Định” means “to intend to” and is placed before a verb to indicate intention. For example, “Tôi định học tiếng Việt” (I intend to study Vietnamese).

faqs.question: What’s the difference between muốn and định ?
faqs.answer: “Muốn” expresses a desire (want) to do something, while “định” specifically indicates an intention or plan. For example, “Tôi muốn đi du lịch” (I want to travel) versus “Tôi định đi du lịch” (I intend to travel).

faqs.question: Can “sẽ” be used to express intention, or is it only for the future tense?
faqs.answer: “ Sẽ ” generally indicates a future action but can imply intent if the context is clear. However, “ định ” or “muốn” are more specific for intentional actions.

faqs.question: Can “đang định” be used to indicate an immediate intention?
faqs.answer: Yes, “đang định” implies an intention that you are actively considering or about to do soon. For example, “Tôi đang định gọi cho bạn” (I am about to call you).

units.title: Will (sẽ)

modules.title: Expressing surprise in Vietnamese
modules.description: In Vietnamese, expressing surprise is often vivid and emotional, using short exclamations that convey shock, disbelief, or amazement. This lesson will introduce common phrases like Thật à , Không ngờ , and Trời ơi to help you sound more natural in everyday conversations.

faqs.question: What is the difference between “Thật à?
faqs.answer: ” and “

faqs.question: Thật không?
Both express surprise, but “Thật à?
faqs.answer: ” is more neutral/informal and used in spoken

faqs.question: Vietnamese, while “Thật không?
faqs.answer: ” can carry more disbelief or request for confirmation. Is “Trời ơi!” considered rude or inappropriate? No, “Trời ơi!” is very common and expressive in daily conversation, but tone and context matter. Use it carefully in formal settings.

faqs.question: Can “Không ngờ” be used at the beginning of a sentence?
faqs.answer: Yes , “Không ngờ…” (I didn’t expect…) often starts a sentence to show surprise or shock about an outcome.

faqs.question: Are there any formal ways to express surprise in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: While most surprise expressions are informal, phrases like “Tôi thật sự ngạc nhiên” (I’m truly surprised) are more formal or written.

faqs.question: Can I combine these expressions in one sentence?
faqs.answer: Yes, native speakers often layer expressions for emphasis, like “Trời ơi, không ngờ luôn đó!” , especially in spoken language.

modules.title: Expressing regret in Vietnamese
modules.description: In Vietnamese, there are few phrases to express regret or a sense of sorrow, wishing things were different, or acknowledging a missed opportunity. This lesson will show you how to express regret in Vietnamese.

faqs.question: Can I use “đáng lẽ ra” in both spoken and written Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes, “đáng lẽ ra” is used in both formal and informal contexts, but it’s more commonly found in reflective or narrative speech and writing to express regret or missed opportunities.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “thật tiếc là” and “đáng lẽ ra”?
faqs.answer: “Thật tiếc là” simply expresses regret or sympathy over something unfortunate, while “đáng lẽ ra” suggests that something should have happened differently, implying a sense of missed obligation or expectation.

faqs.question: How do I use “biết vậy thì” in a sentence?
faqs.answer: “Biết vậy thì…” means “If I had known, then…” and is usually followed by a statement indicating what the speaker would have done instead. It expresses regret based on hindsight.

faqs.question: Are there other common phrases to express regret in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes, other expressions include giá mà (if only), ước gì (I wish), and lẽ ra (should have), all of which can express similar feelings of regret or missed chances.

faqs.question: What level of Vietnamese do I need to use these structures correctly?
faqs.answer: These expressions are generally suited for learners at the B1 (intermediate) level or above, as they require some familiarity with conditional and past narrative forms.

modules.title: Expressing hope in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, you’ll learn how to express hope in Vietnamese using common phrases like hy vọng , mong , and more. These expressions are useful in both casual and formal situations to share your wishes, expectations, or optimism about the future.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “hy vọng” and “mong”?
faqs.answer: “Hy vọng” is a more general and neutral way to express hope. While “mong” can sound slightly more formal or polite and is often used in expressions of wish or expectation.

faqs.question: Can “mong” be used with pronouns like “tôi” or “bạn”?
faqs.answer: Yes , “mong” can be used with personal pronouns. For example: Tôi mong bạn thành công (I hope you succeed).

faqs.question: Is there a grammatical structure I should follow when using “hy vọng”?
faqs.answer: Yes , “hy vọng” is often followed by rằng (that) or a clause, e.g., Tôi hy vọng rằng bạn sẽ đến sớm (I hope that you will come early).

faqs.question: Can “mong” be used in formal writing or letters?
faqs.answer: Absolutely . “Mong” is very common in formal or polite Vietnamese, especially in written requests or closing remarks in emails and letters, like Mong nhận được phản hồi sớm (Hope to receive your reply soon).

faqs.question: At what level should I learn to use “hy vọng” and “mong”?
faqs.answer: These expressions are suitable for A2 to B1 level learners, as they involve basic sentence structures and polite forms commonly used in everyday conversation.

modules.title: Probability in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, you will learn how to express probability in Vietnamese using common phrases such as hình như , có lẽ , chắc là , and có thể . These expressions help you talk about uncertainty, possibility, and likelihood in everyday situations.

faqs.question: What is the difference between “hình như” and “có lẽ”?
faqs.answer: Both express uncertainty, but hình như often implies personal perception or assumption, while có lẽ is a more neutral way to say “maybe” or “probably.”

faqs.question: Can I use “chắc là” and “có thể” interchangeably?
faqs.answer: Not exactly. Chắc là implies higher certainty (“surely”), while có thể suggests possibility without commitment (“might”).

faqs.question: Where do these expressions go in a sentence?
faqs.answer: They typically appear at the beginning or before the verb phrase: e.g., Có lẽ anh ấy chưa đến. (“Maybe he hasn’t arrived.”)

faqs.question: Are these expressions formal or informal?
faqs.answer: They are generally neutral and appropriate in both casual and polite contexts, depending on tone and situation.

faqs.question: How can I practice using these expressions naturally?
faqs.answer: Try making predictions about current events or guessing what might happen using these structures, and get feedback from native speakers or a teacher.

faqs.question: Can I go study in Vietnam with ?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can! You can study with us in Saigon or Hanoi, in both group or individual classes. You’ll even have the opportunity to live with a Vietnamese family, thanks to our homestays .

modules.title: Purpose of action in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, you’ll learn how to express the purpose of an action in Vietnamese using common structures like để , nhằm , and vì . These words help explain why someone does something and are essential for forming clear, goal-oriented sentences.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “để” and “nhằm” when expressing purpose?
faqs.answer: “Để” is commonly used in both spoken and written language to express purpose. “Nhằm” is more formal and often appears in written or official contexts.

faqs.question: Can I use “vì” and “để” interchangeably?
faqs.answer: No. “Vì” introduces the reason or cause of an action, while “để” shows the purpose or intended result. They are not interchangeable.

faqs.question: Where in the sentence should “để” or “nhằm” be placed?
faqs.answer: They are typically placed before a verb or verb phrase to introduce the purpose, e.g., Tôi học tiếng Việt để giao tiếp tốt hơn (I study Vietnamese to communicate better).

faqs.question: Is it okay to omit “để” in casual speech?
faqs.answer: While native speakers might occasionally drop “để” in very casual or rushed speech, it’s generally better for learners to use it clearly to avoid confusion.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “vì muốn” and “để”?
faqs.answer: “Vì muốn” introduces a personal motivation ( because [I] want to… ), while “để” focuses on the intended goal of the action.

modules.title: Expressing potential in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, you will learn how to express potential in Vietnamese using phrases like “có thể” , “có cơ hội” , and “có khả năng” . These expressions help you talk about possibilities, opportunities, and abilities in different contexts.

faqs.question: What is the difference between “có thể” and “có khả năng”?
faqs.answer: “Có thể” is often used to express general possibility or permission, while “có khả năng” emphasizes someone’s ability or potential to do something.

faqs.question: Can I use “có cơ hội” in place of “có thể”?
faqs.answer: No, “có cơ hội” refers to having an opportunity, not just the possibility or ability to do something. It’s more context-dependent.

faqs.question: Is “có khả năng” formal or casual?
faqs.answer: “Có khả năng” is more formal and often used in written or professional contexts, while “có thể” is more common in everyday conversation.

faqs.question: How do I negate these expressions of potential?
faqs.answer: You can negate them by adding “không” in front, such as “không thể” (cannot), “không có khả năng” (lack the ability), or “không có cơ hội” (no opportunity).

faqs.question: Can these expressions be used with both verbs and nouns?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially “có thể” and “có khả năng” can be followed by verbs ( có thể đi – can go) or noun clauses ( có khả năng thành công – potential for success).

units.title: Can (có thể)

modules.title: Expressing contrast in Vietnamese
modules.description: In Vietnamese, expressing contrast helps you show differences between ideas, actions, or situations. This lesson will teach you how to use structures like “mặc dù” , “trong khi” , and “ngược lại” to clearly communicate opposition or comparison in your sentences.

faqs.question: Can I use “mặc dù” and “nhưng” in the same sentence?
faqs.answer: Yes . While “mặc dù” introduces the contrast, “nhưng” can be added in the second clause to emphasize it, similar to “although… but…” in English. For example: Mặc dù trời mưa, nhưng tôi vẫn đi học.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “trong khi” and “ngược lại”?
faqs.answer: “Trong khi” means “while” and is used to contrast two simultaneous actions or situations. “Ngược lại” means “on the contrary” or “in contrast” and introduces an opposite idea or result.

faqs.question: Is “mặc dù” formal or informal?
faqs.answer: “Mặc dù” is neutral and commonly used in both spoken and written Vietnamese. It is slightly more formal than “dù” but both are acceptable in most contexts.

faqs.question: Can I start a sentence with “ngược lại”?
faqs.answer: Yes . “Ngược lại” can begin a sentence to introduce a contrasting idea. Example: Tôi thích ở nhà. Ngược lại, anh ấy thích đi chơi.

faqs.question: Are there other ways to express contrast in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes. Besides “mặc dù”, “trong khi”, and “ngược lại”, you can also use “tuy nhiên” (however), “dù sao đi nữa” (anyway), and “trái lại” (conversely) depending on the tone and context.

units.title: Even Though (mặc dù...nhưng)

modules.title: Giving advice in Vietnamese
modules.description: Giving advice is a common part of everyday conversation in Vietnamese. In this lesson, you’ll learn how to use expressions like khuyên , thử , and nghĩ to offer suggestions, make recommendations, and gently guide others in a natural and culturally appropriate way.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “khuyên” and “góp ý”?
faqs.answer: Khuyên is used for giving advice with the intent to help or guide someone, often from a position of more experience. Góp ý is more about offering suggestions or constructive feedback, often in a neutral or collaborative tone.

faqs.question: Can I use “nên” instead of “khuyên” when giving advice?
faqs.answer: Yes. Nên is often used directly in sentences to suggest what someone should do (e.g. Bạn nên nghỉ ngơi. ). Khuyên typically introduces the act of advising (e.g. Tôi khuyên bạn nên nghỉ ngơi. ).

faqs.question: Is “thử” always used to suggest something?
faqs.answer: Not always. Thử literally means “to try.” It can be used to suggest trying something ( Bạn thử làm cái này đi. ), but can also describe an attempt ( Tôi thử học tiếng Việt. ).

faqs.question: How do I soften my advice to make it sound more polite?
faqs.answer: You can add softeners like nhé , xem sao , or use a questioning tone (e.g.

faqs.question: Bạn thử làm như vậy xem sao nhé?
faqs.answer: ) to avoid sounding too direct.

faqs.question: When should I use “nghĩ là” in giving advice?
faqs.answer: Nghĩ là (I think that…) introduces a personal opinion and is often used to gently suggest an action, especially when you don’t want to impose (e.g. Tôi nghĩ là bạn nên nói chuyện với cô ấy. ).

modules.title: How to order food in Vietnamese
modules.description: When dining in Vietnam, knowing how to order food and ask for the bill is essential for a smooth experience. In this lesson, we’ll go over the most common phrases and structures used when ordering at a restaurant in Vietnam.
modules.mainPattern: Cho + 1st pronoun + counter + name of the dish or drink

faqs.question: What is the most polite way to order food in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: The most polite way is to use “Cho tôi…” (Give me…) or “Tôi muốn…” (I would like…). You can also add “làm ơn” (please) to sound more courteous.

faqs.question: You can say: “Cho tôi xem thực đơn được không?
faqs.answer: ” which means “

faqs.question: May I see the menu?
How do I ask for the bill at a restaurant?
faqs.answer: To ask for the bill, simply say: “Tính tiền, nhé!” or more politely, “Làm ơn cho tôi xin hóa đơn.”

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “món này” and “cái này” when ordering?
faqs.answer: “Món này” refers to this dish (used specifically for food), while “cái này” means this thing in general and is less specific when talking about food.

faqs.question: Is it okay to point at the menu when ordering?
faqs.answer: Yes, it’s quite common and acceptable to politely point at the menu while saying the name of the dish or “Tôi muốn món này.”

modules.title: Adjective Clause with "Đến mức" in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, you’ll learn how to use “đến mức” in Vietnamese to express the extent or result of an action or quality — similar to “so… that” or “to the point that” in English. This structure helps add depth and clarity when describing intensity or consequences.

faqs.question: What does “đến mức” mean in Vietnamese grammar?
faqs.answer: “Đến mức” means “to the extent that” or “so…that” and is used to express the degree or result of an action or description.

faqs.question: How is “đến mức” different from “quá… đến nỗi”?
faqs.answer: While both indicate result or extent, “quá… đến nỗi” emphasizes excessiveness, whereas “đến mức” can describe both moderate and extreme degrees more neutrally.

faqs.question: Can I use “đến mức” in both spoken and written Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes, “đến mức” is appropriate in both contexts and is commonly used in formal and informal situations to show consequence or intensity.

faqs.question: Where does “đến mức” appear in the sentence?
faqs.answer: “Đến mức” typically follows an adjective or verb phrase and precedes a clause or descriptive phrase showing the outcome or degree.

faqs.question: Are there synonyms for “đến mức” in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes , phrases like “tới mức” or “đến nỗi” can be used similarly, though they may differ slightly in tone or emphasis depending on context.

units.title: So...That (đến mức)
units.explanation: The phrase “ đến mức “ in Vietnamese is used to indicate the extent or degree of something . It is similar to “to the point that” or “to the extent that” in English. This structure helps add depth and emphasis when describing situations or characteristics..

modules.title: Nominalization in Vietnamese
modules.description: Nominalization (danh từ hóa) helps transform actions and qualities into abstract nouns , making your sentences sound more natural and academic. In this lesson, you’ll learn how to use nominalization correctly and effectively in Vietnamese! There are two main ways to create nominalization in Vietnamese:

faqs.question: What is nominalization in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Nominalization is the process of turning verbs or adjectives into nouns using words like sự , việc , or chuyện , allowing abstract ideas or actions to be expressed as nouns.

faqs.question: When should I use “sự” instead of “việc” or “chuyện”?
faqs.answer: Use sự for formal, abstract nouns (e.g. sự thành công – success), while việc refers more to actions or tasks ( việc học – the act of studying), and chuyện is used for events or stories, often informal.

faqs.question: Can I use “sự” before any verb?
faqs.answer: Not all verbs can be nominalized with sự . It typically applies to Sino-Vietnamese words and more formal verbs. Native speakers may not use it with purely native or colloquial words.

faqs.question: Is there a difference between “việc học” and “sự học”?
faqs.answer: Yes. Việc học emphasizes the activity of studying, while sự học is more abstract and formal, referring to the concept or process of education in a broader sense.

faqs.question: Is nominalization common in spoken Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Việc and chuyện are quite common in everyday speech, while sự appears more frequently in written or formal contexts like news, reports, or academic texts.

modules.title: Passive voice in Vietnamese
modules.description: Vietnamese speakers usually use a positive passive voice when they want to stay humble and show their respect to the other person or to express their honor by doing something. We guide you through the structure and usages of được and bị , helping you express actions from a recipient’s perspective.

faqs.question: How to form the passive voicce in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: The passive voice is typically formed using “bị” (when the action has a negative outcome) or “được” (when the action has a positive or neutral outcome) before the main verb. For example, “Tôi bị mắng” (I was scolded) and “Tôi được khen” (I was praised).

faqs.question: Should I use “bị” or “được” in the passive voice?
faqs.answer: Use “bị” when the action has an undesirable effect on the subject (e.g., “Tôi bị mất ví” – “I had my wallet stolen”). Use “được” when the action benefits the subject or is neutral (e.g., “Tôi được tăng lương” – “I got a raise”).

faqs.question: Is the passive voice commonly used?
faqs.answer: The passive voice is less common in Vietnamese compared to English. Active voice is preferred unless it’s necessary to focus on the subject receiving the action.

faqs.question: Can passive be used with all verbs?
faqs.answer: No, the passive voice is generally used with transitive verbs (verbs that can take a direct object). Not all verbs in Vietnamese can form a passive sentence.

modules.title: Quoting someone in Vietnamese
modules.description: In Vietnamese, quoting can be done either directly or indirectly, similar to how it is in English. This lesson will explain how to form both direct and indirect quotes, highlighting the differences in structure and word choice.

faqs.question: How do you form direct quotes in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Direct quotes are enclosed in quotation marks, and the speaker’s exact words are used without changes. For example: “Anh ấy nói, ‘Tôi sẽ đi làm sớm.'”

faqs.question: What difference between direct and indirect?
faqs.answer: Direct quoting uses the speaker’s exact words, while indirect quoting paraphrases the statement, often involving changes in tense, pronouns, or sentence structure. For example: “Anh ấy nói rằng anh ấy sẽ đi làm sớm.”

faqs.question: Do quotation marks get used in indirect quotes in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: No, quotation marks are only used in direct quotes. Indirect quotes do not require quotation marks and often start with a reporting verb like “nói rằng” (said that).

faqs.question: Can indirect quotes omit the word “rằng” in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes, in informal speech, “rằng” (that) can sometimes be omitted in indirect quotes. For example, “Anh ấy nói anh ấy sẽ đến” (He said he would come) can omit “rằng.”

modules.title: Expressing hearsay in Vietnamese
modules.description: In Vietnamese, expressing hearsay or indirect information is essential for everyday communication, especially when you’re not the original source of the news. This lesson introduces common structures like nói rằng , nghe nói là , đồn rằng , and theo , helping you share what you’ve heard or read from others.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “nghe nói là” and “đồn rằng”?
faqs.answer: “Nghe nói là” is often used when the speaker has personally heard something from someone, while “đồn rằng” implies that something is a rumor or gossip that is being spread around.

faqs.question: Can I use “nói rằng” in both written and spoken Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes , “nói rằng” is neutral and can be used in both contexts, though in casual conversation, people often omit “rằng” and use just “nói…” .

faqs.question: Is “theo” always followed by a source?
faqs.answer: Yes, “theo” is used to introduce the source of the information (e.g., “Theo báo Tuổi Trẻ…” ), similar to “according to” in English.

faqs.question: Are these hearsay expressions interchangeable?
faqs.answer: Not always. While they all relate to reporting information, they differ in tone and context. For example, “nghe nói” is more casual, while “nói rằng” is more formal or direct.

faqs.question: Can these structures be used to report opinions as well as facts?
faqs.answer: Yes , hearsay expressions in Vietnamese can be used to report both factual information and personal opinions, depending on the context.

modules.title: Expressing degree in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, you’ll learn how to express different degrees or intensities in Vietnamese using words like hết sức , rất , càng ngày càng , and quá . These expressions help you emphasize how strong, extreme, or gradual an action or quality is, allowing for more vivid and accurate communication.

faqs.question: What is the difference between “rất” and “hết sức”?
faqs.answer: Both mean “very,” but “hết sức” is more intense and formal than “rất” . “Hết sức” can translate to “ extremely ” or “utmost.”

faqs.question: Can I use “quá” in both positive and negative sentences?
faqs.answer: Yes , but “quá” often carries a negative tone (e.g., nóng quá! = “too hot!”), unless it’s clearly meant to emphasize excitement or praise.

faqs.question: How do I use “càng ngày càng”?
faqs.answer: “Càng ngày càng” means “more and more” or “increasingly.” It is used before an adjective or verb to show a growing degree over time (e.g., càng ngày càng đẹp = “more and more beautiful”).

faqs.question: Is it okay to combine these words in one sentence?
faqs.answer: Usually, no. Since each word already emphasizes degree, combining them (e.g., rất quá đẹp ) would sound unnatural. Use only one degree modifier per idea. Which of these words is used in formal vs. informal contexts? “Rất” and “quá” are used in both casual and formal situations. “Hết sức” is more formal, while “càng ngày càng” is neutral and suits all contexts.

units.title: A Little (hơi/một chút)

modules.title: How to say "only" in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson we will learn how to use chỉ and mỗi to express “only” in Vietnamese. Both are used to convey exclusivity or limitations, and need to be used correctly in a sentence. Let’s have a look together.

faqs.question: How to say only in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Only in Vietnamese can be expressed using the words chỉ and mỗi , as well as both words under the expression chỉ…mỗi… .

faqs.question: Love you only How to use “chỉ” in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: This is a general term used to indicate that something is limited or restricted. Subject + chỉ + verb/adjective Em chỉ ngủ khi trời sáng. I only sleep in the morning.

faqs.question: How to say if in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: To express if in Vietnamese you’ll need to use the words Nếu or Nếu như. Nếu/ Nếu như + Clause 1, Clause 2 Nếu anh không đến được, nhớ báo em nhá! If you can’t come, let me know! — Learn more about how to say if in Vietnamese here.

units.title: Only with chỉ
units.explanation: Only in Vietnamese can be expressed in three ways, the first one uses the word Chỉ . This is a general term used to indicate that something is limited or restricted. It is used with verbs and adjectives, and could be translated in English by “only”, “just”.

examples.vi: Em chỉ mệt khi chạy hơn
examples.en: 2km I am only tired after 2-km-running

examples.vi: Em chỉ chạy bộ
examples.en: Sau khi

units.title: Only/Each with mỗi
units.explanation: Mỗi is a second way to express only in Vietnamese, and is followed by nouns. PATTERN Mỗi (only) + noun (except for time and date) ăn mỗi cơm eat only rice uống mỗi nước drink only water thích mỗi anh love you only.

modules.title: How to say "instead" in Vietnamese
modules.description: To suggest an alternative or express doing one thing “instead” of doing another in Vietnamese, two terms are commonly used. In this lesson we teach you how to use “thay vì” and “thay vào đó” .
modules.mainPattern: Thay vì + clause A, clause B (alternative option)

faqs.question: How to say instead in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: To express doing one thing “instead” of doing another thing in Vietnamese is Thay vào đó . It is used to introduce an alternative or replacement action, often after stating what was done or considered. It’s like saying “in place of that” or “instead of that.” Clause A + Thay vào đó + clause B (alternative option) Anh ngủ ở nhà cả ngày rồi! Thay vào đó, anh nên chạy bộ 5 phút You’ve been sleeping all day!You should go running in 5 minutes instead !

faqs.question: How to say instead of in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: To express doing one thing “instead” of doing another in Vietnamese, the following structure is used. It introduces an alternative action or choice that replaces something else.

faqs.question: How to say if not in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: If not in Vietnamese is Nếu không . You need to use the following structure: Nếu không + Verb, Clause Nếu không thích, anh cứ về If (you) not like it, just leave — Learn more about if in Vietnamese here.

units.title: Instead (thay vì)
units.pattern: Thay vì + clause A, clause B (alternative option)
units.explanation: IN VIETNAMESE To suggest an alternative or express doing one thing “instead” of doing another in Vietnamese, two terms are commonly used. In this lesson we teach you how to use “thay vì” and “thay vào đó” . INSTEAD OF… To express doing one thing “instead” of doing another in Vietnamese, the following structure is used. It introduces an alternative action or choice that replaces something else. PATTERN Thay vì + clause A, clause B (alternative option) Thay vì chị chia tay anh ấy, chị nên lắng nghe anh ấy giải thích Instead of breaking up with him, you should listen to his explanation Thay vì ăn bánh mì, mình muốn ăn phở Instead of eating banh mi, I want to eat Pho Thay vì đi du lịch Nhật Bản, mình muốn đi du lịch Hàn Quốc Instead of traveling to Japan, I want to travel to Korea.

modules.title: How to say "even though" in Vietnamese
modules.description: The phrase “even though” is commonly expressed as a contrast between two clauses. The primary patterns used in Vietnamese for “even though” are “mặc dù,” “dù,” and “tuy…nhưng.” All these expressions indicate a contrast or concession.

faqs.question: How to say “even though” in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: In Vietnamese, “even though” can be expressed with phrases like mặc dù, dù, or tuy.

faqs.question: Can I use “mặc dù” and “dù” interchangeably?
faqs.answer: Yes, mặc dù and dù both mean “even though,” but mặc dù is more formal, while dù is often used in informal contexts.

faqs.question: How to say “with” in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: With in Vietnamese can be said by using multiple words. The most common sentence structures are: Subject 1 + Verb + với + Subject 2 Tôi về nhà với mẹ tôi. I come home with my mother someone, something “with” something: Subject 1 + Verb + cùng + Subject 2 Tôi về nhà cùng mẹ tôi. I come home with my mother Subject 1 + với (with) + Subject 2 + verb + cùng nhau (together) Tôi với mẹ về nhà cùng nhau . I come home together with my mom — Learn more about how to use with in Vietnamese here.

faqs.question: Is Vietnamese SVO or SOV?
faqs.answer: The Vietnamese language structure is SVO, meaning sentences are built according to Subject + Verb + Object.

faqs.question: Where to find more lessons like this?
faqs.answer: Check out our Vietnamese Grammar Bank , where you will find free lessons for levels A1 to B1. If you prefer to study from home, check out our online courses .

units.title: Although: mặc dù...nhưng
units.explanation: “Mặc dù…nhưng” emphasizes the contrast between two clauses, similar to “even though” or “despite” in English. It’s commonly used in both spoken and written language, especially in formal or official contexts. 1, nhưng + Clause 2 Mặc dù trời mưa, nhưng tôi vẫn đi ra ngoài Even though it rains, I still go outside Mặc dù cô ấy bận, nhưng cô vẫn giúp tôi Even though she is busy, she still helps me Mặc dù họ không thích món ăn này, nhưng họ vẫn ăn Even though they don’t like this dish, they still eat it Mặc dù anh ấy không khỏe, nhưng anh đi làm Even though he is not well, he goes to work Mặc dù trời lạnh, nhưng họ vẫn chơi bóng đá Even though it’s cold, they still play soccer Mặc dù việc khó khăn, nhưng tôi vẫn cố gắng Even though the task is difficult, I still try.

units.explanation: “Mặc dù…nhưng” emphasizes the contrast between two clauses, similar to “even though” or “despite” in English. It’s commonly used in both spoken and written language, especially in formal or official contexts. 1, nhưng + Clause 2 Mặc dù trời mưa, nhưng tôi vẫn đi ra ngoài Even though it rains, I still go outside Mặc dù cô ấy bận, nhưng cô vẫn giúp tôi Even though she is busy, she still helps me Mặc dù họ không thích món ăn này, nhưng họ vẫn ăn Even though they don’t like this dish, they still eat it Mặc dù anh ấy không khỏe, nhưng anh đi làm Even though he is not well, he goes to work Mặc dù trời lạnh, nhưng họ vẫn chơi bóng đá Even though it’s cold, they still play soccer Mặc dù việc khó khăn, nhưng tôi vẫn cố gắng Even though the task is difficult, I still try DÙ … NHƯNG “Dù…nhưng” is often used interchangeably with “mặc dù” but is less formal. modules.title: How to say "for now" in Vietnamese
modules.description: In Vietnamese, the phrase “tạm thời” effectively communicates temporary situations or decisions. It helps us express what is applicable at the moment but may change later.

faqs.question: How do you say for now in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: You can say “tạm thời” to indicate “for now” or “temporarily.” For example, “Tôi sẽ làm việc này tạm thời” means “I will do this for now.”

faqs.question: Can “tạm thời” be used with formal and informal?
faqs.answer: Yes, “tạm thời” is versatile and can be used in both formal and informal situations when referring to something temporary.

faqs.question: Is “tạm thời” used in everyday conversations?
faqs.answer: Yes, “tạm thời” is frequently used in everyday Vietnamese to refer to temporary situations or arrangements, making it a practical expression for learners.

faqs.question: How to say after all in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: In Vietnamese, “sau tất cả” or “rốt cuộc” can be used to mean “after all” when summing up or reaching a conclusion. — Learn more about how to say after all in Vietnamese here.

units.title: For Now (tạm thời)

modules.title: Expressing "seem to be" in Vietnamese
modules.description: In Vietnamese, expressions like “hình như” , “dường như” , and “có vẻ như” are used to convey uncertainty or make assumptions, similar to “seem to be” in English. This lesson will show you how to use these structures naturally in different contexts.

faqs.question: What is the difference between “hình như” and “dường như”?
faqs.answer: Both mean “seem” or “apparently,” but hình như is more commonly used in spoken Vietnamese and can suggest a bit more uncertainty. Dường như tends to sound slightly more formal or literary.

faqs.question: Can I use “hình như” and “dường như” at the beginning of a sentence?
faqs.answer: Yes! Both expressions usually appear at the beginning of the sentence to indicate uncertainty or assumption, similar to “It seems that…” in English.

faqs.question: Are there other ways to say “seem to be” in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes. In addition to hình như and dường như , you can use có vẻ như (it appears that) or dường như là (it seems that) depending on the context and formality.

faqs.question: Is “hình như” used in questions?
faqs.answer: Yes, it can be. Using hình như in a question implies that the speaker is unsure and seeking confirmation, e.g.,

faqs.question: Hình như bạn chưa ăn sáng?
You haven’t eaten breakfast, have you?
Can these expressions be used with different tenses?
faqs.answer: Yes. Hình như , dường như , and có vẻ như are compatible with past, present, or future contexts. The time reference is understood from the rest of the sentence.

units.title: Apparently (hình như)

modules.title: Include & exclude in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, you’ll learn how to express inclusion and exclusion in Vietnamese using common phrases like gồm có , bao gồm , không tính , and trừ . Mastering these structures will help you clearly state what is or isn’t part of a group, list, or total.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “không tính” and “trừ” when excluding something?
faqs.answer: Both express exclusion, but “trừ” is often used in more formal or written contexts, while “không tính” sounds more conversational and is common in speech.

faqs.question: Can “gồm có” and “bao gồm” be used the same way?
faqs.answer: Yes, they both mean “include,” but “bao gồm” is a bit more formal. “Gồm có” is commonly used in lists or descriptions.

faqs.question: What does “bao hàm” mean compared to “bao gồm”?
faqs.answer: “Bao hàm” also means “to include” but usually refers to abstract or conceptual inclusion, like ideas or meanings, whereas “bao gồm” often lists tangible elements.

faqs.question: How do I say “The price includes breakfast” in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: You can say: Giá bao gồm bữa sáng or Giá gồm có bữa sáng.

faqs.question: Is it correct to use “tính cả” to express inclusion?
faqs.answer: Yes, “tính cả” is a natural and informal way to say “including,” especially when adding extra elements: Tính cả tôi thì có 5 người.

modules.title: Certainty & uncertainty in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, you’ll learn how to express certainty and uncertainty in Vietnamese using common words like chắc chắn , có thể , có lẽ , and more. These expressions are essential for sharing opinions, making assumptions, or stating facts with varying degrees of confidence.

faqs.question: What is the difference between chắc chắn and có thể ?
faqs.answer: Chắc chắn expresses certainty (definitely/surely), while có thể indicates possibility (might/may). For example: Tôi chắc chắn anh ấy sẽ đến vs. Anh ấy có thể sẽ đến .

faqs.question: Can có lẽ and có thể be used interchangeably?
faqs.answer: Not always. Both express uncertainty, but có lẽ often implies a stronger guess or assumption based on context, while có thể emphasizes possibility.

faqs.question: How do you politely express uncertainty in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: You can use phrases like tôi nghĩ là… , có lẽ là… , or theo tôi thì… to soften your opinion and avoid sounding too direct.

faqs.question: Is there a word for “probably” in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes, có lẽ and chắc là can both be translated as “probably,” depending on the tone and certainty level intended.

faqs.question: Can I use chắc by itself to express certainty?
faqs.answer: Yes, c hắc is a shortened form of chắc chắn and is commonly used in casual speech. However, it can also mean “probably” depending on intonation and context.

units.title: Surely (chắc chắn)

modules.title: Expressing excessiveness in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, you will learn how to express excessiveness in Vietnamese using phrases like quá mức , thật sự , hơn mong đợi , and rất . These expressions help you describe situations, feelings, or actions that go beyond the usual or expected level.

faqs.question: What is the difference between “quá mức” and “rất”?
faqs.answer: “Quá mức” means “excessively” or “too much,” implying something has gone beyond a reasonable limit, while “rất” simply means “very” and is a neutral intensifier.

faqs.question: Can “thật sự” be used interchangeably with “rất”?
faqs.answer: Not always. “Thật sự” emphasizes truth or sincerity (e.g., “really”), while “rất” emphasizes degree. They serve slightly different functions even if both add emphasis.

faqs.question: When do I use “hơn mong đợi”?
faqs.answer: Use “hơn mong đợi” when something exceeds expectations. It implies a positive or surprising excess, rather than a negative one.

faqs.question: Can I use “quá mức” in both positive and negative contexts?
faqs.answer: It’s generally used in negative contexts to express that something is excessive or overdone, such as “ăn quá mức” (eating too much).

faqs.question: Are these expressions commonly used in daily conversation?
faqs.answer: Yes. While some like “quá mức” are more formal, words like “rất” and “thật sự” are frequently used in everyday Vietnamese.

modules.title: Expressing inaction in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, we’ll learn how to express inaction or negative actions in Vietnamese using common structures like “đừng” (don’t), “chưa” (not yet), and “không bao giờ” (never) . These expressions are essential for forming negative sentences, giving polite commands, or talking about things that haven’t happened.

faqs.question: What is the difference between “đừng” and “không”?
faqs.answer: “Đừng” is used to tell someone not to do something (a command) , while “không” simply states that something does not happen or is not true.

faqs.question: Can I use “chưa” and “không bao giờ” interchangeably?
faqs.answer: No. “Chưa” means “not yet” (suggesting the action may happen later), while “không bao giờ” means “never” , indicating the action will not happen at all .

faqs.question: Is it polite to use “đừng” when speaking to someone older or of higher status?
faqs.answer: “Đừng” can sound direct or even rude if not softened. To be polite, add particles like “nhé” or use a gentler phrase, such as “xin đừng.”

faqs.question: Can “chưa” be used with completed actions?
faqs.answer: No. “Chưa” is used to talk about incomplete or unaccomplished actions , often in the present or past.

faqs.question: How do I form negative commands in Vietnamese using “đừng”?
faqs.answer: Place “đừng” at the beginning of the sentence, followed by the verb: e.g., “Đừng nói chuyện!” = “Don’t talk!”.

units.title: Don't (không)

modules.title: Giving opinion in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, we’ll explore how to use expressions to express your opinion or personal thoughts correctly in Vietnamese. In order to master this lesson, just have a quick look at the Personal Pronouns in Vietnamese lesson here !

faqs.question: Can I use “nghĩ” on its own, or do I need to follow it with a clause?
faqs.answer: You can use “nghĩ” on its own in informal speech, but for clarity, it’s often followed by “rằng” and a full clause to state your opinion more precisely (e.g. Tôi nghĩ rằng điều đó đúng ).

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “nghĩ”, “tin”, and “cho rằng”?
faqs.answer: “Nghĩ” means “to think,” “tin” means “to believe,” and “cho rằng” often implies a stronger or more formal opinion, closer to “to assume” or “to state that.”

faqs.question: Is it polite to use “tôi nghĩ là…” when giving opinions in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes , “tôi nghĩ là…” is a polite and commonly used way to express personal opinions. It’s widely accepted in both formal and informal contexts.

faqs.question: When should I use “chắc chắn rằng” instead of “nghĩ”?
faqs.answer: Use “chắc chắn rằng” when you want to express certainty or strong confidence in your opinion, rather than just a personal thought or guess.

faqs.question: Can I omit “rằng” in spoken Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes , “rằng” is often omitted in casual speech, especially after verbs like nghĩ or biết , but it’s still useful in formal or written Vietnamese to clearly mark the beginning of a subordinate clause.

modules.title: Compliments in Vietnamese
modules.description: In Vietnamese, giving compliments is a subtle yet meaningful way to build relationships and show appreciation. This lesson explores common expressions used to compliment others at work, with friends, or in social situations, while helping you understand the cultural context behind them.

faqs.question: Can I use the same compliments with coworkers and close friends?
faqs.answer: Not always. Compliments at work are usually more formal and focused on achievements, while with friends, they can be casual and personal.

faqs.question: Are compliments commonly given in Vietnamese culture?
faqs.answer: Compliments are appreciated but often expressed more subtly than in Western cultures. Overuse can sometimes feel insincere.

faqs.question: How do I respond to a compliment in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Common responses include “Cảm ơn” (Thank you) or modest replies like “Không có gì đâu” (It’s nothing).

faqs.question: Is it appropriate to compliment someone’s appearance in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes , but it depends on the context and relationship. Keep it respectful, especially with new acquaintances or in formal settings.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between praising someone and flattering them in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Praise (khen) is genuine and appropriate for achievements. Flattery (nịnh) can come across as insincere or manipulative if overdone.

units.title: Compliments at Work
units.explanation: In Vietnam, it’s common to compliment someone’s effort , skills, or work after they finish a task successfully. Here are some compliments for such situations: Tốt lắm! Well done! Xuất sắc! Excellent! Rất giỏi! Very good! Bạn làm tốt lắm! You did well! Cảm ơn bạn, bạn đã làm rất tốt! Thank you, you did really well! Công việc của bạn thật tuyệt vời! Your work is amazing!

modules.title: Expressing emphasis in Vietnamese
modules.description: In Vietnamese, emphasis is used to draw special attention to a word or idea, helping speakers clarify meaning or express strong emotions. This lesson explores common structures like chính , tuyệt đối , and chính xác that add emphasis in both spoken and written language.

faqs.question: What is the most common way to express emphasis in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Words like chính , rất , or tuyệt đối are often used to place strong focus on a noun, verb, or adjective depending on the sentence context.

faqs.question: Can I use both “chính” and “tuyệt đối” in the same sentence?
faqs.answer: Yes, but it depends on the structure. Chính emphasizes identity or exactness, while tuyệt đối intensifies absoluteness. Using both is possible but should be done thoughtfully to avoid redundancy.

faqs.question: Are these emphasis words formal or informal?
faqs.answer: Some are neutral and used in everyday conversation (like rất ), while others like tuyệt đối or chính xác may appear more in formal or written contexts.

faqs.question: What’s the difference between “rất” and “vô cùng”?
faqs.answer: Both mean “very,” but vô cùng is more intense and emotional. It’s often used in expressive speech or writing for dramatic emphasis.

faqs.question: Can emphasis words come at the beginning of a sentence in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Yes, particularly for stylistic or rhetorical purposes. For example, Chính tôi đã làm điều đó (“It was I who did it”) places emphasis at the start.

modules.title: Approval/Disapproval in Vietnamese
modules.description: In this lesson, you’ll learn how to express approval and disapproval in Vietnamese using common phrases and expressions. Mastering these will help you respond naturally in conversations, whether you’re agreeing with a friend or politely disagreeing in a formal setting.

faqs.question: What are the most common ways to express approval in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: Expressions like Tôi đồng ý (I agree), Hay đấy! (That’s great!), and Tốt lắm (Very good) are commonly used to show approval.

faqs.question: How do I politely disagree or disapprove of something in Vietnamese?
faqs.answer: You can use phrases like Tôi không đồng ý (I don’t agree), Tôi không nghĩ vậy (I don’t think so), or Không ổn lắm (Not very good) for polite disapproval.

faqs.question: Can tone or body language affect how approval or disapproval is received?
faqs.answer: Yes . In Vietnamese, tone and facial expression play a big role. Even neutral words can sound harsh or supportive depending on how they’re said.

faqs.question: Are there formal and informal ways to show approval/disapproval?
faqs.answer: Definitely . For example, Tôi đồng ý với anh/chị is more formal, while Chuẩn rồi! (Exactly!) is casual and friendly.

faqs.question: Can these expressions be used in professional settings?
faqs.answer: Yes, but choose formal expressions like Tôi tán thành với ý kiến này (I support this opinion) in business or academic environments for a respectful tone.

levels.label: Upper-Intermediate
levels.description: Advanced connectors, reported speech, emphasis, nuanced conditionals and aspect — the grammar of fluent, organized expression.

modules.title: Contrast & Concession Connectors
modules.description: This module teaches the formal connectors Vietnamese uses to link contrasting and concessive clauses ("although," "however," "on the contrary"). These structures appear in essays, news, and careful speech, where a simpler nhưng would sound too plain.
modules.mainPattern: mặc dù / dù / cho dù + clause, (nhưng) + clause; tuy nhiên / trái lại + sentence

faqs.question: What is the difference between 'nhưng' and 'tuy nhiên'? They both seem to mean 'but'.
faqs.answer: 'Nhưng' is a coordinating conjunction that joins two clauses inside one sentence: 'Trời mưa nhưng chúng tôi vẫn đi.' (It rained but we still went.) 'Tuy nhiên' is a sentence-level adverbial that starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma; it is more formal and signals a contrast with the whole preceding idea: 'Kế hoạch rất tốt. Tuy nhiên, chi phí quá cao.' (The plan is very good. However, the cost is too high.) Use 'nhưng' for tight clause-to-clause contrast and 'tuy nhiên' to open a contrasting sentence in writing.

faqs.question: Do I need 'nhưng' in the second clause after 'mặc dù'?
faqs.answer: It is optional but very common. 'Mặc dù' sets up the concession, and Vietnamese often adds 'nhưng' (or the adverb 'vẫn') to mark the main clause: 'Mặc dù mệt, (nhưng) cô ấy vẫn làm việc.' (Although tired, she still worked.) Including 'nhưng' or 'vẫn' makes the contrast clearer and sounds natural; dropping both is acceptable but feels more clipped.

units.title: mặc dù… (nhưng)… — concessive 'although'
units.explanation: 'Mặc dù' introduces a concession: a fact that you might expect to block the main clause, but doesn't. The main clause typically carries 'nhưng' and/or the adverb 'vẫn' (still) to complete the contrast. 'Mặc dù' is the most formal of the 'although' set and is common in writing.
units.note: 'Mặc dù' attaches to the conceded clause, never the result clause. Don't pair it with a second contrast word at the start of the same clause (no 'mặc dù… tuy nhiên'); the contrast marker goes on the main clause as 'nhưng/vẫn'.

examples.vi: Mặc dù trời mưa rất to, nhưng họ vẫn quyết định lên đường.
examples.en: Although it was raining very hard, they still decided to set off.

examples.vi: Mặc dù đã cố gắng hết sức, anh ấy vẫn không vượt qua kỳ thi.
examples.en: Although he tried his hardest, he still did not pass the exam.

examples.vi: Mặc dù công ty thua lỗ năm ngoái, ban giám đốc vẫn giữ nguyên nhân sự.
examples.en: Although the company made a loss last year, the board kept all the staff.

examples.vi: Mặc dù không có nhiều kinh nghiệm, cô ấy vẫn được nhận vào vị trí đó.
examples.en: Although she didn't have much experience, she was still accepted for that position.

units.title: tuy… nhưng… — clause-internal 'though'
units.explanation: 'Tuy' works like 'mặc dù' but is slightly lighter and pairs almost obligatorily with 'nhưng' in the second clause. It marks the conceded clause and is very frequent in both writing and careful speech. Treat 'tuy… nhưng…' as a fixed correlative pair.
units.note: Don't confuse the subordinator 'tuy' (paired with 'nhưng' inside one sentence) with the sentence adverb 'tuy nhiên', which starts a new sentence. 'Tuy' alone needs a following 'nhưng' clause; 'tuy nhiên' stands at the head of its own sentence.

examples.vi: Tuy nhà xa, nhưng cô ấy chưa bao giờ đi học muộn.
examples.en: Though her house is far away, she has never been late for school.

examples.vi: Tuy còn trẻ, nhưng anh ấy đã rất chín chắn.
examples.en: Though he is still young, he is already very mature.

examples.vi: Tuy giá cao, nhưng sản phẩm này bán rất chạy.
examples.en: Though the price is high, this product sells very well.

examples.vi: Tuy chỉ học trực tuyến, nhưng kết quả của lớp vẫn rất tốt.
examples.en: Though they only studied online, the class's results were still very good.

units.title: dù / cho dù… vẫn… — 'even if / no matter'
units.pattern: dù / cho dù + clause, (thì) + subject + vẫn + verb
units.explanation: 'Dù' and the stronger 'cho dù' express 'even if / even though / no matter', stressing that the outcome holds regardless of the condition. The main clause almost always contains 'vẫn' (still) and often an optional 'thì' bridging the two clauses. This pattern can describe both real facts and hypothetical conditions.
units.note: 'Cho dù' leans hypothetical/emphatic ('even if it were the case'), while plain 'dù' covers both real and hypothetical. With question-word phrases ('dù ai', 'dù thế nào', 'dù bao nhiêu') it means 'no matter who/how/how much' — a key B2 use.

examples.vi: Dù khó khăn đến đâu, chúng tôi vẫn sẽ hoàn thành dự án.
examples.en: No matter how difficult it gets, we will still finish the project.

examples.vi: Cho dù bạn có nói gì, tôi vẫn không thay đổi quyết định.
examples.en: No matter what you say, I still won't change my decision.

examples.vi: Dù ai phản đối thì kế hoạch này vẫn được tiến hành.
examples.en: No matter who objects, this plan will still go ahead.

examples.vi: Cho dù phải làm lại từ đầu, anh ấy vẫn không bỏ cuộc.
examples.en: Even if he had to start over from scratch, he still wouldn't give up.

units.title: tuy nhiên — sentence-opening 'however'
units.explanation: 'Tuy nhiên' is a formal sentence-level adverbial meaning 'however / nevertheless'. It opens a new sentence, is followed by a comma, and contrasts with the entire preceding statement rather than a single clause. It is the standard contrast connector in essays, reports, and news.
units.note: Always start a new sentence (or independent clause after a semicolon) with 'tuy nhiên'; it cannot glue two clauses the way 'nhưng' does. 'Song' is a more literary synonym; 'thế nhưng' is a slightly more conversational equivalent.

examples.vi: Doanh thu năm nay tăng mạnh. Tuy nhiên, lợi nhuận lại giảm.
examples.en: Revenue rose sharply this year. However, profit fell.

examples.vi: Phương pháp này rất hiệu quả. Tuy nhiên, nó đòi hỏi nhiều thời gian.
examples.en: This method is very effective. However, it demands a lot of time.

examples.vi: Đa số đồng ý với đề xuất. Tuy nhiên, vẫn còn một vài ý kiến trái chiều.
examples.en: Most people agreed with the proposal. However, there were still a few dissenting opinions.

examples.vi: Cô ấy đã chuẩn bị rất kỹ. Tuy nhiên, buổi phỏng vấn vẫn không như mong đợi.
examples.en: She had prepared very carefully. However, the interview still did not go as expected.

units.title: trái lại / ngược lại — 'on the contrary'
units.pattern: Sentence 1 (negative/false expectation). Trái lại / Ngược lại, + sentence 2.
units.explanation: 'Trái lại' and 'ngược lại' mean 'on the contrary / conversely'. They introduce a statement that is the opposite of what the previous sentence implied, often after a negation. Unlike 'tuy nhiên' (which adds a qualifying or limiting contrast), these flip the idea to its direct opposite.
units.note: Use these only when the second idea genuinely reverses the first; if you merely add a limiting contrast, use 'tuy nhiên'. 'Ngược lại' can also mean 'vice versa' in comparisons, while 'trái lại' is almost always 'on the contrary'.

examples.vi: Anh ấy không hề tức giận. Trái lại, anh ấy còn cảm ơn tôi.
examples.en: He wasn't angry at all. On the contrary, he even thanked me.

examples.vi: Việc tăng giá không làm giảm doanh số. Ngược lại, khách hàng còn mua nhiều hơn.
examples.en: Raising the price didn't reduce sales. On the contrary, customers bought even more.

examples.vi: Cô ấy không buồn vì thất bại. Trái lại, cô ấy coi đó là một bài học quý giá.
examples.en: She wasn't sad about the failure. On the contrary, she saw it as a valuable lesson.

examples.vi: Công nghệ mới không khiến công việc khó hơn. Ngược lại, nó giúp mọi thứ đơn giản hơn nhiều.
examples.en: The new technology didn't make the work harder. On the contrary, it made everything much simpler.

modules.title: Cause, Result & Consequence
modules.description: This module teaches advanced ways to link a cause to a strong or notable result in Vietnamese — going beyond the basic "vì…nên" of earlier levels. You use these patterns in narration, argument, and formal speech to express that something caused, triggered, or led to a significant consequence.
modules.mainPattern: Vì / Do + [cause], (cho) nên + [result]  •  [cause] + đến nỗi + [extreme result]  •  [cause] + khiến (cho) + [affected party] + [result]  •  [cause] + dẫn đến + [consequence]

faqs.question: What is the difference between 'nên', 'khiến', and 'dẫn đến' — they all seem to mean 'so / causing'?
faqs.answer: They differ in structure and tone. 'Nên' (often 'cho nên') simply links two clauses: cause → result, e.g. 'Trời mưa nên tôi ở nhà' (It rained, so I stayed home). 'Khiến (cho)' takes an object — it says a cause MAKES someone/something do or feel something: 'Tin đó khiến cô ấy bật khóc' (That news made her burst into tears). 'Dẫn đến' is more formal and abstract, used for chains of consequence, usually negative: 'Sự chủ quan dẫn đến thất bại' (Complacency leads to failure). Roughly: nên = neutral logical link, khiến = causes an affected party to react, dẫn đến = results in a (often serious) outcome.

faqs.question: When do I use 'đến nỗi' versus just 'nên'?
faqs.answer: Use 'đến nỗi' only when the result is extreme or surprising — it means 'to the point that'. Compare 'Tôi mệt nên tôi đi ngủ' (I was tired so I went to sleep, neutral) with 'Tôi mệt đến nỗi không đứng nổi' (I was so tired that I couldn't even stand). 'Đến nỗi' always implies the cause reached an intensity that produced a striking consequence, so it sounds odd with mundane results.

units.title: Do / Vì … (cho) nên — formal cause → result
units.explanation: At B2 you refine the basic 'vì…nên'. 'Do' replaces 'vì' in formal, written, or explanatory registers and often introduces an objective or impersonal cause. The full connector 'cho nên' is slightly more emphatic and formal than bare 'nên'. The cause clause comes first; 'nên' / 'cho nên' introduces the consequence. Note the asymmetry: 'vì/do' may be dropped if 'nên' is present, and 'nên' may be dropped if 'vì/do' is present, but in careful writing both are kept.
units.note: Do NOT pair 'nên' (so) with the homophone modal 'nên' (should) in the same breath — context disambiguates, but learners often confuse 'Tôi nên đi' (I should go) with 'Trời mưa nên tôi đi' (It rained so I went).

examples.vi: Do thời tiết xấu, cho nên chuyến bay đã bị hoãn.
examples.en: Due to bad weather, the flight was postponed.

examples.vi: Vì anh ấy chuẩn bị kỹ nên buổi phỏng vấn diễn ra rất suôn sẻ.
examples.en: Because he prepared carefully, the interview went very smoothly.

examples.vi: Do giá nguyên liệu tăng cao nên công ty buộc phải nâng giá sản phẩm.
examples.en: Because raw-material prices rose sharply, the company was forced to raise its product prices.

examples.vi: Cô ấy đến muộn, cho nên chúng tôi phải bắt đầu cuộc họp mà không có cô.
examples.en: She arrived late, so we had to start the meeting without her.

units.title: … đến nỗi — so much that (extreme result)
units.explanation: 'Đến nỗi' (also written 'đến mức') means 'to the point that' and marks a result so strong it is remarkable. It attaches to a verb or adjective describing intensity, then introduces the striking consequence. Unlike 'nên', it inherently signals that a threshold was crossed. The result clause frequently contains 'không … nổi' / 'không … được' (couldn't manage to…) to stress the extreme.
units.note: 'Đến nỗi' carries an evaluative, often negative or dramatic colour. For a plain neutral result, use 'nên' instead — '#Tôi vui đến nỗi đi ngủ' sounds wrong because going to sleep isn't an extreme outcome of joy.

examples.vi: Trời nóng đến nỗi nhựa đường như chảy ra.
examples.en: It was so hot that the asphalt seemed to melt.

examples.vi: Nó cười nhiều đến nỗi đau cả bụng.
examples.en: He laughed so much that his whole stomach hurt.

examples.vi: Bài toán khó đến mức cả lớp không ai giải được.
examples.en: The problem was so hard that no one in the whole class could solve it.

examples.vi: Cô ấy xúc động đến nỗi không nói nên lời.
examples.en: She was so moved that she couldn't get a word out.

units.title: … khiến (cho) … — to cause / make someone (react)
units.explanation: 'Khiến' (optionally 'khiến cho') is a causative verb meaning 'to cause / make'. Crucially it takes an affected party as object, then states what that party does, feels, or becomes. It is the natural way to say that an event provoked a reaction or change in someone or something. More elegant and slightly more formal than the colloquial 'làm cho', and far more common in writing than a bare 'nên' when there is a clear party being affected.
units.note: Don't omit the affected party: 'khiến' needs something to act upon. Say 'Tin đó khiến mọi người lo lắng' (That news made everyone anxious), not '#Tin đó khiến lo lắng'. With no object, use 'nên' or 'dẫn đến' instead.

examples.vi: Lời nói vô tâm của anh đã khiến cô ấy tổn thương sâu sắc.
examples.en: His thoughtless words deeply hurt her.

examples.vi: Đại dịch khiến cho hàng triệu người mất việc làm.
examples.en: The pandemic caused millions of people to lose their jobs.

examples.vi: Thất bại lần này khiến tôi nhận ra nhiều điều.
examples.en: This failure made me realise a great deal.

examples.vi: Tiếng ồn ngoài đường khiến tôi không tài nào tập trung được.
examples.en: The noise from the street made it impossible for me to concentrate.

units.title: … dẫn đến / gây ra — to lead to / bring about (consequence)
units.pattern: [cause / action] + dẫn đến / gây ra + [noun-phrase consequence]
units.explanation: For abstract chains of consequence — especially in formal, academic, or news writing — Vietnamese uses 'dẫn đến' (lead to) and 'gây ra' (cause / give rise to). Both take a NOUN PHRASE as the consequence, not a full clause: you say 'dẫn đến thất bại' (lead to failure), not a finite clause. 'Dẫn đến' frames the outcome as the end of a causal chain; 'gây ra' frames the cause as actively producing a (usually harmful) result such as damage, accidents, or conflict.
units.note: Both require a nominalised consequence. To attach a full clause, switch to 'khiến' or 'nên': 'gây ra tai nạn' (cause an accident) but '#gây ra xe đâm nhau' is wrong — say 'khiến hai xe đâm nhau' instead.

examples.vi: Việc khai thác rừng bừa bãi dẫn đến lũ lụt nghiêm trọng.
examples.en: Reckless deforestation leads to severe flooding.

examples.vi: Sự bất cẩn của tài xế đã gây ra một vụ tai nạn thảm khốc.
examples.en: The driver's carelessness caused a horrific accident.

examples.vi: Áp lực công việc kéo dài có thể dẫn đến trầm cảm.
examples.en: Prolonged work pressure can lead to depression.

examples.vi: Quyết định vội vàng đó đã gây ra nhiều hậu quả khôn lường.
examples.en: That hasty decision brought about many unforeseeable consequences.

modules.title: Purpose Clauses
modules.description: This module teaches how to express purpose in Vietnamese ("in order to / so that") and the negative-purpose construction "lest / so as to avoid." It covers the everyday connector để alongside the more formal nhằm and emphatic cốt để, and contrasts them with kẻo, which warns against an unwanted outcome.
modules.mainPattern: clause₁ + để / nhằm / cốt để + purpose-clause  |  clause₁ + kẻo + (unwanted) outcome

faqs.question: What is the difference between để and kẻo? They both seem to link to a result.
faqs.answer: để introduces the positive purpose you are aiming AT — the thing you want to happen: 'Tôi học chăm để đậu kỳ thi.' (I study hard in order to pass the exam.) kẻo introduces a negative outcome you want to AVOID, and the main clause is usually advice or a warning: 'Mặc áo ấm vào kẻo bị cảm.' (Put on a warm jacket, or else you'll catch a cold.) A quick test: if you can rephrase it as 'so as not to / otherwise...', use kẻo, not để.

faqs.question: When should I use nhằm instead of để?
faqs.answer: nhằm is the formal, written-register equivalent of để and is common in news, official documents, and business Vietnamese. Compare conversational 'Họ giảm giá để bán hết hàng.' with the more formal 'Công ty giảm giá nhằm thúc đẩy doanh số.' (The company cut prices in order to boost sales.) In speech, để is almost always the natural choice; reserve nhằm for serious or institutional contexts.

units.title: để — stating the purpose
units.explanation: để is the default connector for purpose, equivalent to 'in order to / so that / to'. The clause after để states the goal of the action in the main clause. The subject of the purpose clause is usually the same as the main clause and is normally dropped. Note that để also means 'to let/allow' and 'to put/leave'; here it functions purely as a purpose connector.
units.note: Don't confuse purpose để with the standalone verb để ('to put/place') or with để cho meaning 'so that (someone else) can'. When the purpose has a DIFFERENT subject, you generally need để cho: 'Tôi nói nhỏ để cho con ngủ.' (I speak quietly so that the child can sleep.)

examples.vi: Cô ấy dậy sớm để kịp chuyến tàu đầu tiên.
examples.en: She gets up early in order to catch the first train.

examples.vi: Chúng tôi họp trước để thống nhất quan điểm.
examples.en: We meet beforehand so as to align our views.

examples.vi: Anh ghi lại số điện thoại để khỏi quên.
examples.en: Write down the phone number so you don't forget it.

examples.vi: Họ tiết kiệm tiền để mua một căn nhà nhỏ.
examples.en: They save money in order to buy a small house.

units.title: nhằm — formal purpose (written register)
units.explanation: nhằm expresses purpose in formal, written, or institutional Vietnamese — newspapers, reports, policy, and business communication. It is interchangeable in meaning with để but raises the register noticeably. It frequently appears as nhằm mục đích ('with the aim of') before a noun or nominalised phrase.
units.note: nhằm sounds stiff or bureaucratic in casual conversation; among friends, switch back to để. Also distinguish it from the verb nhằm/nhắm ('to aim at, to target'), which takes a direct object rather than a clause.

examples.vi: Chính phủ ban hành quy định mới nhằm bảo vệ người tiêu dùng.
examples.en: The government issued new regulations in order to protect consumers.

examples.vi: Hội thảo được tổ chức nhằm nâng cao nhận thức về môi trường.
examples.en: The seminar was held with the aim of raising environmental awareness.

examples.vi: Công ty cắt giảm chi phí nhằm mục đích tăng lợi nhuận.
examples.en: The company cut costs with the aim of increasing profits.

examples.vi: Các biện pháp này nhằm hạn chế tình trạng ùn tắc giao thông.
examples.en: These measures are intended to reduce traffic congestion.

units.title: cốt để / cốt là để — emphasising the sole purpose
units.explanation: cốt để (or cốt là để) emphasises that the purpose is the ONE essential, real reason behind an action — 'purely in order to / with the sole aim of'. cốt by itself means 'the essential thing / the core', so the phrase frames everything else as secondary. It often carries a slightly evaluative tone, sometimes implying the action is done only for that reason.
units.note: cốt để is emphatic and a bit colloquial-literary; it is not a neutral substitute for để. Using it suggests 'the whole point is just to...', which can sound dismissive if the purpose is trivial.

examples.vi: Anh ấy nói vậy cốt để làm vừa lòng mọi người.
examples.en: He said that purely to please everyone.

examples.vi: Tôi đến đây cốt là để gặp anh một lần.
examples.en: I came here with the sole purpose of seeing you just once.

examples.vi: Nó học thuộc lòng cốt để qua môn chứ chẳng hiểu gì.
examples.en: He memorises it only to pass the course, without understanding anything.

examples.vi: Bà cụ dành dụm cả đời cốt để lo cho các cháu.
examples.en: The old lady saved her whole life with the single aim of providing for her grandchildren.

units.title: kẻo — negative purpose (avoiding an outcome)
units.explanation: kẻo introduces the bad outcome you act to AVOID — 'lest / or else / otherwise'. The main clause is typically a piece of advice, a suggestion, or a gentle command, and kẻo links it to the consequence that would follow if the advice were ignored. It is the negative counterpart of để: instead of aiming at a goal, you act so as not to let something happen.
units.note: Unlike để, kẻo is NOT followed by your goal but by the thing you're warning against, so it is almost always paired with an undesirable verb (bị cảm, muộn, hỏng, ngã). It belongs to spoken and friendly register; in formal writing prefer để tránh ('in order to avoid') + noun.

examples.vi: Đi nhanh lên kẻo trễ giờ làm.
examples.en: Hurry up, or else you'll be late for work.

examples.vi: Cất tiền cẩn thận kẻo mất.
examples.en: Put your money away carefully, lest you lose it.

examples.vi: Ăn ít đồ ngọt thôi kẻo sâu răng.
examples.en: Eat fewer sweets, otherwise you'll get cavities.

examples.vi: Nhớ tưới cây mỗi ngày kẻo nó héo.
examples.en: Remember to water the plant every day, or else it'll wither.

units.title: để tránh / để khỏi — avoiding an outcome with để
units.pattern: clause₁ + để tránh + noun  /  để khỏi + verb
units.explanation: When you want the 'so as not to' meaning but in neutral or formal register, use để tránh ('in order to avoid') before a noun/nominalised phrase, or để khỏi ('so as not to / to keep from') before a verb. These are the register-flexible alternatives to kẻo: the same avoidance logic, but they slot into the để frame and work in writing as well as speech.
units.note: để tránh wants a noun phrase after it (để tránh hiểu lầm), while để khỏi wants a verb (để khỏi hiểu lầm). Mixing them up is a common mistake. Unlike kẻo, the main clause here need not be advice — it can be a plain statement of fact.

examples.vi: Cô ấy nói rõ từng chi tiết để tránh hiểu lầm.
examples.en: She spelled out every detail in order to avoid misunderstandings.

examples.vi: Chúng tôi đặt vé sớm để khỏi hết chỗ.
examples.en: We booked tickets early so as not to miss out on seats.

examples.vi: Nhà máy lắp hệ thống lọc để tránh ô nhiễm nguồn nước.
examples.en: The factory installed a filtration system to avoid water pollution.

examples.vi: Anh nên sao lưu dữ liệu để khỏi mất khi máy hỏng.
examples.en: You should back up your data so as not to lose it if the computer breaks.

modules.title: Relative Clauses with mà
modules.description: This module teaches how to attach a full clause to a noun using mà, forming relative clauses like "the person who...", "the thing that...", or "the book I bought." It covers when mà is used, when it is dropped, and how to relativize subjects, objects, and prepositional/possessive relationships in natural Vietnamese.

faqs.question: When do I use mà, and when do I drop it?
faqs.answer: When the head noun is the SUBJECT of the relative clause, Vietnamese normally DROPS mà and attaches the verb directly: 'người giúp tôi' (the person who helped me), not 'người mà giúp tôi' (which sounds wrong). mà is used — and is the natural choice — when the clause has its OWN subject and the head noun is the OBJECT or another role, e.g. 'cuốn sách (mà) tôi mua' (the book that I bought). Here tôi is the subject and the head noun is the object, so mà marks the boundary and prevents misreading. Even in object relatives mà can sometimes be dropped in casual speech ('cuốn sách tôi mua'), but keeping it is always safe and clear.

faqs.question: Is 'cái mà' the same as English 'the thing that' / 'what'?
faqs.answer: Often yes. 'cái mà' nominalizes a clause into 'the thing that...': 'Cái mà tôi cần là thời gian' = 'What I need is time.' Note 'cái' here is the generic noun 'thing/one'; you can also use a more specific noun — 'điều mà', 'thứ mà', 'người mà'. 'điều mà' tends to be used for abstract matters/ideas, while 'cái mà' and 'thứ mà' lean toward concrete things.

units.title: Subject relative clauses: Noun + clause (no mà)
units.explanation: When the head noun is the subject of the embedded clause (the one doing the action), Vietnamese attaches the clause directly to the noun WITHOUT mà. The clause describes who or what the noun is by what it does. The natural form is 'người giúp tôi' (the person who helped me); inserting mà before the verb ('người mà giúp tôi') sounds wrong to native speakers and should be avoided.
units.note: A bare subject relative can look identical to a verb simply following the noun, but context and word order make the meaning clear. Do not add mà here to 'disambiguate' — native speakers leave it out in subject relatives.

examples.vi: Người giúp tôi hôm qua là bác sĩ.
examples.en: The person who helped me yesterday is a doctor.

examples.vi: Tôi thích những bài hát nói về tuổi trẻ.
examples.en: I like the songs that talk about youth.

examples.vi: Đó là con chó hay sủa vào ban đêm.
examples.en: That is the dog that often barks at night.

examples.vi: Cô gái ngồi cạnh tôi là người Huế.
examples.en: The girl who sits next to me is from Huế.

units.title: Object relative clauses: Noun (mà) + Subject + Verb
units.explanation: When the head noun is the OBJECT of the embedded verb, the clause has its own subject before the verb, and the object 'gap' is the head noun itself. This is the most common and most natural use of mà. Here mà clearly marks where the main noun ends and the modifying clause begins, so it is the preferred choice (though it can be dropped in casual speech).
units.note: Do not repeat the object inside the clause with a pronoun — say 'cuốn sách mà tôi mua' (the book that I bought), NOT 'cuốn sách mà tôi mua nó'. The head noun already fills the object slot.

examples.vi: Cuốn sách mà tôi mua hôm qua rất hay.
examples.en: The book that I bought yesterday is very good.

examples.vi: Người mà chúng ta gặp ở quán cà phê là sếp của tôi.
examples.en: The person whom we met at the café is my boss.

examples.vi: Món ăn mà mẹ tôi nấu ngon nhất là phở.
examples.en: The dish that my mother cooks best is phở.

examples.vi: Ngôi nhà mà họ vừa bán nằm gần biển.
examples.en: The house that they just sold is near the sea.

units.title: cái mà / điều mà: nominalizing a clause into 'what / the thing that'
units.explanation: By using a generic noun (cái, điều, thứ, người) plus mà, you turn a whole clause into a noun phrase meaning 'the thing/one that...' — close to English 'what'. This is very useful for cleft-like emphasis: 'Cái mà tôi cần là...' (What I need is...). Use điều for abstract matters/ideas, cái or thứ for concrete things, người for people.
units.note: Choose the generic noun to match the meaning: 'điều mà anh nói' (the thing/point that you said — abstract) sounds better than 'cái mà anh nói' when referring to a statement or idea.

examples.vi: Cái mà tôi cần nhất bây giờ là thời gian.
examples.en: What I need most right now is time.

examples.vi: Điều mà tôi lo lắng là sức khỏe của bố.
examples.en: The thing I worry about is my father's health.

examples.vi: Thứ mà anh ấy quan tâm chỉ là tiền.
examples.en: The only thing he cares about is money.

examples.vi: Người mà cô ấy yêu đã chuyển đi xa rồi.
examples.en: The person whom she loves has already moved far away.

units.title: Relativizing oblique roles: place, time, and possession with mà
units.pattern: Noun + mà + Subject + Verb + (ở/vào đó · của ...)
units.explanation: mà can also relativize nouns that play a place, time, or possessor role in the clause. For place and time you may keep a resumptive 'đó/ấy' or a locative, e.g. 'nơi mà ... ở đó'; in everyday speech the resumptive is frequently dropped and sounds lighter. For possession, the relationship is shown with 'của' inside the clause.
units.note: For pure location/time, native speakers often prefer 'nơi', 'chỗ', 'lúc', 'khi' as the head noun and drop the resumptive: 'nơi tôi lớn lên' is lighter than 'thành phố mà tôi lớn lên ở đó'. Reserve heavier 'mà ... ở đó' relatives for when you genuinely need to spell out the location.

examples.vi: Thành phố mà tôi lớn lên bây giờ đã thay đổi nhiều.
examples.en: The city where I grew up has changed a lot now.

examples.vi: Cái ngày mà chúng tôi gặp nhau lần đầu, trời mưa rất to.
examples.en: The day (when) we first met, it rained very hard.

examples.vi: Người đàn ông mà con trai của ông ấy học cùng lớp với tôi vừa qua đời.
examples.en: The man whose son studies in the same class as me just passed away.

examples.vi: Quán ăn mà chúng ta đã ăn tối ở đó đã đóng cửa.
examples.en: The restaurant where we had dinner has closed down.

modules.title: Reported speech & indirect questions
modules.description: This module teaches how to embed someone's words, thoughts, or questions inside a larger sentence in Vietnamese — reporting statements with nói rằng / bảo là and reporting questions with hỏi xem / hỏi liệu and the không biết…có…không frame. Use it when relaying what others said, asking embedded (indirect) questions, or softening a direct question into a polite or uncertain one.

faqs.question: Does Vietnamese change the tense or pronouns when reporting speech, like English does ("I am" → "he was")?
faqs.answer: No tense backshift — Vietnamese verbs do not conjugate, so the embedded verb stays the same: time is shown by markers like đã, đang, sẽ if needed, not by changing the verb. What you DO change is the pronouns/perspective. Direct: Anh ấy nói: "Tôi sẽ đến." (He said: "I will come.") Reported: Anh ấy nói rằng anh ấy sẽ đến. (He said that he would come.) Notice "tôi" becomes "anh ấy" to match the reporter's viewpoint, but "sẽ" stays exactly the same.

faqs.question: What is the difference between rằng and là after nói/bảo?
faqs.answer: Both introduce a reported clause and both translate as "that." Rằng is slightly more formal/literary; là is more colloquial and far more common in speech. You can also drop both entirely: Cô ấy nói (rằng/là) cô ấy bận. = Cô ấy nói cô ấy bận. (She said she was busy.) For reported questions, however, you cannot use rằng/là — you must switch to xem or liệu: Tôi hỏi xem cô ấy có bận không. (I asked whether she was busy.)

units.title: Reporting statements: nói rằng / nói là
units.explanation: To report a statement, use a speech verb (nói = say, bảo = tell/say, cho biết = state/inform) followed optionally by rằng (more formal) or là (colloquial), then the reported clause. There is no tense backshift; instead you adjust pronouns to the reporter's point of view. Rằng/là can be omitted entirely in casual speech.
units.note: bảo carries a nuance of telling/instructing someone and is very common in speech, but it can sound informal or even slightly bossy in writing; prefer nói or cho biết in formal/written contexts.

examples.vi: Cô ấy nói rằng cô ấy sẽ nghỉ việc vào cuối tháng.
examples.en: She said that she would quit her job at the end of the month.

examples.vi: Mẹ tôi bảo là trời sắp mưa nên đừng đi xa.
examples.en: My mom said it was about to rain, so I shouldn't go far.

examples.vi: Giám đốc cho biết công ty sẽ tuyển thêm người vào năm sau.
examples.en: The director stated that the company would hire more people next year.

examples.vi: Anh ấy nói anh ấy không hề biết chuyện đó.
examples.en: He said he had no idea about that (no rằng/là, dropped).

units.title: Reported yes/no questions: hỏi xem … có … không
units.pattern: S + hỏi (xem) + [clause] + có … không / đã … chưa
units.explanation: To report a yes/no question, use hỏi (ask) followed by xem (whether) and keep the original question frame có…không (for general yes/no) or đã…chưa (for "yet"). Unlike English, the word order does not invert and there is no "if/whether" conjunction beyond xem. Xem can be dropped, but keeping it makes the embedded-question reading clearer.
units.note: Don't use rằng or là to report a question — that's a frequent error. Rằng/là are only for statements; questions take xem or liệu.

examples.vi: Cô ấy hỏi xem tôi có rảnh vào cuối tuần không.
examples.en: She asked whether I was free on the weekend.

examples.vi: Tôi hỏi xem họ đã ăn tối chưa.
examples.en: I asked whether they had had dinner yet.

examples.vi: Sếp hỏi xem dự án có kịp tiến độ không.
examples.en: The boss asked whether the project was on schedule.

examples.vi: Anh ấy hỏi tôi có muốn đi cùng không.
examples.en: He asked whether I wanted to come along (xem dropped).

units.title: Reported wh-questions: hỏi + question word
units.pattern: S + hỏi (xem) + [clause with ai/gì/đâu/khi nào/tại sao/thế nào]
units.explanation: To report an information (wh-) question, use hỏi followed by the same question word the original speaker used — ai (who), gì (what), ở đâu (where), khi nào / bao giờ (when), tại sao / vì sao (why), thế nào / như thế nào (how). The question word stays in its normal in-situ position; there is no fronting or inversion as in English.
units.note: The position of khi nào/bao giờ signals time reference: before the verb it points to the future, after the verb it points to the past — this carries over into the embedded clause, so place it carefully.

examples.vi: Cô ấy hỏi tôi đang làm gì.
examples.en: She asked what I was doing.

examples.vi: Họ hỏi xem cuộc họp sẽ diễn ra ở đâu.
