examples.en: They asked where the meeting would take place.

examples.vi: Tôi hỏi anh ấy tại sao lại đổi ý vào phút chót.
examples.en: I asked him why he had changed his mind at the last minute.

examples.vi: Khách hàng hỏi khi nào hàng mới về.
examples.en: The customer asked when the new stock would arrive.

units.title: Embedding uncertainty: không biết … có … không
units.explanation: The frame không biết ("[I] don't know / I wonder") embeds a question as an expression of the speaker's own uncertainty rather than reporting someone else's question. Pair it with có…không for yes/no wondering, or with a wh-word for open wondering. It works both as a genuine statement of not-knowing and as a soft, indirect way to raise a question or make a polite request.
units.note: As a softener, không biết … có thể … không is a polite request formula: Không biết anh có thể giúp tôi một chút không? = "I wonder if you could help me a little?" — much gentler than a bare Anh giúp tôi được không?

examples.vi: Tôi không biết cô ấy có nhận được tin nhắn của tôi không.
examples.en: I don't know / I wonder whether she got my message.

examples.vi: Không biết ngày mai trời có mưa không nhỉ.
examples.en: I wonder whether it'll rain tomorrow.

examples.vi: Tôi không biết phải bắt đầu từ đâu.
examples.en: I don't know where I should start.

examples.vi: Không biết anh có thể nói rõ hơn một chút không ạ?
examples.en: I wonder if you could explain it a bit more clearly? (polite request)

units.title: Formal/written embedding: hỏi liệu … (có) … (hay) không
units.pattern: S + hỏi/băn khoăn/tự hỏi + liệu + [clause] + (có) … (hay) không
units.explanation: Liệu is a more formal, often written, marker for embedding a yes/no question expressing deliberation or doubt. It pairs naturally with verbs of wondering (tự hỏi = wonder to oneself, băn khoăn = be unsure) and with hỏi. The closing can be …có…không or the more literary …hay không. Liệu adds a reflective, weighing-the-possibilities tone that plain xem lacks.
units.note: Liệu sounds bookish in everyday chat — in casual speech native speakers default to hỏi xem … có … không. Reserve liệu for writing, formal speech, or deliberate, contemplative statements.

examples.vi: Tôi tự hỏi liệu quyết định của mình có đúng hay không.
examples.en: I wondered whether my decision was right or not.

examples.vi: Nhiều người băn khoăn liệu nền kinh tế có phục hồi trong năm nay không.
examples.en: Many people wonder whether the economy will recover this year.

examples.vi: Họ hỏi liệu công ty có sẵn sàng đàm phán lại hợp đồng hay không.
examples.en: They asked whether the company was willing to renegotiate the contract.

examples.vi: Cô ấy đắn đo liệu có nên nói ra sự thật hay không.
examples.en: She agonized over whether she should tell the truth or not.

modules.title: Emphasis & Cleft Sentences
modules.description: This module teaches how to single out and highlight one element of a sentence in Vietnamese using focusing constructions built on chính, chỉ có…mới, and là. These structures let you stress "exactly this one / it is precisely X that…" in a way that plain word order cannot, and they are common in argument, correction, and emphatic spoken and written Vietnamese.
modules.mainPattern: chính + (noun/pronoun) + (là) + …  /  chỉ có + X + mới + verb phrase

faqs.question: What is the difference between using chính and just stressing the word with my voice?
faqs.answer: In speech you can stress almost any word, but chính grammatically marks that element as the unique, exact focus and rules out alternatives. 'Anh ấy làm việc này' just states who did it; 'Chính anh ấy đã làm việc này' (It was he who did this / He himself did it) insists it was that person and nobody else. chính is also stable in writing, where vocal stress is invisible, so it is the reliable way to encode emphasis.

faqs.question: When do I use chỉ có…mới versus just chỉ?
faqs.answer: Plain chỉ means 'only' and simply limits quantity or scope: 'Tôi chỉ có hai cuốn sách' (I only have two books). The frame chỉ có…mới is a cleft of exclusivity meaning 'only X (and no one/nothing else) is able to / does…', and the mới is obligatory before the verb: 'Chỉ có anh ấy mới hiểu được vấn đề này' (Only he can understand this problem). Dropping mới makes it sound incomplete or merely quantitative.

units.title: chính + noun/pronoun: 'the very / precisely this one'
units.explanation: Placing chính directly before a noun or pronoun marks it as the exact, identical referent — 'the very (one)', 'precisely', '…itself/himself'. It tightens identification and excludes any other candidate. The marked phrase can be the subject ('Chính anh ấy…' = He himself…) or an object/complement ('…tại chính nơi này' = at this very place).
units.note: Do not confuse this chính ('exact, the very') with the adjective chính meaning 'main/primary' (as in cửa chính 'main door'). As a focus marker, chính comes before the noun; as 'main', it comes after.

examples.vi: Chính anh ấy đã giúp tôi vượt qua giai đoạn khó khăn nhất.
examples.en: It was he himself who helped me through the hardest period.

examples.vi: Tôi gặp lại cô ấy tại chính nơi chúng tôi đã chia tay.
examples.en: I met her again at the very place where we had broken up.

examples.vi: Chính sự im lặng của anh đã khiến mọi chuyện trở nên tồi tệ hơn.
examples.en: It was precisely your silence that made everything worse.

units.title: chính là: 'is exactly / is none other than'
units.explanation: chính là is an emphatic equative 'to be', stronger than plain là. It identifies the predicate as the one exact answer — 'is exactly / is precisely / is none other than'. It is the natural way to deliver a reveal, a conclusion, or a firm definition, often answering 'who/what exactly is it?'.
units.note: chính là links to a noun phrase, not directly to a bare verb. To emphasise an action, recast it as a noun ('Điều tôi cần chính là sự trung thực' — What I need is exactly honesty), rather than putting chính là before a verb.

examples.vi: Người đứng sau dự án này chính là giám đốc cũ của chúng ta.
examples.en: The person behind this project is none other than our former director.

examples.vi: Điều quan trọng nhất chính là sức khỏe của bạn.
examples.en: The most important thing is precisely your health.

examples.vi: Đó chính là lý do tại sao tôi không đồng ý.
examples.en: That is exactly the reason why I do not agree.

units.title: chỉ có + X + mới: exclusive cleft 'only X (and no one else) can'
units.explanation: This frame singles out X as the sole entity for which the predicate holds — 'only X, and nobody/nothing else, does/can…'. The mới before the verb phrase is obligatory and carries the sense of 'it takes X (for it) to…'. X is typically the subject but can be a condition or time. An optional thôi at the end reinforces the exclusivity.
units.note: Omitting mới breaks the construction: 'Chỉ có anh ấy hiểu' sounds truncated. Keep chỉ có…mới as a fixed frame whenever you mean exclusive capability or the unique condition for something.

examples.vi: Chỉ có anh ấy mới hiểu được vấn đề phức tạp này.
examples.en: Only he can really understand this complicated problem.

examples.vi: Chỉ có nỗ lực thật sự mới mang lại kết quả.
examples.en: Only genuine effort brings results.

examples.vi: Chỉ có lúc đó tôi mới nhận ra mình đã sai.
examples.en: Only then did I realise I had been wrong.

units.title: là cleft: fronting the focused element with là
units.pattern: (Fronted element) + là + (rest of clause) / Sở dĩ … là vì …
units.explanation: Vietnamese forms English-style 'it is X that…' clefts by fronting the focused phrase and joining it with là. A very common reasoning variant is the frame sở dĩ + clause + là (do/vì) + cause, literally 'the reason that… is because…', which clefts the cause for emphasis. This is more formal and argumentative than ordinary word order.
units.note: In the sở dĩ…là vì… frame, both halves are needed: sở dĩ introduces the result and là vì introduces the cause. Using sở dĩ without the là vì half sounds unfinished.

examples.vi: Sở dĩ tôi đến muộn là vì xe của tôi bị hỏng giữa đường.
examples.en: The reason I came late is that my car broke down on the way.

examples.vi: Người tôi tin tưởng nhất là cô ấy, chứ không phải anh ta.
examples.en: The person I trust most is her, not him.

examples.vi: Cái mà chúng ta cần bây giờ là một kế hoạch rõ ràng.
examples.en: What we need now is a clear plan.

units.title: chính … chứ không phải …: emphatic contrast
units.pattern: chính + X + … chứ không phải + Y
units.explanation: Combining a chính-focus with chứ không phải ('and not / rather than') makes an explicit corrective contrast: it asserts X as the true focus while denying the wrong alternative Y. This is the standard way to correct a mistaken assumption emphatically ('It was X, not Y').
units.note: chứ không phải negates a noun phrase or whole alternative; to deny a plain verb use chứ không (without phải): 'Tôi đến để giúp chứ không phải để phán xét' vs. 'Tôi đến để giúp chứ không phán xét.'

examples.vi: Chính bạn mới là người quyết định, chứ không phải tôi.
examples.en: It is you who decides, not me.

examples.vi: Chính cách làm mới là vấn đề, chứ không phải con người.
examples.en: It is the method that is the problem, not the people.

examples.vi: Chính anh ấy là người gây ra chuyện này, chứ không phải tôi.
examples.en: It was he who caused this, not me.

modules.title: Conditional Nuance
modules.description: This module teaches the family of Vietnamese conditional connectors that go beyond basic nếu…thì — covering habitual/automatic conditions, counterfactual regret, minimum requirements, and exceptions. Use these to express precise shades of condition, hypothesis, and stipulation in natural spoken and written Vietnamese.
modules.mainPattern: hễ + clause + (là/thì) + clause; giá (như) + clause + (thì) + clause

faqs.question: What's the difference between nếu and hễ? They both seem to mean 'if'.
faqs.answer: nếu marks a single, possible (often one-off) condition: 'if it happens'. hễ marks a habitual, automatic, repeated condition closer to English 'whenever / every time': the result follows reliably each time. Compare 'Nếu trời mưa thì tôi ở nhà' (If it rains [this once], I'll stay home) with 'Hễ trời mưa là tôi ở nhà' (Whenever it rains, I stay home). hễ very commonly pairs with là rather than thì, and implies a near-certain, almost reflexive consequence.

faqs.question: How do I say 'if only…' to express regret about something that didn't happen?
faqs.answer: Use giá (như) or giá mà for counterfactual / unreal conditions, especially regrets about the past: 'Giá như tôi nghe lời anh thì đã không sao' (If only I'd listened to you, nothing would have gone wrong). The clue that it's counterfactual is often a following đã and a wistful tone. This is different from nếu, which leaves the condition open and realistic rather than contrary to fact.

units.title: hễ…là/thì — habitual, automatic condition
units.explanation: hễ introduces a condition that recurs and triggers its result automatically and reliably, like English 'whenever' or 'every time… without fail'. It is most natural with repeated, habitual situations, and the second clause is very often introduced by là (rather than thì), stressing the immediacy of the consequence.
units.note: Don't use hễ for a single hypothetical future event — that's nếu. hễ implies repetition or a law-like pattern, so 'hễ ngày mai trời mưa' sounds wrong; use 'nếu ngày mai trời mưa'.

examples.vi: Hễ rảnh là tôi lại đọc sách.
examples.en: Whenever I'm free, I read a book.

examples.vi: Hễ trời trở lạnh là bà tôi lại đau lưng.
examples.en: Every time it turns cold, my grandmother's back aches.

examples.vi: Hễ nó mở miệng thì ai cũng cười.
examples.en: Whenever he opens his mouth, everyone laughs.

examples.vi: Hễ uống cà phê buổi tối là tôi mất ngủ.
examples.en: Whenever I drink coffee at night, I can't sleep.

units.title: giá (như)…thì — counterfactual 'if only'
units.explanation: giá, giá như, and giá mà express an unreal or counterfactual condition — a wish or regret about something contrary to fact, equivalent to English 'if only…' or 'had I…'. It frequently refers to the past, in which case the result clause often takes đã to mark the unrealized outcome.
units.note: The tone is wistful or regretful, not neutral. Using nếu here would lose the 'contrary to fact' meaning and just sound like an open, realistic condition.

examples.vi: Giá như tôi nghe lời mẹ thì đã không ra nông nỗi này.
examples.en: If only I'd listened to my mother, things wouldn't have come to this.

examples.vi: Giá mà hồi đó tôi chăm học hơn.
examples.en: If only I'd studied harder back then.

examples.vi: Giá như trời đừng mưa thì chuyến đi đã vui hơn.
examples.en: If only it hadn't rained, the trip would have been more fun.

examples.vi: Giá mà em ở đây lúc này.
examples.en: If only you were here right now.

units.title: miễn là — 'as long as / provided that' (sole condition)
units.pattern: clause + miễn là + condition; or miễn (là) + condition + (thì) + clause
units.explanation: miễn là sets out a single sufficient condition under which the main statement holds — English 'as long as', 'so long as', or 'provided that'. The speaker signals that nothing else matters; meeting this one requirement is enough. The shorter form miễn (without là) is common in speech.
units.note: miễn là states a minimum requirement that licenses the result; it is not interchangeable with chỉ cần ('all you need is'), though they overlap. Avoid confusing it with the verb miễn ('to exempt'), as in miễn phí ('free of charge').

examples.vi: Đi đâu cũng được, miễn là có em đi cùng.
examples.en: Anywhere is fine, as long as you come with me.

examples.vi: Tôi sẽ giúp cậu, miễn là cậu thành thật.
examples.en: I'll help you, provided that you're honest.

examples.vi: Miễn là con khỏe mạnh, bố mẹ không đòi hỏi gì hơn.
examples.en: As long as you're healthy, your parents ask for nothing more.

examples.vi: Ăn gì cũng được, miễn là rẻ.
examples.en: Any food's fine, as long as it's cheap.

units.title: trừ khi — 'unless' (the only exception)
units.pattern: clause + trừ khi + exception; or trừ khi + exception + (thì) + clause
units.explanation: trừ khi means 'unless' — it carves out the single exception that would cancel the main statement. The default holds in all cases except the one named after trừ khi.
units.note: trừ khi negates the exception, so the main clause stays affirmative: 'Tôi sẽ đi, trừ khi trời mưa' = 'I'll go unless it rains' (i.e. I'll go in every case except rain). Don't add a second negation in the main clause expecting English 'unless… not'.

examples.vi: Tôi sẽ đến đúng giờ, trừ khi xe hỏng.
examples.en: I'll arrive on time, unless the car breaks down.

examples.vi: Trừ khi có việc gấp, đừng gọi tôi sau mười giờ.
examples.en: Unless it's urgent, don't call me after ten.

examples.vi: Nó không bao giờ nghỉ học, trừ khi ốm nặng.
examples.en: He never skips class unless he's seriously ill.

examples.vi: Chúng ta sẽ thắng, trừ khi đối thủ chơi xấu.
examples.en: We'll win, unless the opponents play dirty.

units.title: cứ…là — 'every time / as soon as' (reflexive trigger)
units.explanation: The cứ…là pattern expresses that one event invariably and immediately triggers another — 'every time X, then Y' or 'the moment X, Y'. It overlaps with hễ…là but adds a sense of inevitability or stubborn regularity, often with a slightly exasperated or matter-of-fact tone.
units.note: Here cứ is not the imperative cứ ('go ahead, just…'); it is the conditional-frequency cứ that must be completed by là. Leaving out là breaks the pattern.

examples.vi: Cứ đến cuối tháng là tôi lại hết tiền.
examples.en: Every time the end of the month comes, I run out of money again.

examples.vi: Cứ nhắc đến chuyện đó là nó im lặng.
examples.en: The moment you bring that up, he goes quiet.

examples.vi: Cứ ăn đồ cay là bụng tôi khó chịu.
examples.en: Every time I eat spicy food, my stomach acts up.

examples.vi: Cứ mưa to là khu này lại ngập.
examples.en: Whenever it rains hard, this area floods again.

modules.title: Aspect & Phases of an Action
modules.description: This module teaches the fine-grained aspect markers Vietnamese uses to pinpoint where an action sits in time: experience in the past, ongoing continuation, imminence, and very recent completion. Use it to express nuances that plain past/present/future markers (đã, đang, sẽ) cannot, such as "have ever done", "still", "about to", and "just finished".
modules.mainPattern: đã từng / vẫn còn / sắp (sửa) / vừa mới / mới + V (...) + xong

faqs.question: What is the difference between đã and đã từng? Aren't they both just 'past tense'?
faqs.answer: đã simply marks that an action happened (completed past): 'Tôi đã ăn rồi' = 'I already ate.' đã từng adds an experiential nuance — 'to have ever / once done' something, often something now finished or no longer true: 'Tôi đã từng sống ở Hà Nội' = 'I once lived in Hanoi (but not anymore).' Use từng for life experiences and past states that contrast with the present, not for a single recent event. Note the negative: 'chưa từng' = 'have never (yet)', e.g. 'Tôi chưa từng ăn sầu riêng' = 'I've never eaten durian.'

faqs.question: vừa, mới, and vừa mới all seem to mean 'just'. How do I choose?
faqs.answer: All three mark very recent past, and in everyday speech they overlap heavily. vừa and mới are near-interchangeable for 'just (a moment ago)': 'Anh ấy vừa đi' / 'Anh ấy mới đi' = 'He just left.' vừa mới combines them for emphasis on immediacy: 'Tôi vừa mới gọi cho anh' = 'I just this second called you.' A separate use of mới is 'only then / not until', signalling something happened later than expected: 'Mãi đến 10 giờ anh ấy mới về' = 'He didn't get home until 10.' Watch for that second meaning — it is not about recency at all.

units.title: đã từng — past experience ('have ever / once')
units.pattern: S + (đã) từng + V (+ rồi) | negative: S + chưa (từng) + V
units.explanation: từng (often đã từng) expresses that the subject has had the experience of doing something at some point, or once did/was something that is typically no longer the case. It is the experiential perfect — closer to English 'have ever done' or 'used to' than to a plain completed past. The negative counterpart is 'chưa từng' / 'chưa bao giờ' = 'have never (yet)'.
units.note: Don't use từng for a single, specific recent action — say 'Tôi đã gặp cô ấy hôm qua' (I met her yesterday), not 'đã từng'. từng implies experience or a discontinued past state, not a one-off recent event.

examples.vi: Tôi đã từng làm việc ở một công ty Nhật.
examples.en: I once worked at a Japanese company (but not now).

examples.vi: Bạn đã từng đến Đà Lạt bao giờ chưa?
examples.en: Have you ever been to Da Lat?

examples.vi: Cô ấy chưa từng nói dối tôi.
examples.en: She has never lied to me.

examples.vi: Anh ấy từng là vận động viên chuyên nghiệp.
examples.en: He used to be a professional athlete.

units.title: vẫn còn — continuation ('still')
units.pattern: S + vẫn (còn) + V / Adj | S + vẫn chưa + V (still not yet)
units.explanation: vẫn còn marks that a state or action persists up to and including now, against an expectation that it might have ended — English 'still'. vẫn alone stresses 'nevertheless/still the same', còn alone stresses 'remaining/yet'; together they reinforce ongoing continuation. The negative 'vẫn chưa' means 'still hasn't (yet)'.
units.note: còn on its own can also mean 'there is still / remaining' (existential), e.g. 'Còn ghế trống không?' (Are there still empty seats?). In that existential sense it doesn't pair with vẫn.

examples.vi: Trời vẫn còn mưa to lắm.
examples.en: It's still raining hard.

examples.vi: Tôi vẫn còn nhớ ngày đầu tiên gặp em.
examples.en: I still remember the first day I met you.

examples.vi: Anh ấy vẫn chưa trả lời tin nhắn của tôi.
examples.en: He still hasn't replied to my message.

examples.vi: Dù đã muộn, cô ấy vẫn còn làm việc.
examples.en: Even though it was late, she was still working.

units.title: sắp (sửa) — imminent future ('about to')
units.explanation: sắp, or the more colloquial sắp sửa, marks an action as imminent — about to happen very soon. It is more immediate and certain than sẽ ('will'). The sentence-final 'rồi' is extremely common and adds the sense 'it's about to happen any moment now'.
units.note: sắp focuses on imminence regardless of distance, but it implies 'soon'; for a vague or distant future use sẽ instead. 'sắp ... rồi' is the natural, idiomatic pairing — leaving out rồi sounds flatter but is still correct.

examples.vi: Tàu sắp chạy rồi, nhanh lên!
examples.en: The train is about to leave, hurry up!

examples.vi: Tôi sắp sửa ra ngoài thì trời đổ mưa.
examples.en: I was just about to go out when it started to rain.

examples.vi: Con gái họ sắp tốt nghiệp đại học.
examples.en: Their daughter is about to graduate from university.

examples.vi: Mọi người ơi, phim sắp bắt đầu rồi.
examples.en: Everyone, the film is about to start.

units.title: vừa / mới / vừa mới — very recent past ('just')
units.pattern: S + vừa / mới / vừa mới + V
units.explanation: These markers place an action in the immediate past — it happened just a moment ago. vừa and mới are largely interchangeable; vừa mới stacks them to emphasise how recent it is. They answer 'when?' with 'just now', and contrast with đã (general completed past).
units.note: Beware a second meaning of mới: placed after a time expression it means 'only then / not until', highlighting lateness — 'Đến tối anh ấy mới ăn' (He didn't eat until evening). Context and word order disambiguate it from the 'just' meaning.

examples.vi: Tôi vừa ăn cơm xong.
examples.en: I just finished eating.

examples.vi: Cô ấy mới đi khỏi đây mấy phút trước.
examples.en: She left just a few minutes ago.

examples.vi: Chúng tôi vừa mới chuyển đến khu này.
examples.en: We've just moved to this neighbourhood.

examples.vi: Em vừa nhận được email của anh.
examples.en: I just received your email.

units.title: mới ... xong — just-completed action ('just finished V-ing')
units.explanation: Bracketing a verb with mới ... xong marks an action as having just been completed at the moment of speaking — 'have just finished doing X'. xong is a completive/resultative marker ('finished') that follows the verb (and its object), while mới/vừa mới at the front signals recency. Together they stress a fresh result.
units.note: With a short object, xong normally sits at the very end of the clause: 'làm bài tập xong' (finished the homework). When the object is long, the order 'V + xong + object' is also fully standard and often preferred — 'làm xong bài tập về nhà' (finished the homework). Both orders are correct native Vietnamese; choose by rhythm and object length.

examples.vi: Tôi vừa mới làm bài tập xong thì bạn gọi.
examples.en: I had just finished my homework when you called.

examples.vi: Mẹ mới nấu cơm xong, vào ăn đi.
examples.en: Mum has just finished cooking, come and eat.

examples.vi: Họ mới họp xong nên ai cũng mệt.
examples.en: They just finished the meeting, so everyone is tired.

examples.vi: Anh ấy mới rửa xe xong thì trời lại mưa.
examples.en: He had just finished washing the car when it rained again.

levels.label: Advanced
levels.description: Nominalization, formal register, discourse cohesion, scalar focus, counterfactuals and stance — precise, sophisticated Vietnamese.

modules.title: Nominalization & Abstract Nouns
modules.description: This module teaches how Vietnamese turns verbs and adjectives into abstract nouns using nominalizing classifiers (sự, việc, cuộc, tính, niềm, nỗi). These constructions are essential for formal writing, academic prose, journalism, and abstract discussion, where Vietnamese prefers noun phrases over plain verb clauses.
modules.mainPattern: sự / việc / cuộc / tính / niềm / nỗi + verb/adjective → abstract noun

faqs.question: Vietnamese verbs and adjectives can already act like nouns without any marker. So why bother with sự, việc, niềm, etc.?
faqs.answer: Bare verbs/adjectives work fine in casual speech (Tôi thích đọc sách = I like reading). But formal Vietnamese, especially written prose, treats nominalizers as a register signal and a clarity device. Sự phát triển (development) reads as a defined abstract concept, whereas phát triển alone reads as the action 'to develop'. Compare casual Anh ấy thành công (He succeeds/is successful) with formal sự thành công của anh ấy (his success), which can take adjectives and stand as a subject: Sự thành công của anh ấy là điều không thể phủ nhận (His success is undeniable). Nominalizers also let you attach modifiers and possessors cleanly, which bare verbs resist.

faqs.question: How do I know whether to use sự or việc?
faqs.answer: Use sự + adjective/stative or abstract verb for qualities and states that have no concrete 'event' (sự im lặng = silence, sự khác biệt = the difference, sự tồn tại = existence). Use việc + dynamic verb for an action/affair treated as a concrete matter or task, often as a subject or object (Việc học tiếng Việt rất quan trọng = Learning Vietnamese is very important; Tôi phản đối việc tăng giá = I oppose raising prices). Rule of thumb: if you could say 'the matter/act of ___', use việc; if you mean 'the quality/fact of ___', use sự.

units.title: sự + adjective/stative verb (abstract qualities & facts)
units.pattern: sự + adjective / stative verb → abstract noun
units.explanation: 'Sự' is the default nominalizer for turning adjectives and stative/abstract verbs into abstract nouns denoting a quality, state, or fact. The result behaves like a full noun: it can take a possessor with 'của', be modified, and serve as subject or object. This is the workhorse of formal and academic Vietnamese.
units.note: Sự pairs naturally with adjectives and abstract/stative verbs, not with everyday concrete actions. You say sự im lặng (silence) but not normally 'sự ăn' for 'eating' — for ordinary dynamic actions use việc instead.

examples.vi: Sự im lặng của cả phòng họp khiến anh ấy bối rối.
examples.en: The silence of the whole meeting room left him flustered.

examples.vi: Chúng ta cần thừa nhận sự khác biệt giữa hai nền văn hóa.
examples.en: We need to acknowledge the difference between the two cultures.

examples.vi: Sự phát triển nhanh chóng của công nghệ đặt ra nhiều thách thức.
examples.en: The rapid development of technology poses many challenges.

examples.vi: Không ai có thể phủ nhận sự tồn tại của vấn đề này.
examples.en: No one can deny the existence of this problem.

units.title: việc + dynamic verb (actions as concrete matters)
units.pattern: việc + verb (phrase) → 'the act/matter of doing X'
units.explanation: 'Việc' nominalizes dynamic verbs and whole verb phrases, packaging an action or affair as a concrete 'matter' or 'task'. It is the preferred way to make a clause function as a grammatical subject or object, especially after verbs of opinion, decision, and evaluation (đồng ý, phản đối, quyết định, ủng hộ).
units.note: Việc keeps the verb's own objects and complements: việc tăng giá xăng (the matter of raising fuel prices), not just việc tăng. Choosing sự here (sự tăng giá) shifts the nuance toward the abstract phenomenon rather than the deliberate act.

examples.vi: Việc học một ngoại ngữ đòi hỏi sự kiên nhẫn.
examples.en: Learning a foreign language demands patience.

examples.vi: Hội đồng đã phản đối việc xây nhà máy gần khu dân cư.
examples.en: The council opposed building a factory near the residential area.

examples.vi: Việc anh ấy từ chối lời mời khiến mọi người ngạc nhiên.
examples.en: His turning down the invitation surprised everyone.

examples.vi: Chính phủ đang cân nhắc việc tăng thuế đối với hàng nhập khẩu.
examples.en: The government is considering raising taxes on imported goods.

units.title: cuộc + verb (bounded events & undertakings)
units.pattern: cuộc + verb/noun → a bounded event, process, or undertaking
units.explanation: 'Cuộc' nominalizes an activity into a single, bounded event or organized undertaking with participants and a duration — a meeting, a struggle, a journey, a revolution. Unlike abstract 'sự', 'cuộc' frames the noun as a concrete happening you can attend, launch, or live through.
units.note: Cuộc collocates with specific verbs/nouns and is largely lexicalized: cuộc họp (meeting), cuộc đời (life), cuộc chiến (war), cuộc cách mạng (revolution). You cannot freely attach it to any verb — learn the high-frequency pairings rather than generating them.

examples.vi: Cuộc đấu tranh giành độc lập kéo dài nhiều thập kỷ.
examples.en: The struggle for independence lasted many decades.

examples.vi: Cuộc cách mạng công nghiệp đã thay đổi hoàn toàn xã hội.
examples.en: The industrial revolution completely transformed society.

examples.vi: Cả nước đang theo dõi cuộc khủng hoảng kinh tế hiện nay.
examples.en: The whole country is watching the current economic crisis.

examples.vi: Cuộc đời của bà là một tấm gương về lòng kiên trì.
examples.en: Her life is a model of perseverance.

units.title: tính + adjective (the '-ness' of a quality)
units.explanation: 'Tính' turns an adjective into the name of the inherent property or characteristic it denotes, much like English '-ity', '-ness', or '-ness of'. It is heavily used in academic, scientific, and technical writing to label abstract attributes (feasibility, accuracy, stability).
units.note: 'Tính' (property) overlaps with but differs from 'sự': tính chính xác = accuracy as an inherent trait of something; sự chính xác leans toward 'the fact of being accurate' in a given case. Many tính-words are fixed scientific terms (tính khả thi, tính bền vững) and should be memorized as units.

examples.vi: Các nhà nghiên cứu đã đánh giá tính khả thi của dự án.
examples.en: The researchers assessed the feasibility of the project.

examples.vi: Tính chính xác của số liệu là yếu tố quyết định.
examples.en: The accuracy of the data is the decisive factor.

examples.vi: Báo cáo nhấn mạnh tính bền vững của mô hình phát triển này.
examples.en: The report stresses the sustainability of this development model.

examples.vi: Tính minh bạch trong quản lý tài chính ngày càng được coi trọng.
examples.en: Transparency in financial management is increasingly valued.

units.title: niềm vs nỗi + emotion (positive vs negative feelings)
units.pattern: niềm + positive emotion / nỗi + negative emotion → named feeling
units.explanation: 'Niềm' and 'nỗi' nominalize emotion words, but they split by valence: 'niềm' takes positive or uplifting feelings (joy, pride, hope, faith), while 'nỗi' takes negative or painful ones (sorrow, fear, longing, worry). The choice is semantic, not free, and getting it wrong sounds jarring to natives. Both are common in literary and emotive formal prose.
units.note: Match the classifier to the feeling's valence: niềm vui / niềm tự hào / niềm hy vọng vs nỗi buồn / nỗi sợ / nỗi nhớ. Saying 'nỗi vui' or 'niềm buồn' is incorrect. A few feelings can take either with a meaning shift, but as a learner, treat the valence rule as firm.

examples.vi: Niềm tự hào dân tộc được thể hiện rõ trong từng trang sử.
examples.en: National pride is clearly expressed on every page of history.

examples.vi: Thành công của con cái là niềm hạnh phúc lớn nhất của cha mẹ.
examples.en: Their children's success is parents' greatest happiness.

examples.vi: Nỗi cô đơn của người già là một vấn đề xã hội đáng quan tâm.
examples.en: The loneliness of the elderly is a social issue worth attention.

examples.vi: Chiến tranh để lại nỗi đau khó nguôi trong lòng nhiều thế hệ.
examples.en: The war left a pain hard to soothe in the hearts of many generations.

modules.title: Formal & Written Register
modules.description: This C1 module teaches how Vietnamese shifts into a formal, written register (văn viết) — favouring Sino-Vietnamese (Hán-Việt) vocabulary, structured passive constructions with được/bị, and impersonal connectives. Use it for academic writing, official documents, journalism, and formal speeches, where everyday spoken phrasing (văn nói) would sound careless or unprofessional.
modules.mainPattern: [Hán-Việt lexis] + được/bị + [động từ] (passive); văn nói → văn viết register shift

faqs.question: When should I choose a Sino-Vietnamese (Hán-Việt) word over its native Vietnamese equivalent?
faqs.answer: Use the Hán-Việt word in formal, written, technical or ceremonial contexts; use the native word in everyday speech. They often share a core meaning but differ sharply in register. For example, 'phụ nữ' (women) is neutral-to-formal and standard in writing, while 'đàn bà' is colloquial and can sound blunt or even disrespectful: 'Hội nghị bàn về quyền của phụ nữ' (The conference discusses women's rights) vs. spoken 'Mấy bà đàn bà ngồi nói chuyện' (The women sit chatting). Similarly, written 'tử vong' replaces spoken 'chết', and 'phu nhân' replaces 'vợ' in diplomatic contexts: 'Tổng thống và phu nhân' (The President and his wife). The pitfall is overcorrection — piling on Hán-Việt where it isn't idiomatic (e.g. 'mua' is always fine in ordinary prose; you don't need 'thu mua' or 'mua sắm' unless the context is specifically commercial or about shopping).

faqs.question: Is the được/bị passive really necessary, or can I just keep the active voice like in speech?
faqs.answer: In văn nói, Vietnamese strongly prefers the active voice or topic-comment word order, so the passive can feel heavy. But in văn viết — especially reports, science and law — the passive with được (favourable/neutral outcome) or bị (adverse outcome) is the register-correct choice when the agent is unknown, unimportant, or deliberately backgrounded: 'Dự luật đã được Quốc hội thông qua' (The bill was passed by the National Assembly) sounds far more official than the spoken 'Quốc hội thông qua dự luật rồi'. Choosing được vs bị also encodes evaluation: 'được khen' (praised — positive) vs 'bị phê bình' (criticised — negative).

units.title: Hán-Việt for native words in formal register
units.pattern: native word (văn nói) → Hán-Việt synonym (văn viết)
units.explanation: Most formal Vietnamese writing replaces high-frequency native words with their Sino-Vietnamese (Hán-Việt) equivalents, which carry a more abstract, dignified or technical tone. The pairs are often near-synonyms in meaning but not interchangeable in register: the native form is warm and spoken, the Hán-Việt form is detached and written. Mastering these pairs is the single biggest lever for sounding educated in writing.
units.note: Do not over-Sinicise. Many everyday verbs (ăn, đi, mua, làm) have no natural Hán-Việt replacement in ordinary prose; forcing one (e.g. using 'thực' for 'ăn' outside fixed compounds) sounds pretentious or wrong.

examples.vi: Nhiều người đã tử vong trong vụ tai nạn.
examples.en: Many people died in the accident. (written 'tử vong' vs spoken 'chết')

examples.vi: Phụ nữ và trẻ em được ưu tiên sơ tán trước.
examples.en: Women and children were prioritised for evacuation. (written 'phụ nữ' vs spoken 'đàn bà')

examples.vi: Quý vị vui lòng cung cấp thông tin cá nhân.
examples.en: Please provide your personal information. (formal 'cung cấp' vs spoken 'đưa / cho')

examples.vi: Công trình sẽ được khởi công vào quý ba.
examples.en: The project will commence in the third quarter. (formal 'khởi công' vs spoken 'bắt đầu xây')

units.title: The được passive for neutral or favourable outcomes
units.explanation: In formal writing, 'được' forms a passive whose subject undergoes an action with a neutral or positive/beneficial result. The agent, if mentioned, sits between 'được' and the verb. This construction lets the writer foreground the result or the affected entity and background or omit the doer — a hallmark of objective, institutional prose.
units.note: 'được' is not a generic English-style passive marker: it specifically signals a neutral/favourable reading. Using it for a clearly harmful event ('*được thương' for 'injured') is wrong — use 'bị' instead.

examples.vi: Đề xuất này đã được hội đồng phê duyệt.
examples.en: This proposal was approved by the council.

examples.vi: Báo cáo sẽ được công bố vào tuần tới.
examples.en: The report will be published next week. (agent omitted)

examples.vi: Tác phẩm được giới phê bình đánh giá cao.
examples.en: The work was highly rated by critics.

examples.vi: Các quy định mới đã được ban hành kể từ đầu năm.
examples.en: The new regulations have been promulgated since the start of the year.

units.title: The bị passive for adverse outcomes
units.explanation: 'bị' forms the counterpart passive used when the action affects the subject negatively or undesirably. In formal registers (journalism, law, science) it is the precise, neutral way to report harm, failure, sanction or loss while keeping the affected party in topic position. The contrast được/bị is obligatory and meaning-bearing, not stylistic.
units.note: Avoid the spoken habit of stacking 'bị' on neutral facts (e.g. '*bị tăng' for a price merely rising). Use 'bị' only when the writer frames the outcome as unfavourable to the subject; otherwise use 'được' or an active clause.

examples.vi: Giám đốc bị cách chức sau vụ bê bối.
examples.en: The director was dismissed after the scandal.

examples.vi: Nhiều hộ dân bị ảnh hưởng bởi trận lũ.
examples.en: Many households were affected by the flood.

examples.vi: Dự án bị đình chỉ do thiếu kinh phí.
examples.en: The project was suspended due to a lack of funding.

examples.vi: Bị cáo bị tuyên phạt năm năm tù.
examples.en: The defendant was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

units.title: Formal connectives and impersonal framing
units.pattern: Theo + nguồn; Nhằm + mục đích; Do/Vì + nguyên nhân, ...
units.explanation: Written Vietnamese signals logical relations with a dedicated set of formal connectives that replace casual spoken links. 'Theo' (according to) attributes a claim impersonally; 'nhằm' (in order to / with the aim of) states purpose more formally than spoken 'để'; 'do' and 'vì' introduce cause in reports; 'tuy nhiên' / 'song' (however) and 'đồng thời' (at the same time) structure argument. These keep the prose objective and source-attributed.
units.note: 'nhằm' is purpose-only and formal; don't substitute it for plain 'để' in casual contexts. 'song' (however) is markedly literary — fine in editorials, too stiff for an email, where 'tuy nhiên' or 'nhưng' is safer.

examples.vi: Theo báo cáo của Bộ Y tế, số ca nhiễm đang giảm.
examples.en: According to the Ministry of Health's report, the number of cases is falling.

examples.vi: Nhằm nâng cao chất lượng dịch vụ, công ty đã tái cơ cấu.
examples.en: In order to improve service quality, the company restructured.

examples.vi: Doanh thu tăng mạnh; tuy nhiên, lợi nhuận lại giảm.
examples.en: Revenue rose sharply; however, profit fell.

examples.vi: Do điều kiện thời tiết bất lợi, sự kiện đã bị hoãn.
examples.en: Owing to unfavourable weather conditions, the event was postponed.

units.title: Nominalisation with sự / việc / tính / hóa
units.pattern: sự/việc + [động từ]; [tính từ] + tính; [danh/tính từ] + hóa
units.explanation: Formal Vietnamese turns verbs and adjectives into abstract nouns to build dense, objective sentences. 'sự' nominalises states/changes (sự phát triển — development), 'việc' nominalises actions/facts (việc thực hiện — the carrying-out), the prefix 'tính' forms abstract qualities (tính khả thi — feasibility), and the suffix '-hóa' forms 'X-isation' processes (hiện đại hóa — modernisation). This packing of information into noun phrases is typical of academic and bureaucratic writing.
units.note: Nominalisation is powerful but easy to overuse: stacking too many 'sự/việc' phrases makes prose clunky and is a known flaw of weak bureaucratic Vietnamese. Prefer it where it adds precision, not as automatic padding.

examples.vi: Sự phát triển của nền kinh tế phụ thuộc vào nhiều yếu tố.
examples.en: The development of the economy depends on many factors.

examples.vi: Việc triển khai dự án cần được giám sát chặt chẽ.
examples.en: The implementation of the project needs to be closely monitored.

examples.vi: Tính khả thi của phương án vẫn đang được xem xét.
examples.en: The feasibility of the plan is still under consideration.

examples.vi: Quá trình công nghiệp hóa, hiện đại hóa đất nước.
examples.en: The process of industrialising and modernising the country.

modules.title: Discourse Markers & Cohesion
modules.description: This module teaches sentence-initial discourse markers that Vietnamese speakers use to organize ideas, signal reframing, generalize, summarize, and rephrase across a stretch of discourse. These connectors are essential for sounding coherent and fluent in essays, presentations, and extended spoken argumentation.
modules.mainPattern: [Discourse marker] + (là/thì) + clause — e.g. "Thật ra (thì) ...", "Nói chung (là) ...", "Tóm lại (thì) ..."

faqs.question: What's the difference between 'nói chung' and 'nhìn chung'? They both seem to mean 'in general.'
faqs.answer: They overlap but carry different registers and angles. 'Nói chung' (literally 'speaking generally') is the everyday workhorse — it generalizes or wraps up loosely, and works in speech and writing: 'Nói chung là ổn' (Generally it's fine). 'Nhìn chung' (literally 'viewing generally / on the whole') is more formal and analytical; it takes a bird's-eye view of data or a situation, and is common in reports and essays: 'Nhìn chung, nền kinh tế đang phục hồi' (On the whole, the economy is recovering). Use 'nói chung' for casual summing-up and 'nhìn chung' when you survey a whole picture objectively.

faqs.question: Can I just stack English-style connectors like 'in other words' literally, or are there fixed Vietnamese forms?
faqs.answer: Vietnamese has fixed lexical chunks you should learn whole rather than translate word-by-word. 'In other words' is 'nói cách khác', 'to sum up' is 'tóm lại', 'actually/in fact' is 'thật ra' (or 'thực ra'). They sit at the front of the sentence and are often followed by an optional 'là' or 'thì': 'Nói cách khác, đây là một sai lầm' (In other words, this is a mistake). Inserting 'là'/'thì' makes it sound more natural and spoken; dropping it is crisper and more written.

units.title: Reframing with thật ra / thực ra
units.explanation: 'Thật ra' (or the equally common 'thực ra') means 'actually, in fact, the truth is.' It introduces a correction or a more accurate reframing of what was just said or assumed — signalling that the real situation differs from appearances. It typically opens the sentence and may be followed by an optional 'thì'.
units.note: 'Thật ra' contradicts a prior assumption; don't confuse it with 'thật là' (= 'how / really' as an intensifier, e.g. 'thật là đẹp' = 'how beautiful'). They are not interchangeable.

examples.vi: Nhiều người nghĩ anh ấy lạnh lùng, nhưng thật ra anh ấy rất tình cảm.
examples.en: Many people think he's cold, but in fact he's very warm-hearted.

examples.vi: Thật ra thì tôi không phản đối ý tưởng đó, tôi chỉ lo về chi phí.
examples.en: Actually, I'm not against the idea; I'm just worried about the cost.

examples.vi: Trông có vẻ phức tạp, nhưng thực ra cách làm rất đơn giản.
examples.en: It looks complicated, but actually the method is very simple.

examples.vi: Thực ra, đây không phải lần đầu tiên chuyện này xảy ra.
examples.en: In fact, this isn't the first time this has happened.

units.title: Generalizing with nói chung
units.explanation: 'Nói chung' means 'in general, generally speaking, all in all.' It signals that the speaker is setting aside details and stating a broad, overall judgment, often to wrap up a list or smooth over exceptions. Adding 'là' gives it a natural, conversational rhythm.
units.note: In casual speech 'nói chung là' can become a filler ('like, basically...'). In formal writing, prefer it sparingly and lean on 'nhìn chung' for analytical summaries.

examples.vi: Có vài chỗ chưa hoàn hảo, nhưng nói chung tôi hài lòng với kết quả.
examples.en: There are a few imperfect spots, but in general I'm satisfied with the result.

examples.vi: Nói chung là dịch vụ ở đây khá tốt, chỉ hơi chậm thôi.
examples.en: Generally speaking, the service here is pretty good, just a bit slow.

examples.vi: Thời tiết tháng này nói chung là dễ chịu.
examples.en: The weather this month is generally pleasant.

examples.vi: Nói chung, ai cũng đồng ý rằng cần thay đổi.
examples.en: All in all, everyone agrees that change is needed.

units.title: Surveying the whole with nhìn chung
units.explanation: 'Nhìn chung' means 'on the whole, overall, broadly viewed.' Compared with 'nói chung', it is more formal and takes an objective, bird's-eye perspective over a whole situation, dataset, or body of work — making it the go-to marker for reports, reviews, and academic essays.
units.note: Because it implies surveying a whole picture, 'nhìn chung' fits assessments and conclusions; it sounds odd attached to a single trivial fact. Reserve it for genuinely aggregate judgments.

examples.vi: Nhìn chung, chất lượng sản phẩm năm nay đã được cải thiện đáng kể.
examples.en: On the whole, product quality this year has improved considerably.

examples.vi: Nhìn chung, các số liệu cho thấy xu hướng tích cực.
examples.en: Overall, the figures show a positive trend.

examples.vi: Nhìn chung, học sinh tiếp thu bài tốt, dù vẫn còn một số em gặp khó khăn.
examples.en: Broadly, the students absorbed the lesson well, though some still struggled.

examples.vi: Nhìn chung, dự án đã đạt được mục tiêu đề ra.
examples.en: On the whole, the project achieved its stated objectives.

units.title: Rephrasing with nói cách khác
units.explanation: 'Nói cách khác' means 'in other words, put another way.' It signals that the next sentence restates the previous point in different terms — clarifying, simplifying, or drawing out the implication. It is a fixed chunk and opens the sentence.
units.note: Don't follow 'nói cách khác' with brand-new information; it must paraphrase what came before. For adding a fresh point, use 'hơn nữa' (moreover) instead.

examples.vi: Chi phí tăng nhưng doanh thu không đổi; nói cách khác, lợi nhuận đang giảm.
examples.en: Costs rose but revenue stayed flat; in other words, profit is shrinking.

examples.vi: Anh ấy luôn đến muộn và không hoàn thành việc — nói cách khác, anh ấy thiếu trách nhiệm.
examples.en: He's always late and never finishes his work — in other words, he's irresponsible.

examples.vi: Nói cách khác, chúng ta cần một chiến lược hoàn toàn mới.
examples.en: In other words, we need an entirely new strategy.

examples.vi: Cô ấy từ chối lời mời, nói cách khác là không muốn tham gia.
examples.en: She declined the invitation; put another way, she doesn't want to take part.

units.title: Concluding with tóm lại & highlighting with đáng nói là
units.pattern: Tóm lại, + clause / Đáng nói là + clause
units.explanation: Two closing-stage markers. 'Tóm lại' means 'in short, to sum up' and introduces the bottom-line conclusion after a longer discussion. 'Đáng nói là' means 'notably, what's worth mentioning is' and flags the single most significant or surprising point in a stretch of discourse, directing the listener's attention to it.
units.note: 'Tóm lại' belongs at the very end of an argument — using it mid-discussion sounds premature. 'Đáng nói (là)' often carries an evaluative or critical tone, so it suits points the speaker finds striking, not neutral facts.

examples.vi: Tóm lại, nếu không hành động ngay, chúng ta sẽ mất cơ hội này.
examples.en: In short, if we don't act now, we'll lose this opportunity.

examples.vi: Tóm lại, ưu điểm nhiều hơn nhược điểm.
examples.en: To sum up, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

examples.vi: Dự án bị trễ tiến độ, và đáng nói là chi phí đã vượt ngân sách gấp đôi.
examples.en: The project fell behind schedule, and notably the cost has overrun the budget twofold.

examples.vi: Đáng nói là không ai trong ban lãnh đạo lên tiếng nhận trách nhiệm.
examples.en: What's worth mentioning is that no one in management spoke up to take responsibility.

modules.title: Correlative Gradience
modules.description: This module teaches paired correlative constructions in Vietnamese that link two clauses so the second varies in proportion to, simultaneously with, or in exact measure to the first. Use these to express proportional change ("the more... the more"), matched quantity ("as much as"), and bundled simultaneous predicates with precision and natural flow.
modules.mainPattern: càng + X, (lại) càng + Y  •  bao nhiêu… bấy nhiêu  •  vừa + V1, vừa + V2

faqs.question: What is the difference between 'càng…càng' and 'càng ngày càng'?
faqs.answer: 'càng A càng B' links two correlated variables: as one rises, so does the other (e.g. 'Càng học, tôi càng thấy mình thiếu sót' — The more I study, the more I see my own shortcomings). 'Càng ngày càng' is a fixed idiom meaning 'more and more (over time)' with no second variable; it tracks change against the passage of time itself: 'Tiếng Việt của anh ấy càng ngày càng giỏi' (His Vietnamese gets better and better). Use 'càng ngày càng' (or its colloquial reduction 'ngày càng') only for gradual change over time, not for a true cause-effect proportion.

faqs.question: Can 'vừa…vừa' join two nouns or only verbs?
faqs.answer: In its core simultaneity sense it joins verbs/verb phrases performed by one subject at the same time: 'Cô ấy vừa lái xe vừa nghe nhạc' (She drives and listens to music at the same time). It also joins two adjectives to mean 'both… and…': 'Món này vừa rẻ vừa ngon' (This dish is both cheap and tasty). It does not directly conjoin two plain nouns — for that, use 'cả… lẫn…' instead: 'cả cà phê lẫn trà' (both coffee and tea).

units.title: Proportional càng…càng
units.explanation: The core proportional construction: as the first quantity or quality increases, the second increases (or decreases) in step. English 'the more…, the more…'. Each 'càng' immediately precedes the verb or adjective it scales. The optional 'lại' before the second 'càng' adds an emphatic 'all the more' nuance. The subject may differ across the two clauses or be shared and dropped.
units.note: 'càng' scales gradable predicates, not nouns — you cannot say 'càng tiền'. To scale a noun, attach it to a verb/adjective: 'càng có nhiều tiền' (the more money one has), not 'càng tiền'.

examples.vi: Càng học, tôi càng thấy mình còn thiếu sót.
examples.en: The more I study, the more I realize how much I still lack.

examples.vi: Trời càng về khuya, gió lại càng lạnh.
examples.en: The later into the night it got, the colder the wind became.

examples.vi: Anh càng giải thích, mọi người càng khó hiểu.
examples.en: The more he explained, the harder it was for everyone to understand.

examples.vi: Càng nghĩ về chuyện đó, cô ấy càng thấy bất an.
examples.en: The more she thought about it, the more uneasy she felt.

units.title: càng ngày càng (steady change over time)
units.pattern: (Subject) càng ngày càng + V/Adj   (colloquial: ngày càng + V/Adj)
units.explanation: A fixed idiom meaning 'more and more' as time passes — the change is tracked against time itself rather than a second variable. The reduced form 'ngày càng' is common and slightly more formal/written; 'càng ngày càng' is fully idiomatic in speech. It attaches directly to a gradable predicate.
units.note: Do not confuse with proportional 'càng…càng'. Here there is only one variable changing over time; there is no paired clause. Saying 'Càng ngày anh ấy càng giỏi' is also possible but the unbroken 'càng ngày càng + Adj' is the unmarked, most natural form.

examples.vi: Tiếng Việt của anh ấy càng ngày càng tốt.
examples.en: His Vietnamese is getting better and better.

examples.vi: Giá nhà ở thành phố ngày càng đắt đỏ.
examples.en: Housing prices in the city are getting more and more expensive.

examples.vi: Khí hậu càng ngày càng khắc nghiệt.
examples.en: The climate is becoming more and more extreme.

examples.vi: Cô ấy càng ngày càng ít nói chuyện với gia đình.
examples.en: She talks to her family less and less.

units.title: bao nhiêu… bấy nhiêu (matched measure)
units.explanation: A paired quantifier construction expressing that the second quantity matches the first in exact measure — 'as much as', 'however much… that much'. 'bao nhiêu' (interrogative 'how much/many') sets the scale; 'bấy nhiêu' (correlative 'that much') mirrors it. Often used to convey that effort, reward, love, or hardship is repaid in equal proportion. It frequently carries a rhetorical or proverbial tone.
units.note: Word order is fixed: the 'bao nhiêu' clause comes first and 'bấy nhiêu' answers it. When both predicates are gradable adjectives, the structure implies an inverse-or-equal balance and can read as a polished, almost literary register — heavier than everyday 'càng…càng'.

examples.vi: Bạn bỏ ra bao nhiêu công sức, bạn sẽ nhận lại bấy nhiêu thành quả.
examples.en: However much effort you put in, that's exactly how much reward you'll get back.

examples.vi: Yêu nhau bao nhiêu, giận nhau bấy nhiêu.
examples.en: However deeply they love each other, that's exactly how bitterly they quarrel.

examples.vi: Anh ấy có bao nhiêu tiền thì tiêu bấy nhiêu.
examples.en: He spends every bit of however much money he has.

examples.vi: Chúng tôi gom được bao nhiêu thì quyên góp bấy nhiêu.
examples.en: We donated however much we managed to gather.

units.title: vừa… vừa (simultaneous predicates)
units.explanation: Bundles two predicates of a single subject. With verbs it marks two actions done at the same time ('while…'); with adjectives it means 'both… and…', stacking two qualities. Each predicate takes its own 'vừa'. The actions/qualities must belong to the same subject — for two distinct subjects, use other coordinators.
units.note: Beware the homograph: 'vừa' alone also means 'just (recently)' as in 'tôi vừa ăn' (I just ate), and 'vừa' can mean 'to fit'. The simultaneity reading requires the paired 'vừa… vừa…' frame; a single 'vừa' before a verb is the recent-past sense, not simultaneity.

examples.vi: Cô ấy vừa khóc vừa kể lại chuyện đã xảy ra.
examples.en: She recounted what had happened while crying.

examples.vi: Quán này vừa rẻ vừa sạch sẽ nên lúc nào cũng đông.
examples.en: This place is both cheap and clean, so it's always crowded.

examples.vi: Anh đừng vừa lái xe vừa nhắn tin, nguy hiểm lắm.
examples.en: Don't text and drive at the same time — it's very dangerous.

examples.vi: Đứa bé vừa chạy vừa cười khanh khách.
examples.en: The child ran along giggling out loud.

units.title: vừa… đã… (no sooner… than…)
units.explanation: A sequential correlative built on 'vừa': it pairs a barely-completed first event with an immediately following second one — 'no sooner had… than…', 'as soon as…'. 'vừa' (often reinforced as 'vừa mới') marks the first event as just finished; 'đã' marks the second as already happening. This stresses how little time separated the two, often with surprise.
units.note: This is distinct from simultaneity 'vừa…vừa…': here the two events are sequential and very close, not concurrent. The 'thì' is optional and adds a slight pause/emphasis; 'đã' in the second clause is what fixes the 'already/so soon' reading.

examples.vi: Tôi vừa đặt lưng xuống giường thì điện thoại đã reo.
examples.en: No sooner had I lain down than the phone rang.

examples.vi: Nó vừa mới ra khỏi nhà thì trời đã đổ mưa.
examples.en: He had just left the house when it started to pour.

examples.vi: Khách vừa đến, cô ấy đã dọn cơm ra sẵn.
examples.en: The guests had barely arrived before she'd already laid out the meal.

examples.vi: Chúng tôi vừa ký hợp đồng xong thì đối tác đã đổi ý.
examples.en: We had just finished signing the contract when the partner changed their mind.

modules.title: Scalar Focus Particles: "even / let alone"
modules.description: This module teaches the Vietnamese particles used to place a referent at the extreme end of a likelihood scale — ngay cả, đến (cả), thậm chí for "even," and huống chi/huống hồ for "let alone." Use them to mark a surprising or extreme case and to draw the listener toward an implied stronger conclusion.
modules.mainPattern: ngay cả / đến (cả) / thậm chí + [extreme element] (... cũng/còn ...) ; ... huống chi/hồ + [easier case]

faqs.question: What's the difference between ngay cả, đến, and thậm chí — they all seem to mean 'even'?
faqs.answer: They overlap but differ in register and structure. 'Ngay cả' and 'đến (cả)' mark a noun phrase as the surprising case and almost always pair with 'cũng' or 'còn' in the predicate: 'Ngay cả giám đốc cũng không biết' / 'Đến giám đốc cũng không biết' (Even the director didn't know). 'Thậm chí' is more like English sentence-adverb 'even/in fact' — it can introduce a whole clause or an escalated second statement and does not require 'cũng': 'Nó lười, thậm chí không thèm trả lời tin nhắn' (He's lazy; he won't even bother to reply to messages). In short: ngay cả/đến scope over a phrase + cũng; thậm chí escalates a clause.

faqs.question: How do I say 'let alone' as in 'I can't afford a bike, let alone a car'?
faqs.answer: Use 'huống chi' (or the more literary 'huống hồ'), placed before the easier/more extreme case, after you've stated the harder one — usually with 'đến...còn/cũng' in the first clause: 'Xe đạp tôi còn chẳng mua nổi, huống chi (là) ô tô' (I can't even afford a bike, let alone a car). The logic is reversed from English word order: Vietnamese states the difficult case first, then 'huống chi' introduces what is even more out of reach. You can add 'là' after it for emphasis: 'huống chi là ô tô'.

units.title: ngay cả ... cũng/còn — "even X (does/is) ..."
units.explanation: 'Ngay cả' marks a noun phrase as the most extreme or least expected member of a set, implying that if even this case holds, all easier cases hold too. The predicate almost always carries 'cũng' (also/even) or 'còn' (still); dropping it sounds incomplete to native ears. 'Ngay cả' can sit at the front of the sentence or directly before the focused phrase.
units.note: Don't omit 'cũng'/'còn'. *'Ngay cả nó không đến' is wrong; it must be 'Ngay cả nó cũng không đến.' The 'cũng' is what closes the scalar implication.

examples.vi: Ngay cả những người giàu kinh nghiệm nhất cũng mắc sai lầm này.
examples.en: Even the most experienced people make this mistake.

examples.vi: Hôm đó lạnh đến mức ngay cả nước trong bình cũng đóng băng.
examples.en: It was so cold that day that even the water in the bottle froze.

examples.vi: Cô ấy bận đến nỗi ngay cả bữa trưa cũng không có thời gian ăn.
examples.en: She was so busy that she didn't even have time to eat lunch.

examples.vi: Ngay cả anh ấy còn không giải được bài này thì nói gì đến chúng tôi.
examples.en: Even he couldn't solve this problem, so what hope is there for us.

units.title: đến (cả) ... cũng/còn — colloquial "even, to the point of"
units.explanation: 'Đến' (literally 'reaching/up to') used as a focus particle is the everyday spoken equivalent of 'ngay cả.' It pushes a case to the limit of the scale: 'even as far as X.' 'Cả' is often added for emphasis ('đến cả'). Like 'ngay cả,' it pairs with 'cũng' or 'còn.' This is the form you hear most in casual speech and complaints.
units.note: This focus-particle 'đến' is distinct from the verb 'đến' (to arrive) and from 'đến mức/nỗi' (to the extent that). Context and the following 'cũng/còn' disambiguate it.

examples.vi: Mệt quá, đến nói chuyện tôi cũng chẳng buồn.
examples.en: I'm so tired I don't even feel like talking.

examples.vi: Nó vô tâm đến mức đến sinh nhật mẹ cũng quên.
examples.en: He's so thoughtless that he even forgot his own mother's birthday.

examples.vi: Đến trẻ con còn hiểu điều đó, sao anh lại không?
examples.en: Even a child understands that — how come you don't?

examples.vi: Đói đến cả cơm nguội tôi cũng ăn được.
examples.en: I'm so hungry I'd even eat cold leftover rice.

units.title: thậm chí — clause-level escalation "in fact / even"
units.explanation: 'Thậm chí' works like an English sentence adverb. It introduces an escalated second statement that goes beyond the first, often with 'còn' to reinforce the step up. Unlike 'ngay cả'/'đến,' it does not need to scope over a single noun phrase and does not require 'cũng' — it can lead a whole verb phrase or clause. Use it to add a surprising, intensifying afterthought.
units.note: When 'thậm chí' focuses a noun phrase rather than a clause, native speakers often still add 'cũng': 'Thậm chí bố mẹ nó cũng không tin' (Even its parents don't believe it). For clausal escalation, 'còn' is the natural partner instead.

examples.vi: Bộ phim không hề dở, thậm chí còn hay hơn phần đầu.
examples.en: The film isn't bad at all; in fact, it's even better than the first part.

examples.vi: Anh ta không xin lỗi, thậm chí còn đổ lỗi cho người khác.
examples.en: He didn't apologize; he even blamed someone else.

examples.vi: Dự án bị chậm, thậm chí có nguy cơ bị hủy hoàn toàn.
examples.en: The project is delayed, and in fact risks being cancelled altogether.

examples.vi: Thậm chí những chuyên gia hàng đầu cũng chưa có lời giải.
examples.en: Even the top experts don't have an answer yet.

units.title: ... huống chi / huống hồ — "let alone, much less"
units.explanation: 'Huống chi' (formal/literary: 'huống hồ') expresses 'let alone / much less.' Vietnamese states the harder case first — usually with 'đến ... còn' or '... còn chẳng/không' to stress that even that fails — then 'huống chi' introduces the case that is even more out of the question. Optionally add 'là' after it. The result is an a-fortiori argument: if even the lesser thing fails, the greater one certainly does.
units.note: Mind the order: it is the reverse of English. English says 'X, let alone Y' (Y harder); Vietnamese puts the already-difficult case first and lets 'huống chi' point to the even more extreme one. Putting the easy case first breaks the logic.

examples.vi: Việc đơn giản thế này nó còn làm hỏng, huống chi việc khó hơn.
examples.en: He even botches a simple task like this, let alone a harder one.

examples.vi: Đi bộ một cây số tôi còn thấy mệt, huống hồ chạy marathon.
examples.en: I get tired walking one kilometre, let alone running a marathon.

examples.vi: Người lớn còn không chịu nổi cái nóng này, huống chi là trẻ nhỏ.
examples.en: Even adults can't stand this heat, let alone small children.

examples.vi: Tiếng mẹ đẻ nó còn viết sai chính tả, huống chi tiếng nước ngoài.
examples.en: He even makes spelling mistakes in his mother tongue, let alone a foreign language.

modules.title: Counterfactual & Regret
modules.description: This module teaches how Vietnamese expresses unreal past situations and regret — wishing things had been different and stating what should have happened. You use these patterns to talk about missed opportunities, hindsight, and reproach, where English would use "if only," "should have," and the third conditional.
modules.mainPattern: giá (mà) / phải chi + clause [thì (đã) + clause] ; đáng lẽ / lẽ ra + clause [(đã) ... rồi / nhưng ...]

faqs.question: What's the difference between giá mà and phải chi? They both seem to mean 'if only.'
faqs.answer: Both introduce an unreal wish about the past, but the register differs. Giá mà (and the shorter giá) is neutral and works everywhere — speech, writing, formal contexts: Giá mà tôi nghe lời anh thì đã không ra nông nỗi này (If only I had listened to you, it wouldn't have come to this). Phải chi is warmer, more emotional and colloquial, with a strong Southern flavour, often sighed out loud: Phải chi hồi đó tao đừng bỏ học (If only I hadn't dropped out back then). For an essay or a measured tone, prefer giá mà; for raw, spoken regret, phải chi sounds more native.

faqs.question: How do I say 'should have' as in blaming someone, versus just expressing regret?
faqs.answer: Use đáng lẽ / lẽ ra for 'should have' — what the correct or expected action was. It is naturally evaluative, so it carries blame or reproach when aimed at another person: Đáng lẽ anh phải gọi cho tôi trước (You should have called me first). For pure inward regret with no judgement, giá mà / phải chi is softer because it only voices a wish: Giá mà mình gọi sớm hơn (If only I'd called sooner). A common combo states the wrong outcome with đáng lẽ … nhưng …: Lẽ ra tôi đã đỗ, nhưng tôi làm sai câu cuối (I should have passed, but I got the last question wrong).

units.title: giá mà / giá — counterfactual wish about the past
units.explanation: Giá mà (or simply giá) introduces a wish about something that did not actually happen — the equivalent of English 'if only' / 'had I only.' The first clause states the unreal condition; an optional result clause, often marked with thì and the past/perfective đã, states what would then have been true. Because the situation is contrary to fact, Vietnamese relies on context and đã rather than any verb-tense change.
units.note: Giá mà is neutral in register and safe in both speech and writing. Don't confuse it with giả sử ('suppose that…'), which sets up a hypothesis for argument's sake and is not necessarily counterfactual.

examples.vi: Giá mà tôi nghe lời anh thì đã không ra nông nỗi này.
examples.en: If only I had listened to you, it wouldn't have come to this.

examples.vi: Giá hồi đó tôi chịu khó học tiếng Anh thì giờ đã khác.
examples.en: If only I'd buckled down and studied English back then, things would be different now.

examples.vi: Giá mà cô ấy đừng nói câu đó thì mọi chuyện đã ổn.
examples.en: If only she hadn't said that, everything would have been fine.

examples.vi: Giá mà tôi biết trước, tôi đã không mua căn nhà đó.
examples.en: Had I only known beforehand, I wouldn't have bought that house.

units.title: phải chi — emotional, colloquial 'if only'
units.explanation: Phải chi expresses the same counterfactual wish as giá mà but with stronger emotional colour — wistful, sometimes self-reproaching. It is markedly more colloquial and carries a Southern Vietnamese flavour, common in everyday speech, song lyrics and heartfelt sighs. Structurally it behaves exactly like giá mà.
units.note: Avoid phải chi in formal writing such as essays or business correspondence — it reads as too informal and emotional. Switch to giá mà / lẽ ra there.

examples.vi: Phải chi hồi đó tao đừng bỏ học thì giờ đã có công việc tử tế.
examples.en: If only I hadn't dropped out back then, I'd have a decent job now.

examples.vi: Phải chi mình gặp nhau sớm hơn vài năm.
examples.en: If only we had met a few years sooner.

examples.vi: Phải chi tôi đừng tin lời hắn thì đã không mất tiền.
examples.en: If only I hadn't believed him, I wouldn't have lost the money.

examples.vi: Phải chi con nghe lời mẹ thì đâu đến mức này.
examples.en: If only I'd listened to you, Mum, it wouldn't have gotten this bad.

units.title: đáng lẽ / đáng lẽ ra — 'should have' (the correct thing that didn't happen)
units.explanation: Đáng lẽ (and the fuller đáng lẽ ra) marks what should or ought to have happened according to reason, duty or expectation — but didn't. It is inherently evaluative, so it often implies fault or regret. It frequently pairs with phải ('must/ought') in the should-have clause and with a nhưng-clause stating the disappointing reality.
units.note: When directed at another person, đáng lẽ sounds like reproach ('you should have…'), so use it carefully. For softer self-directed regret, giá mà is gentler.

examples.vi: Đáng lẽ anh phải gọi cho tôi trước khi quyết định.
examples.en: You should have called me before deciding.

examples.vi: Đáng lẽ ra tôi không nên đồng ý ngay từ đầu.
examples.en: I shouldn't have agreed in the first place.

examples.vi: Đáng lẽ chúng ta đã thắng, nhưng trọng tài thổi sai.
examples.en: We should have won, but the referee made a bad call.

examples.vi: Đáng lẽ ra việc này phải xong từ tuần trước rồi.
examples.en: This should have been finished last week already.

units.title: lẽ ra — 'by rights / one would have expected', formal hindsight
units.explanation: Lẽ ra is a slightly more formal, reasoned near-synonym of đáng lẽ, foregrounding logic and what the natural/proper course of events would have been ('by rights,' 'one would have expected'). It is common in writing and measured speech, and very often introduces a contrast with what actually occurred.
units.note: Lẽ ra and đáng lẽ are largely interchangeable; lẽ ra leans more reasoned/written, đáng lẽ slightly more conversational and reproachful. Both differ from giá mà in that they assert an expected norm, not merely a wish.

examples.vi: Lẽ ra cuộc họp đã bắt đầu lúc chín giờ, nhưng diễn giả đến muộn.
examples.en: The meeting should have started at nine, but the speaker arrived late.

examples.vi: Lẽ ra tôi đã đỗ, nhưng tôi làm sai câu cuối.
examples.en: I should have passed, but I got the last question wrong.

examples.vi: Lẽ ra anh không cần phải xin lỗi; lỗi đâu phải ở anh.
examples.en: By rights you needn't have apologised; the fault wasn't yours.

examples.vi: Lẽ ra với năng lực đó, cô ấy đã được thăng chức từ lâu.
examples.en: With ability like that, she should have been promoted long ago.

units.title: biết thế / biết vậy — 'had I known' hindsight regret
units.explanation: Biết thế (or biết vậy) is a compact, idiomatic way to express hindsight: literally 'had I known it would be like this.' It encapsulates a whole counterfactual condition in two words and is followed by the action one would have taken instead. Very natural in speech and a hallmark of fluent, native-sounding regret.
units.note: Often stands alone as a sigh — Biết thế! ('If only I'd known!'). The negative follow-up uses đã không / đã chẳng: Biết thế đã không đi ('Had I known, I wouldn't have gone').

examples.vi: Biết thế tôi đã không đi làm hôm nay.
examples.en: Had I known, I wouldn't have gone to work today.

examples.vi: Biết vậy thì mình đã đặt vé sớm hơn.
examples.en: If I'd known, I would have booked the tickets earlier.

examples.vi: Trời mưa to thế này, biết thế đã mang theo ô.
examples.en: It's pouring like this — had I known, I'd have brought an umbrella.

examples.vi: Biết thế đã chẳng nói gì cho xong.
examples.en: If only I'd known, I'd have just kept my mouth shut.

modules.title: Rhetorical Questions & Negation Scope
modules.description: This module teaches the high-frequency Vietnamese constructions that pose a question only to assert its opposite — denying, dismissing or contradicting a proposition with emotional colour (disbelief, indignation, resignation). It is used in argument, complaint, banter and persuasion, where a flat negation (không) would sound weak or neutral.
modules.mainPattern: làm gì có + N/clause · sao mà + clause + được · chẳng lẽ + clause (?) · clause + có…đâu

faqs.question: What is the difference between a plain negation with 'không' and a rhetorical negation like 'làm gì có'?
faqs.answer: 'Không' simply states that something is not the case ('Tôi không có tiền' = I don't have money). The rhetorical forms add force and stance: they treat the proposition as absurd or as something the speaker already knows to be false. 'Làm gì có tiền' means roughly 'As if I had any money!' / 'Where would I get money?' — it denies AND signals that the idea was unreasonable to begin with. Compare neutral 'Anh ấy không đến' (He isn't coming) with indignant 'Anh ấy đến làm gì!' (Why on earth would he come? — he won't / it's pointless).

faqs.question: How do I know whether 'chẳng lẽ' expects me to agree or disagree?
faqs.answer: 'Chẳng lẽ' raises a possibility the speaker finds hard to accept, so the expected answer is almost always 'no, surely not'. 'Chẳng lẽ anh ấy lại nói dối?' = 'Surely he wouldn't lie?' — the speaker leans toward 'he wouldn't'. It often pairs with 'lại' for extra incredulity and can trail off with 'sao' ('Chẳng lẽ lại thế sao?'). Use it to express reluctant suspicion, not a genuine information question.

units.title: làm gì có — emphatic denial of existence
units.explanation: 'Làm gì có' literally asks 'doing what is there…?' but functions as a forceful denial that something exists or is the case — close to English 'There's no such thing as…' or 'As if there were…'. It negates more strongly than 'không có' and implies the claim was mistaken or naive. It can take a noun phrase or a whole clause.
units.note: Do not confuse this with the literal question 'làm gì' (= 'doing what / why'). 'Anh làm gì đấy?' = 'What are you doing?', but 'Làm gì có chuyện đó!' = 'No such thing happened!'. Intonation and the following noun/clause disambiguate.

examples.vi: Làm gì có chuyện đó! Tôi chưa bao giờ nói thế.
examples.en: There's no such thing! I never said that.

examples.vi: Mới mùng một mà làm gì có tiền tiêu.
examples.en: It's only the first of the month — as if I'd have any money to spend.

examples.vi: Nó bảo trúng số à? Làm gì có, đùa thôi.
examples.en: He said he won the lottery? No way — he was just joking.

examples.vi: Thành phố này làm gì có tuyết bao giờ.
examples.en: This city never gets any snow at all.

units.title: sao mà…được — denying possibility
units.explanation: 'Sao mà … được' frames an action as impossible or unreasonable: 'how could (one) possibly…?'. The rhetorical question asserts that it cannot happen. 'Được' (be able/allowed) closes the frame and is obligatory. The bare variant 'sao … được' (without 'mà') is equally common and slightly more neutral.
units.note: 'Sao mà' has a second, unrelated use as an exclamation of degree ('Sao mà đẹp thế!' = 'How beautiful!'). The impossibility reading requires the closing '…được'; the exclamatory one does not.

examples.vi: Một mình anh sao mà làm hết đống việc này được.
examples.en: How could you possibly finish all this work on your own?

examples.vi: Trời mưa thế này thì sao mà đi chơi được.
examples.en: With rain like this, there's no way we can go out.

examples.vi: Nó nói nhanh quá, sao mà nghe kịp được.
examples.en: He talks too fast — how is anyone supposed to keep up?

examples.vi: Lương ba cọc ba đồng, sao mà sống được ở đây.
examples.en: On such a tiny salary, how could anyone manage to live here?

units.title: chẳng lẽ — reluctant disbelief
units.explanation: 'Chẳng lẽ' introduces a possibility the speaker finds hard to believe or accept, expecting the hearer to reject it: 'Surely it isn't the case that…?' / 'Don't tell me…'. It frequently combines with 'lại' to heighten the incredulity and may end in 'sao' or 'à'. It can also voice a dilemma the speaker is unwilling to face.
units.note: Although it ends a sentence like a question, 'chẳng lẽ' is rhetorical: it leans toward the negative answer. A genuine yes/no question would use 'có…không' instead. 'Chẳng lẽ anh quên?' expects 'no, he didn't', not real information.

examples.vi: Chẳng lẽ anh ấy lại nỡ bỏ rơi con mình?
examples.en: Surely he wouldn't have the heart to abandon his own child?

examples.vi: Đợi mãi không thấy ai, chẳng lẽ họ quên mất cuộc hẹn?
examples.en: No one's shown up — don't tell me they forgot the appointment?

examples.vi: Chẳng lẽ bao công sức bấy lâu lại đổ sông đổ bể sao?
examples.en: Surely all that effort isn't just going to go down the drain?

examples.vi: Hỏng xe rồi, chẳng lẽ giờ đi bộ về nhà?
examples.en: The car's broken down — am I really supposed to walk home now?

units.title: có…đâu — sentence-final refutation
units.explanation: The discontinuous frame 'có … đâu' refutes an assumption the listener is presumed to hold, scoping the negation over the whole predicate: 'but I didn't / it isn't, you know'. 'Có' opens and the clause-final 'đâu' closes the negation, often softening it into a mild protest or correction. It answers an unspoken or stated belief rather than a direct question.
units.note: Word order matters: 'đâu' must sit at the very end, after the object. 'Tôi có ăn cắp đâu' (I didn't steal — contrary to what you think) is correct; placing 'đâu' before the verb is ungrammatical. Compare neutral 'Tôi không ăn cắp' (a plain denial with no implied accusation).

examples.vi: Tôi có nói gì anh đâu, sao anh giận?
examples.en: I didn't say anything to you — why are you angry?

examples.vi: Cô ấy có biết lái xe đâu mà nhờ.
examples.en: She doesn't even know how to drive, so there's no point asking her.

examples.vi: Có xa xôi gì đâu, đi bộ năm phút là tới.
examples.en: It's not far at all — a five-minute walk and you're there.

examples.vi: Anh tưởng tôi quên à? Tôi có quên đâu.
examples.en: You thought I forgot? I didn't forget at all.

units.title: …làm gì — questioning the point of an action
units.explanation: Clause-final '…làm gì' challenges the purpose of an action, asserting it is pointless or unwarranted: 'what's the use of…?' / 'why bother…?'. It scopes over the verb it follows and implies the speaker thinks the action should not be done. Often paired with 'cho' ('…làm gì cho…') to add a consequence the speaker wants to avoid.
units.note: This sentence-final '…làm gì' (= 'what for / why bother') is distinct from clause-initial 'làm gì có' (denial) in Unit 1. Position is the key: at the end it questions purpose; before a noun it denies existence.

examples.vi: Mua nhiều đồ ăn làm gì cho phí, có ăn hết đâu.
examples.en: Why buy so much food and waste it — we'll never finish it.

examples.vi: Giận nó làm gì cho mệt người.
examples.en: What's the point of being angry at him? It only wears you out.

examples.vi: Biết rồi còn hỏi làm gì.
examples.en: You already know, so why even ask?

examples.vi: Lo xa làm gì, chuyện đâu còn có đó.
examples.en: Why worry so far ahead? Things will sort themselves out when the time comes.

modules.title: Modality & Stance: Certainty, Inference, and Discovery
modules.description: This C1 module teaches how Vietnamese marks epistemic stance — how confident the speaker is, whether a conclusion is inferred from evidence, and how a fact turns out to contradict an earlier assumption. You use these markers to sound nuanced and native rather than flatly factual, especially in opinion, narration, and discussion.
modules.mainPattern: chắc hẳn / hẳn là + clause (high-certainty inference); e rằng + clause (hedged concern); hóa ra / té ra + clause (discovery contrary to expectation)

faqs.question: What's the difference between 'chắc' and 'chắc hẳn'? They both seem to mean 'probably'.
faqs.answer: 'Chắc' is a soft, everyday guess — roughly 'probably / I think so' (Chắc anh ấy quên rồi — 'He probably forgot'). 'Chắc hẳn' (and 'hẳn là') is markedly stronger: it signals a confident inference the speaker has reasoned out from evidence, closer to English 'must / surely' (Đèn còn sáng, chắc hẳn anh ấy vẫn ở nhà — 'The light's still on, so he must still be home'). Use 'chắc' for casual hedging; reserve 'chắc hẳn' for conclusions you feel sure about.

faqs.question: Are 'hóa ra' and 'té ra' interchangeable?
faqs.answer: Semantically yes — both mean 'it turns out (that)', introducing a fact that overturns what you'd assumed. The difference is register: 'hóa ra' is neutral and works everywhere, including writing. 'Té ra' (and the variant 'thì ra') is more colloquial and Southern-flavored, common in speech and storytelling. In an essay or formal report, prefer 'hóa ra'.

units.title: chắc hẳn / hẳn là — confident inference
units.explanation: Use 'chắc hẳn' or 'hẳn là' to express a strong, evidence-based inference — the speaker is reasoning toward a conclusion they feel almost certain of, like English 'must (be)' or 'surely'. It is noticeably stronger than plain 'chắc' (a casual guess). 'Hẳn là' typically opens the clause; 'chắc hẳn' can sit before the subject or before the predicate.
units.note: Don't confuse this 'hẳn' with the intensifier 'hẳn' meaning 'completely/outright' (e.g. 'nghỉ hẳn việc' = quit the job altogether). The modal sense requires the inferential reading or the pairing 'hẳn là'.
