examples.vi: Trời tối thế này mà nó chưa về, chắc hẳn đã có chuyện gì rồi.
examples.en: It's this dark and he's still not back — something must have happened.

examples.vi: Hẳn là cô ấy rất giận, nếu không đã chẳng bỏ về sớm như vậy.
examples.en: She must be really angry; otherwise she wouldn't have left so early.

examples.vi: Anh ta nói tiếng Việt trôi chảy thế, chắc hẳn đã sống ở đây nhiều năm.
examples.en: He speaks Vietnamese so fluently — he must have lived here for years.

examples.vi: Bài thi khó như vậy, hẳn là ai cũng phải toát mồ hôi.
examples.en: With a test that hard, surely everyone broke out in a sweat.

units.title: e rằng — hedged apprehension
units.explanation: 'E rằng' (or 'e là', 'e ngại rằng') expresses a tentative fear or concern that something undesirable is or will be the case. It is a polite, slightly formal hedge — 'I'm afraid (that) / I worry (that)'. It softens bad news or a pessimistic forecast and signals the speaker's emotional stance, not just probability.
units.note: 'E rằng' almost always introduces something negative or unwelcome. Using it for good news sounds wrong. For neutral uncertainty, use 'có lẽ' or 'chắc'; reserve 'e rằng' for worry.

examples.vi: Với tình hình này, tôi e rằng dự án khó hoàn thành đúng hạn.
examples.en: Given the situation, I'm afraid the project will struggle to finish on time.

examples.vi: E rằng chúng ta đã đến quá muộn, cửa hàng đóng cửa mất rồi.
examples.en: I'm afraid we've come too late — the shop has already closed.

examples.vi: Ông ấy nói vậy, nhưng tôi e là sự thật không đơn giản như thế.
examples.en: He says so, but I'm afraid the truth isn't that simple.

examples.vi: Nếu cứ chủ quan, tôi e rằng hậu quả sẽ rất khó lường.
examples.en: If we stay complacent, I fear the consequences will be hard to predict.

units.title: hóa ra — discovery contrary to expectation
units.pattern: hóa ra + clause (often after a setup clause)
units.explanation: 'Hóa ra' introduces a fact the speaker has just realized, which contradicts or revises what they previously assumed — 'it turns out (that) / as it turns out'. It marks a shift from a prior belief to the real state of affairs, and frequently follows a clause describing the original assumption. Neutral in register and common in both speech and writing.
units.note: Pair it with the prior assumption for full effect: '...tưởng X, hóa ra Y' (I thought X, but it turns out Y). Standing alone it still works, but the contrast with an expectation is what gives 'hóa ra' its punch.

examples.vi: Tôi cứ tưởng anh ấy là người Hàn, hóa ra anh ấy là người Việt sinh ra ở Seoul.
examples.en: I'd assumed he was Korean — turns out he's Vietnamese, born in Seoul.

examples.vi: Tìm mãi không thấy chìa khóa, hóa ra nó nằm ngay trong túi áo.
examples.en: I searched forever for the key — turns out it was right in my jacket pocket.

examples.vi: Mọi người trách cô ấy vô tâm, hóa ra cô ấy đã âm thầm giúp đỡ từ lâu.
examples.en: Everyone blamed her for being indifferent; it turns out she'd been quietly helping all along.

examples.vi: Cứ ngỡ đề thi sẽ rất khó, hóa ra lại dễ hơn mình nghĩ nhiều.
examples.en: We figured the exam would be brutal — turns out it was much easier than expected.

units.title: té ra / thì ra — colloquial 'so that's why'
units.explanation: 'Té ra' (Southern/colloquial) and 'thì ra' are spoken variants of 'hóa ra'. They express the same sudden realization but carry a stronger flavor of 'aha, so THAT'S the reason' — the speaker connects a puzzling fact to its newly understood cause. Best in casual conversation and storytelling.
units.note: Register pitfall: 'té ra' is markedly informal and Southern-leaning. In formal writing or with strangers, switch to 'hóa ra'. 'Thì ra' is a touch more neutral than 'té ra' but still conversational.

examples.vi: Thảo nào dạo này nó cứ cười suốt, té ra là sắp cưới vợ.
examples.en: No wonder he's been grinning lately — turns out he's about to get married.

examples.vi: Thì ra cái mùi khét nãy giờ là do tôi quên tắt bếp.
examples.en: So that's what the burnt smell was — I'd forgotten to turn off the stove.

examples.vi: Hèn gì cửa mở sẵn, té ra mẹ về từ trưa rồi.
examples.en: No wonder the door was open — turns out Mom got back at noon.

examples.vi: Anh tìm tôi nãy giờ à? Thì ra là chuyện đó, tưởng gì nghiêm trọng.
examples.en: You've been looking for me? Oh, so it's about that — I thought it was something serious.

units.title: Stacking stance: from worry to realization
units.pattern: tưởng / e rằng ... → hóa ra / chắc hẳn ... (chained stance shift)
units.explanation: At C1, fluent speakers chain these markers across a discourse to track how their assessment evolves: an initial assumption or worry ('tưởng', 'e rằng'), then a revision ('hóa ra') or a firmed-up inference ('chắc hẳn'). Mastering the sequencing — not just each marker alone — is what makes narration and argument sound native.
units.note: Keep the markers consistent in register within one stretch of speech: mixing formal 'e rằng' with casual 'té ra' in the same breath sounds jarring unless done deliberately for effect.

examples.vi: Ban đầu tôi e rằng nó giận, nhưng hóa ra nó chỉ mệt nên ít nói thôi.
examples.en: At first I was afraid he was angry, but it turned out he was just tired and so spoke little.

examples.vi: Cả nhà cứ tưởng ông cụ lẫn, hóa ra ông nhớ mọi chuyện rõ hơn ai hết — chắc hẳn ông giả vờ quên cho yên thân.
examples.en: The whole family assumed the old man was senile; turns out he remembered everything better than anyone — he must have been feigning forgetfulness for some peace.

examples.vi: Tôi e là kế hoạch đã đổ bể, nào ngờ hóa ra mọi thứ vẫn đang đi đúng hướng.
examples.en: I feared the plan had fallen apart, but who'd have thought — it turns out everything was still on track.

examples.vi: Nghe tin đồn, ai cũng e rằng công ty sắp phá sản; hóa ra đó chỉ là tin thất thiệt, và chắc hẳn có người tung ra để trục lợi.
examples.en: Hearing the rumor, everyone feared the company was about to go bankrupt; it turned out to be false news, and surely someone spread it for profit.

levels.label: Mastery
levels.description: Idioms, Sino-Vietnamese compounds, reduplication, pragmatic particles, literary style and register-shifting — near-native command.

modules.title: Proverbs & idioms (thành ngữ, tục ngữ)
modules.description: This C2 module teaches the internal architecture of Vietnamese fixed sayings—how four- and six-part idioms (thành ngữ) and proverbs (tục ngữ) are built from balanced, parallel halves—and how to deploy them naturally in speech and writing without sounding stilted or misquoting them.
modules.mainPattern: [A B] // [C D] — paired four-syllable halves with syntactic parallelism and tonal balance (e.g., "ăn cây nào, rào cây nấy")

faqs.question: What's the actual difference between thành ngữ and tục ngữ, and does it matter when I use them?
faqs.answer: It matters for how you frame them. A thành ngữ is an idiom — a fixed phrase, not a full sentence, that functions like a vocabulary item inside your own clause. You weave it in grammatically: 'Anh ấy làm việc đầu voi đuôi chuột' (He works in a grand-start-small-finish way). A tục ngữ is a proverb — a complete, self-standing sentence expressing folk wisdom, which you usually quote whole and set off, often with 'các cụ có câu' (the elders have a saying) or 'ông bà ta thường nói': 'Ông bà ta thường nói: Có công mài sắt, có ngày nên kim' (Our forebears used to say: grind iron with effort and one day it becomes a needle). Rule of thumb: an idiom slots into your sentence; a proverb is its own sentence you cite.

faqs.question: How do I use a proverb without sounding like a textbook or an old person?
faqs.answer: Three habits make it natural. First, quote only the first half and let the listener complete it — Vietnamese speakers do this constantly: someone says 'Đi một ngày đàng...' and trails off, and everyone hears '...học một sàng khôn'. Second, frame it, don't dump it: 'Đúng là cha nào con nấy' (Truly, like father like son) lands better than firing the bare proverb. Third, match register — proverbs suit warm, reflective, or persuasive moments (advice, toasts, essays), not crisp transactional talk. Misquoting (wrong word, broken parallelism) is the fastest way to sound non-native, so learn each saying as an unbreakable unit.

units.title: The 2+2 four-syllable idiom (thành ngữ bốn chữ)
units.pattern: [A B] + [C D] — two two-syllable halves in parallel
units.explanation: The core unit of Vietnamese idiom is four syllables split into two balanced halves. Each half mirrors the other syntactically (verb+noun // verb+noun) and the two often contrast or escalate. The idiom is not a sentence; it behaves like an adjective or adverbial chunk that you insert into your own clause, typically after a noun it describes or as the predicate's complement. You never inflect or rearrange the four syllables — they are frozen.
units.note: Treat the four syllables as a single lexical block. Swapping in a synonym (e.g., saying 'đầu voi cuối chuột' instead of 'đầu voi đuôi chuột') breaks the fixed form and immediately marks you as a learner.

examples.vi: Dự án này đúng kiểu đầu voi đuôi chuột, lúc đầu rầm rộ, sau chẳng đâu vào đâu.
examples.en: This project is the classic elephant-head-rat-tail type — a roaring start, then nothing comes of it.

examples.vi: Cô ấy ăn nói nhỏ nhẹ nhưng làm việc thì nhanh như chớp.
examples.en: She speaks softly and gently, but she works as fast as lightning.

examples.vi: Hai anh em nó được nuôi dạy đến nơi đến chốn.
examples.en: The two brothers were raised properly, thoroughly to the end.

examples.vi: Cách giải quyết nửa vời ấy chẳng khác gì bắt cá hai tay.
examples.en: That half-hearted solution is no different from grabbing fish with both hands (trying to have it both ways).

units.title: Conditional/relational proverbs with the X nào … X nấy frame
units.explanation: A highly productive proverb pattern pairs the indefinite 'nào' (which/whichever) in the first half with the correlative 'nấy' (that very one) in the second. It encodes a tight cause-and-consequence or like-begets-like logic: whichever X you act on, that same X you get. The two halves are rigidly parallel — crucially, the same noun is repeated in both halves (cây…cây, cha…con as a fixed pair) — and 'nào … nấy' is the grammatical hinge that locks them together. These function as complete tục ngữ (self-standing sentences) but can also be folded into your speech with a framing word like 'đúng là' (truly).
units.note: 'Nấy' here is the correlative pronoun, not the everyday 'này' (this). Pronouncing or writing it as 'này' destroys the proverb. Keep the falling-then-rising contrast: nào (huyền) … nấy (sắc).

examples.vi: Ăn cây nào, rào cây nấy — đã hưởng lợi từ công ty thì phải có trách nhiệm với công ty.
examples.en: Eat from whichever tree, fence that very tree — if you benefit from the company, you owe it loyalty.

examples.vi: Đúng là cha nào con nấy, ông bố mê bóng đá thì thằng con cũng nghiện.
examples.en: Truly, like father like son — the dad is football-mad and the boy is hooked too.

examples.vi: Rau nào sâu nấy, đám bạn thế nào thì tính nó thế ấy.
examples.en: Each vegetable has its own pest — as the friends are, so the character turns out.

examples.vi: Ở bầu thì tròn, ở ống thì dài; gần người nào thì nhiễm tính người nấy.
examples.en: In a gourd you grow round, in a tube you grow long — whoever you keep close to, you take on that very person's character.

units.title: Six-eight (lục bát) proverbs and the comma-paired couplet
units.pattern: [6-syllable line] // [8-syllable line] OR [4 // 4] split by a comma, with tonal/rhyme balance
units.explanation: Many tục ngữ are built on rhythmic, quasi-poetic frames — either a lục bát couplet (a six-syllable line answered by an eight-syllable line, with internal rhyme) or a longer saying split by a comma into two weighted halves. The structure relies on rhyme and tonal contrast (bằng/trắc) to make the saying memorable and 'lockable.' Because the form is musical, the safest way to use these is to quote the whole couplet, ideally introduced as a citation, so the rhythm stays intact.
units.note: The rhyme is load-bearing: in 'Có công mài sắt, có ngày nên kim', the parallel 'có công … có ngày' and the imagery (sắt→kim) are fixed. Paraphrasing kills both the rhyme and the recognisability.

examples.vi: Bầu ơi thương lấy bí cùng, tuy rằng khác giống nhưng chung một giàn.
examples.en: Gourd, do love the squash — though of different kinds, you share one trellis (we should love one another despite differences).

examples.vi: Có công mài sắt, có ngày nên kim — cứ kiên trì luyện tập thì sẽ giỏi thôi.
examples.en: Grind iron with effort and one day it becomes a needle — keep practising patiently and you'll master it.

examples.vi: Ăn quả nhớ kẻ trồng cây, đó là đạo lý mà ai cũng nên nhớ.
examples.en: When you eat the fruit, remember who planted the tree — that's a principle everyone should keep in mind.

examples.vi: Một cây làm chẳng nên non, ba cây chụm lại nên hòn núi cao.
examples.en: One tree makes no grove; three trees clustered make a tall mountain (unity is strength).

units.title: Truncating a proverb — quoting only the first half
units.pattern: [first half] + … (let the hearer supply the rest)
units.explanation: A hallmark of native fluency is truncation: you utter only the opening half of a well-known proverb and trail off, trusting the listener to mentally complete it. This works precisely because the form is fixed and the two halves are inseparable, so the missing half is unambiguous. It signals shared cultural knowledge and an in-group, conversational tone — far more natural than reciting the whole saying. Mark the cut-off in writing with an ellipsis (…) and in speech with a falling, suggestive intonation.
units.note: Only truncate proverbs that are genuinely famous and unambiguous; truncating an obscure saying just leaves the listener stranded. Also, the half you give must be the canonical first half — you can't lead with the second half.

examples.vi: Thôi, đi một ngày đàng… cứ đi đi rồi sẽ học được nhiều.
examples.en: Come on, 'a day on the road…' — just go and you'll learn a great deal (…learn a basketful of wisdom).

examples.vi: Nó vừa mới khoe là chắc chắn đỗ, mà gieo gió thì…
examples.en: He just boasted he'd surely pass — but sow the wind and… (…reap the storm).

examples.vi: Anh đừng vội tin, tin người quá thì…
examples.en: Don't be quick to trust — trust people too much and… (you'll suffer for it).

examples.vi: Đời cha ăn mặn… nên cẩn thận với những gì mình làm hôm nay.
examples.en: 'The father eats salty…' — so be careful about what you do today (…the child goes thirsty).

units.title: Embedding an idiom as a predicate or adverbial via 'như', 'kiểu', 'theo kiểu'
units.pattern: Subject + (làm/sống/đối xử) + như / kiểu / theo kiểu + [thành ngữ]
units.explanation: To fold a four-syllable idiom into a normal sentence smoothly, Vietnamese uses light connectors: 'như' (like/as) for similes, and 'kiểu / theo kiểu' (in the manner of) to frame an idiom as a style of behaviour. This lets the frozen idiom act as a manner adverbial or predicate complement without grammatical friction. It is the standard, register-neutral way to use thành ngữ in everyday and written prose, and it keeps the idiom intact while clearly subordinating it to your own clause.
units.note: Don't stack two idioms in one breath ('vừa … vừa' with two idioms) unless you intend a heightened rhetorical effect — in ordinary speech it sounds overwrought. One idiom per clause is the natural ceiling.

examples.vi: Anh ta đối xử với nhân viên theo kiểu vắt chanh bỏ vỏ.
examples.en: He treats his staff in the squeeze-the-lemon-throw-away-the-rind manner (uses people then discards them).

examples.vi: Cứ làm kiểu được chăng hay chớ thì không bao giờ thành công đâu.
examples.en: Keep working in that take-it-or-leave-it, careless way and you'll never succeed.

examples.vi: Họ sống với nhau như cá với nước.
examples.en: They live together like fish and water (inseparable, in perfect harmony).

examples.vi: Đừng có nói kiểu nước đôi như thế, hãy trả lời thẳng vào.
examples.en: Don't speak in that two-sided, hedging way — answer directly.

modules.title: Sino-Vietnamese four-character compounds
modules.description: This module teaches thành ngữ Hán-Việt — fixed four-syllable expressions borrowed from Classical Chinese — covering their internal grammatical architecture (parallelism, antithesis, subject-predicate framing) and the formal, literary register in which educated Vietnamese deploy them. It is aimed at advanced learners who already read newspapers and want to write and speak with the density and authority expected in editorials, speeches, and academic prose.
modules.mainPattern: [Hán-Việt 2 + Hán-Việt 2] = a balanced 2+2 four-syllable idiom (e.g. an cư + lạc nghiệp), used as a standalone clause or noun-like chunk in formal register

faqs.question: How do I tell a fixed Sino-Vietnamese four-character idiom (thành ngữ Hán-Việt) from just four Hán-Việt words strung together?
faqs.answer: A true thành ngữ Hán-Việt is lexicalised: it has a fixed order, a non-compositional or culturally conventional meaning, and a 2+2 prosodic balance you cannot rearrange. 'An cư lạc nghiệp' cannot become 'lạc nghiệp an cư' and means more than the sum of its parts (a whole settled life). By contrast, a free combination like 'phát triển kinh tế' (develop the economy) is just two ordinary disyllables and can be paraphrased or reordered freely. Test it: if swapping the halves or substituting a synonym breaks it, it is a fixed idiom.

faqs.question: Are these idioms understood in everyday speech, or only by educated people?
faqs.answer: The common ones — 'an cư lạc nghiệp', 'đồng cam cộng khổ', 'quốc thái dân an' — are widely understood across the population because they recur in news, songs, and Tết greetings. Rarer literary ones (e.g. 'thượng vàng hạ cám') may puzzle some listeners. The safe rule for a learner: deploy the high-frequency ones in formal writing or speeches, and in casual conversation prefer a plain paraphrase, e.g. 'gắn bó lúc khó khăn' instead of 'đồng cam cộng khổ', unless you specifically want a literary tone.

units.title: The 2+2 parallel frame (tiểu đối)
units.pattern: [V/Adj + N] + [V/Adj + N] → two mirrored disyllabic halves
units.explanation: The prototypical thành ngữ Hán-Việt splits into two two-syllable units that mirror each other grammatically: each half is typically a verb-or-adjective + noun pair, and the two halves stand in parallel (đối). 'An cư lạc nghiệp' = an (settle) cư (dwelling) // lạc (delight in) nghiệp (occupation): 'settle one's home and find joy in one's work.' Recognising this 2+2 spine lets you parse, and even coin, these compounds rather than memorising them as opaque blocks. The whole behaves syntactically like a single predicate or an abstract noun.
units.note: Word order is Sino-Vietnamese (verb-object internally, Chinese-style head order), so you cannot translate the four syllables one-by-one into native Vietnamese order. 'Lạc nghiệp' means 'enjoy [one's] occupation', not 'occupation enjoys'.

examples.vi: Sau bao năm tha hương, ông chỉ mong an cư lạc nghiệp nơi quê nhà.
examples.en: After so many years living far from home, he wishes only to settle down and live contentedly with his work back in his native village.

examples.vi: Chính sách mới hướng tới mục tiêu giúp người dân an cư lạc nghiệp.
examples.en: The new policy aims to help citizens settle their homes and find fulfilment in their livelihoods.

examples.vi: Có an cư thì mới lạc nghiệp được; nhà cửa chưa ổn thì khó mà yên tâm làm ăn.
examples.en: Only once you have a settled home can you enjoy your work; with housing still unstable it is hard to work with peace of mind.

examples.vi: Cả đời họ lam lũ cũng chỉ vì bốn chữ an cư lạc nghiệp.
examples.en: Their whole life of toil came down to just those four words: a settled home and a contented livelihood.

units.title: Antithetical compounds (đối nghĩa)
units.pattern: [A ... B] where the two halves are semantic opposites → totality or contrast
units.explanation: A large class of four-character idioms is built on antithesis: the two halves contain opposed concepts, and the contrast itself carries the meaning. 'Đồng cam cộng khổ' pairs cam (sweetness) against khổ (bitterness) — 'to share the sweet and bear the bitter together', i.e. to go through thick and thin. 'Bán tín bán nghi' (half-believe, half-doubt) and 'thượng vàng hạ cám' (gold above, bran below = goods of every grade) work the same way. The opposed pair often signals completeness ('the whole spectrum from X to Y') or wavering between two states.
units.note: Do not 'repair' the antithesis by making both halves positive. 'Đồng cam cộng khổ' must keep the bitter half; saying only the sweet half destroys the idiom and the sentiment of shared hardship.

examples.vi: Vợ chồng họ đã đồng cam cộng khổ suốt mấy chục năm trời.
examples.en: That couple has shared every joy and hardship together for several decades.

examples.vi: Nghe lời giải thích đó, tôi vẫn bán tín bán nghi.
examples.en: Hearing that explanation, I remained half-convinced, half-doubtful.

examples.vi: Cửa hàng bày bán đủ thứ, thượng vàng hạ cám đều có cả.
examples.en: The shop sells everything, goods of every grade from the finest to the cheapest.

examples.vi: Là người lãnh đạo, ông sẵn sàng đồng cam cộng khổ với anh em công nhân.
examples.en: As a leader, he was ready to share both the good times and the hardships with the workers.

units.title: Subject-predicate idioms (chủ-vị)
units.pattern: [N1 + V/Adj] + [N2 + V/Adj] → two miniature sentences fused into one image
units.explanation: Some four-character compounds are not noun-phrases but two compressed clauses, each with its own subject and predicate, juxtaposed to paint a single scene. 'Quốc thái dân an' = quốc (nation) thái (at peace) // dân (people) an (secure): 'the nation is at peace and the people are secure.' 'Quốc phú dân cường' = quốc (nation) phú (prosperous) // dân (people) cường (strong): 'a prosperous nation and a strong people.' Because each half is a tiny clause, these idioms function as complete propositions and are favoured in wishes, slogans, and ceremonial language.
units.note: These are read as a fused unit, not as a running sentence — do not insert connectors or particles ('là', 'thì', 'và') between the halves. The asyndetic juxtaposition is exactly what marks the elevated register.

examples.vi: Đầu năm, người ta thường cầu cho quốc thái dân an.
examples.en: At the start of the year, people commonly pray for the nation to be at peace and the people secure.

examples.vi: Toàn dân ra sức xây dựng đất nước theo mục tiêu quốc phú dân cường.
examples.en: The whole people strive to build the country toward the goal of a prosperous nation and a strong populace.

examples.vi: Triều đại ấy được ca ngợi là thời kỳ quốc thái dân an, mưa thuận gió hòa.
examples.en: That dynasty is praised as an era of national peace, secure people, and favourable weather.

examples.vi: Ai cũng mong một ngày nước nhà quốc phú dân cường, sánh vai cùng các cường quốc.
examples.en: Everyone hopes for the day the nation grows prosperous and its people strong, standing shoulder to shoulder with the great powers.

units.title: Register and collocation: when (not) to deploy them
units.pattern: [formal context] + thành ngữ Hán-Việt → density and authority; [casual context] → marked / pompous
units.explanation: Four-character Hán-Việt idioms belong to the high register: editorials, speeches, congratulatory couplets, eulogies, legal and academic prose, and deliberately literary speech. Used aptly they compress a whole proposition into four resonant syllables and project erudition. Used in casual chat they sound stiff, archaic, or pretentious — a native speaker would switch to a plain Vietnamese paraphrase. Mastery at C2 is therefore as much about register-matching and frequency as about meaning: knowing that 'an cư lạc nghiệp' fits a policy speech, while over a beer you would just say 'có nhà cửa ổn định, công việc đàng hoàng'.
units.note: Avoid stacking several four-character idioms in one sentence unless writing a deliberately ornate text (e.g. a tribute) — in ordinary prose, two or more in a row reads as showing off (sáo rỗng, 'hollow and clichéd').

examples.vi: Trong bài diễn văn, ông trích dẫn câu thành ngữ một cách rất đắt giá.
examples.en: In his speech he quoted the idiom to powerful effect.

examples.vi: Viết báo cáo khoa học mà dùng quá nhiều thành ngữ Hán-Việt sẽ thành ra sáo rỗng.
examples.en: Using too many Sino-Vietnamese idioms in a scientific report ends up sounding hollow and clichéd.

examples.vi: Nói chuyện đời thường mà cứ 'tâm đầu ý hợp' với 'môn đăng hộ đối' thì nghe khách sáo lắm.
examples.en: Throwing around 'kindred spirits' and 'matched households' in everyday chat comes across as very stilted.

examples.vi: Câu đối ngày Tết thường dùng thành ngữ Hán-Việt để chúc tụng.
examples.en: Lunar New Year parallel couplets typically use Sino-Vietnamese idioms to convey good wishes.

modules.title: Reduplication for nuance (từ láy)
modules.description: A C2-level study of Vietnamese reduplicatives (từ láy) as a tool for fine-grained stylistic control: softening adjectives, intensifying them, and exploiting sound symbolism. It is the resource you reach for when you want to sound like a native writer rather than merely be understood, especially in descriptive prose, literature, and expressive speech.
modules.mainPattern: root + reduplicant (full / partial: alliterative láy âm or rhyming láy vần) → attenuation, intensification, or sound-symbolic colour

faqs.question: How do I know whether a reduplicative softens or intensifies the base word? They look identical in form.
faqs.answer: You can't tell from the reduplication mechanism alone — you have to learn the lexeme, because the same root behaves differently in different pairs. As a strong heuristic, attenuating pairs usually keep the root's tone register level and add a 'spread out, a little bit' feeling (đỏ → đo đỏ = reddish, a touch red), while intensifying pairs add an emphatic, often vivid second syllable (đỏ → đỏ rực = blazing red; đỏ chót = glaringly red). When the reduplicant is a meaningless echo syllable that lowers the pitch, expect attenuation (khác → khang khác = slightly different). When the second syllable is itself a vivid descriptive morpheme, expect intensification. The safest path at C2 is to treat high-frequency pairs as fixed vocabulary and check a dictionary's register notes.

faqs.question: Are từ láy acceptable in formal writing, or are they colloquial?
faqs.answer: They are fully acceptable and in fact prized in formal descriptive and literary registers — Vietnamese newspaper feature writing, essays, and especially poetry lean heavily on them for rhythm and imagery (lác đác, mênh mông, thăm thẳm). What you should avoid in formal prose is the chatty, expressive intensifiers and onomatopoeia of casual speech (ví dụ: đẹp ơi là đẹp, sạch bong, im thin thít in a legal memo). So the dividing line is not 'reduplication vs no reduplication' but which register a given pair belongs to.

units.title: Attenuating adjective reduplication (đo đỏ, tim tím)
units.pattern: X (adj.) → X' X  (echo syllable, often tone-lowered) = 'somewhat / -ish'
units.explanation: Reduplicating a colour or quality adjective with a partial echo syllable softens it to mean 'somewhat X, a little X, X-ish, X here and there'. The echo syllable typically takes a level/lower tone than the root and carries no independent meaning. This is a highly native device for hedging an adjective — often more idiomatic than hơi X ('a bit X'), which can sound flat or clinical. Note that the echo syllable usually precedes the root and undergoes tone change: đỏ → đo đỏ, tím → tim tím, vàng → vàng vàng, xinh → xinh xinh, tối → tôi tối.
units.note: This pattern is restricted to a learnable set of adjectives; you cannot freely coin *to to from to (big) — the idiomatic attenuator is hơi to or to to (with a softening, repeated form for some speakers). Memorise the attested pairs rather than generating them.

examples.vi: Cái áo này màu đo đỏ chứ không đỏ hẳn.
examples.en: This shirt is reddish rather than fully red.

examples.vi: Cô bé có gương mặt xinh xinh, dễ thương.
examples.en: The little girl has a cutish, endearing face.

examples.vi: Trời đã tôi tối, chúng ta nên về thôi.
examples.en: It's getting a bit dark out; we'd better head home.

examples.vi: Bầu trời chiều ngả sang màu tim tím trông rất dịu.
examples.en: The evening sky turned a soft purplish hue, very gentle.

units.title: Intensifying reduplication with a vivid second syllable (đỏ chót, sạch bong)
units.pattern: X (adj.) + Y (vivid descriptive morpheme) = 'intensely / utterly X'
units.explanation: In contrast to attenuation, intensifying reduplicatives pair the root with a second syllable that pushes the quality to its extreme. The second element is often a near-meaningless but highly collocational morpheme bound to one specific root, so each pair is essentially a fixed superlative: đỏ chót (glaringly red), trắng tinh (spotlessly white), đen sì (jet black), sạch bong (squeaky clean), thẳng tắp (dead straight), no nê (stuffed full), mới tinh (brand new). Choosing the correct partner syllable for each adjective is a hallmark of advanced fluency; the wrong partner is immediately non-native.
units.note: The bound partner is root-specific and not transferable: it is trắng tinh / trắng muốt / trắng phau but never *đỏ tinh. Learn each adjective together with its idiomatic intensifier(s).

examples.vi: Đôi môi tô son đỏ chót trông rất nổi bật.
examples.en: Her lips, painted a glaring red, stood out sharply.

examples.vi: Sàn nhà lau sạch bong, không một hạt bụi.
examples.en: The floor was scrubbed squeaky clean, not a speck of dust.

examples.vi: Con đường mới làm thẳng tắp đến tận chân trời.
examples.en: The newly built road runs dead straight to the horizon.

examples.vi: Ăn xong ba bát cơm, nó đã no nê nằm thở.
examples.en: After three bowls of rice, he lay there utterly stuffed.

units.title: Onomatopoeic and sound-symbolic reduplicatives (rì rào, lác đác, ào ào)
units.pattern: (full or rhyming) reduplicant evoking sound, motion, or scattered distribution
units.explanation: A large class of từ láy encodes sound symbolism: the phonetic shape imitates or evokes the sensation. These function as adverbs or predicates and are indispensable in descriptive writing. Recurring sound-symbolic schemas include continuous soft sound (rì rào — rustling/murmuring, thì thầm — whispering), heavy continuous motion (ào ào — gushing/pouring, ầm ầm — rumbling/thundering), and sparse scattered distribution (lác đác — scattered/sporadic, lấm tấm — speckled, lốm đốm — spotted). Vowel quality is meaningful: high front vowels (i, ê) suggest small/light/high-pitched, low back vowels (a, o, u) suggest large/heavy/low-pitched — compare lí nhí (tiny mumbling) with ào ào (a great gushing).
units.note: Sound-symbolic láy are mostly fixed lexemes, not productively coined — and many are strongly tied to one referent (rì rào fits leaves/waves/streams but not, say, a crowd, for which you'd use rì rầm or xôn xao).

examples.vi: Gió thổi qua rặng tre nghe rì rào suốt đêm.
examples.en: The wind through the bamboo rustled softly all night long.

examples.vi: Mưa bắt đầu rơi lác đác rồi đổ ào ào.
examples.en: The rain began falling in scattered drops, then came pouring down.

examples.vi: Hai đứa thì thầm với nhau điều gì đó trong góc lớp.
examples.en: The two of them whispered something to each other in the corner of the class.

examples.vi: Mặt nước trong veo lấm tấm những đốm nắng.
examples.en: The crystal-clear water was speckled with little spots of sunlight.

units.title: Three- and four-syllable expressive reduplication (sạch sành sanh, lôi thôi lếch thếch)
units.pattern: three-syllable láy ba (X X' X'') / four-syllable láy tư (AB → A A' B B' or A B A' B')
units.explanation: Beyond the basic two-syllable form, Vietnamese builds longer reduplicatives for heightened, often emotive or pejorative emphasis. Láy ba (three syllables) maximises a quality: sạch sành sanh (utterly cleaned out / not a thing left), dửng dừng dưng (completely indifferent). Láy tư (four syllables) typically expands a two-syllable base by reduplicating each half: lôi thôi → lôi thôi lếch thếch (a complete shambles, slovenly), hớt hơ hớt hải (in a frantic panic), ấp a ấp úng (stammering and tongue-tied). These belong to vivid, expressive, often colloquial registers and convey the speaker's evaluative attitude as much as a description.
units.note: Four-syllable láy carry strong affect — usually mockery, exasperation, or vivid disorder — so they are pragmatically marked. Dropping one into neutral or formal prose reads as sarcasm or as a register slip.

examples.vi: Trộm vào nhà khoắng sạch sành sanh, chẳng chừa thứ gì.
examples.en: Burglars cleaned the house out completely, leaving nothing behind.

examples.vi: Nó ăn mặc lôi thôi lếch thếch, đầu tóc rối bù.
examples.en: He was dressed in a total shambles, his hair all in a tangle.

examples.vi: Nghe tin dữ, bà chạy hớt hơ hớt hải ra cổng.
examples.en: On hearing the bad news, she rushed to the gate in a frantic panic.

examples.vi: Bị hỏi bất ngờ, cậu ta ấp a ấp úng không nói nên lời.
examples.en: Caught off guard by the question, he stammered and couldn't get a word out.

modules.title: Sentence-final pragmatic particles
modules.description: A C2-level study of Vietnamese clause-final particles (tiểu từ tình thái cuối câu) that carry no propositional meaning but encode stance, politeness, contradiction and emotional alignment. Learners master how chứ, mà, đấy, cơ, ấy, nhé, nha and đi reshape the social register and illocutionary force of an otherwise identical sentence.
modules.mainPattern: [Câu / clause] + tiểu từ tình thái (chứ / mà / đấy / cơ / ấy / nhé / nha / đi)

faqs.question: How do I tell sentence-final stance particles apart from the homophonous conjunctions chứ and mà?
faqs.answer: Use position and prosody. The stance particle is the very last element of the utterance and is not followed by another clause: 'Anh biết chứ.' (You know it, of course) / 'Em bảo rồi mà.' (I told you, after all). The conjunctions, by contrast, link two clauses and sit medially: 'Tôi đùa chứ không nói thật.' (I'm joking, not being serious) / 'Nhà đẹp mà đắt.' (The house is nice but expensive). If you can delete the particle and the sentence still ends grammatically — only the attitude is lost — it is the pragmatic particle.

faqs.question: Can I stack several particles, and does order matter?
faqs.answer: Yes, stacking is common and the order is fixed, moving from propositional emphasis to interpersonal appeal: e.g. 'rồi đấy nhé' (đấy flags the news, nhé seeks your agreement) or 'thế cơ à' (cơ marks the surprising alternative, à the question). You cannot reorder them ('nhé đấy' is wrong). A safe C2 rule: attention/insistence particles (đấy, cơ, mà) come first, then alignment/question particles (nhé, nha, à) close the chain.

units.title: chứ — affirming the obvious / reproachful expectation
units.explanation: Final-particle chứ asserts something the speaker treats as self-evident or expected, often with a tinge of 'of course' or mild reproach that the listener even had to ask. With a rising contour it can also turn a statement into a confirmation-seeking question ('right?'). It presupposes shared ground and pushes back gently against doubt.
units.note: Do not confuse this stance particle with conjunction chứ ('but rather', as in 'tôi nói thật chứ không đùa'). The pragmatic particle sits at the very end of the clause and cannot be followed by a second clause; the conjunction must introduce one.

examples.vi: Anh đi với em chứ?
examples.en: You're coming with me, right? (I assume you are)

examples.vi: Đương nhiên là tôi biết chứ, hỏi gì lạ thế.
examples.en: Of course I know that — what a strange thing to ask.

examples.vi: Ngon chứ còn gì nữa, đầu bếp giỏi nhất vùng mà.
examples.en: Delicious, obviously — he's the best chef in the region, after all.

examples.vi: — Cậu làm được không? — Được chứ!
examples.en: — Can you do it? — Of course I can!

units.title: mà — appealing to a shared or established premise
units.explanation: Clause-final mà flags the proposition as a reminder or justification the listener ought already to accept — 'but I told you', 'after all', 'you know how it is'. It softens insistence by framing the point as common knowledge rather than a fresh claim, and is the natural particle for defending oneself or coaxing.
units.note: Sentence-final mà (stance, falling intonation) is distinct from clause-medial concessive/contrastive mà ('nhà thì đẹp mà đắt'). Beginners often hear only the conjunction; at C2 you must keep the two registers apart by position and prosody.

examples.vi: Em đã bảo anh rồi mà.
examples.en: But I already told you (so don't blame me).

examples.vi: Mua đi, có đắt lắm đâu mà.
examples.en: Just buy it — it's not that expensive, you know.

examples.vi: Thôi đừng giận, anh chỉ đùa thôi mà.
examples.en: Come on, don't be upset — I was only joking, after all.

examples.vi: Cô ấy hát hay là phải, dân chuyên nghiệp mà.
examples.en: No wonder she sings well — she's a professional, after all.

units.title: đấy / ấy — drawing attention and flagging noteworthiness
units.pattern: [Mệnh đề] + đấy (warning / new info) ‖ [Danh ngữ / mệnh đề] + ấy (downtoning / vague reference)
units.explanation: Final đấy spotlights the clause as newsworthy, a warning, or a fact the listener should take note of ('mind you', 'I'm telling you'). Final ấy, by contrast, downtones — it softens an assertion, hedges a reference, or trails off as if the matter is understood ('you know the one', 'sort of'). The pair shows opposite ends of the attention scale.
units.note: Northern đấy corresponds to Southern đó; both can be sharpened into a threat ('liệu hồn đấy!'). Particle ấy must not be read as the demonstrative 'that' here — it is purely a hedging/softening device and carries no deictic weight.

examples.vi: Cẩn thận đấy, đường trơn lắm!
examples.en: Be careful, mind you — the road is very slippery!

examples.vi: Tôi nói trước rồi đấy nhé, đừng có trách.
examples.en: I'm warning you in advance — don't blame me later.

examples.vi: Cái hôm họp ấy, anh nhớ không?
examples.en: That meeting the other day — you know the one — do you remember?

examples.vi: Cái cô ấy là ai ấy nhỉ, tôi quên mất tên rồi.
examples.en: That woman — who was she again — I've forgotten her name.

units.title: cơ — insisting on a preferred alternative (petulant want)
units.pattern: [Điều mong muốn] + cơ (≠ cái được đưa ra)
units.explanation: Final cơ rejects what has been offered and insists on something else the speaker actually wants. It carries an affective, often childlike or coquettish 'I want X, not that' flavour, and presupposes a prior proposal that is being turned down. It is intimate and is avoided in formal speech.
units.note: cơ requires a contrastive context — it cannot open a topic out of nowhere. Combined as 'cơ mà' it becomes a colloquial 'but/however'; do not blend that conjunction sense with the stand-alone insistence particle.

examples.vi: Em không thích cái màu này, em thích màu hồng cơ.
examples.en: I don't like this colour — I want the pink one (not that).

examples.vi: — Mai đi nhé. — Không, hôm nay cơ!
examples.en: — Let's go tomorrow. — No, today! (I insist)

examples.vi: Con muốn mẹ kể chuyện kia cơ.
examples.en: I want you to tell that other story, Mum (not this one).

examples.vi: Đắt thế mà anh ấy vẫn mua những ba cái cơ.
examples.en: Even at that price he went and bought as many as three, no less.

units.title: nhé / nha / đi — managing directives and seeking alignment
units.pattern: [Đề nghị / mệnh lệnh nhẹ] + nhé / nha ‖ [Mệnh lệnh] + đi
units.explanation: These particles tune the force of directives. nhé seeks the listener's agreement and softens a request, suggestion or promise into something collaborative ('okay?'); nha is its warm, Southern-flavoured equivalent. đi, by contrast, energises an imperative into an urging or encouragement ('go on, do it'). Choosing among them, and stacking them (đi nhé), calibrates politeness and warmth precisely.
units.note: đi alone can sound blunt or impatient to a superior; pair it with nhé/nha or a kinship term to stay polite. nhé attached to a first-person statement turns it into a commitment ('mai em gọi nhé' = I'll call tomorrow, okay?), not a command — a distinction learners frequently miss.

examples.vi: Mình đi ăn lẩu nhé?
examples.en: Let's go eat hotpot, shall we?

examples.vi: Nghỉ ngơi đi, trông cậu mệt lắm rồi.
examples.en: Go and rest — you look really worn out.

examples.vi: Chiều em ghé qua nha, đừng đi đâu đấy nhé.
examples.en: I'll drop by this afternoon, okay — make sure you don't go anywhere.

examples.vi: Cố lên đi, sắp đến đích rồi nhé!
examples.en: Keep going — we're almost at the finish, come on!

modules.title: Literary Inversion & Ellipsis
modules.description: This C2 module covers the marked word-order operations of literary Vietnamese: fronting predicates and complements for emphasis, chaining topic-comment structures, and omitting recoverable elements (subjects, copulas, connectors) for compression and rhetorical effect. These patterns belong to poetry, narrative prose, journalism, and elevated speech rather than neutral conversation.
modules.mainPattern: [Predicate/Complement]-fronting + (topic) + comment, with ellipsis of recoverable elements (subject, copula, connectors)

faqs.question: When is it stylistically acceptable to drop the subject in Vietnamese, and how is that different from a beginner just leaving it out?
faqs.answer: Beginners drop the subject when context makes it obvious (e.g. answering 'Đi đâu đấy?' with 'Đi chợ'). Literary ellipsis is a deliberate device: the subject is withheld across a whole passage to create immediacy, suspense, or a roaming 'camera' viewpoint. In narrative prose you'll see chains like 'Mở cửa. Bước ra. Đứng lặng một hồi lâu.' (Opened the door. Stepped out. Stood still for a long while.) — no subject is restated because the writer wants the actions, not the actor, in focus. Note the nuance: this works only when the referent is unambiguous from earlier context; reintroduce the subject the moment reference could shift, or the reader gets lost.

faqs.question: Is fronting in Vietnamese the same as English 'inversion' where the verb and subject swap?
faqs.answer: No — Vietnamese has no subject-verb inversion like English 'Never have I seen...'. Vietnamese 'inversion' is really fronting (topicalization): you move a constituent to the front for emphasis but the core word order does not flip. For example you front a predicate adjective for vividness: 'Đẹp! Đẹp đến nao lòng.' (Beautiful! Beautiful enough to break the heart.), or front an object: 'Cái giá ấy, tôi không trả nổi.' (That price, I can't afford.) The subject 'tôi' stays before its verb; only the object has been displaced to the front and is often echoed or resumed.

units.title: Predicate fronting for emphasis
units.explanation: In neutral Vietnamese the order is Subject-Predicate. For emphatic or evaluative effect, literary style fronts the predicate (an adjective, stative verb, or descriptive phrase) to the head of the clause, leaving the subject — if stated at all — to follow, frequently after 'thì' or 'là'. This throws the spotlight onto the quality or action and is a hallmark of poetry, exclamation, and lyrical prose.
units.note: Do not overuse with an explicit 'thì'/'là' in every sentence — in verse the marker is usually dropped entirely ('Lạnh lùng gió bấc' rather than 'Lạnh lùng thì gió bấc'). Inserting the marker makes it read as analytical prose, not poetry.

examples.vi: Đẹp vô cùng, Tổ quốc ta ơi!
examples.en: Beautiful beyond measure, oh our Motherland!

examples.vi: Lác đác bên sông chợ mấy nhà.
examples.en: Scattered along the river are a few market houses.

examples.vi: Buồn trông cửa bể chiều hôm.
examples.en: Sorrowfully she gazes at the sea-mouth in the evening.

examples.vi: Mênh mông là biển, bao la là trời.
examples.en: Vast is the sea, boundless is the sky.

units.title: Object / complement fronting with resumption
units.explanation: A complement or object can be lifted to clause-initial position as a contrastive or emphatic topic. The remainder of the clause keeps normal Subject-Verb order, so the fronted element is interpreted as 'as for X...'. Often the displaced item is resumed later by a pronoun or classifier, or marked off by 'thì'. This is the standard way to set one element against another or to foreground new-but-anchored information.
units.note: The fronted item must be discourse-anchored (definite or already in play). Fronting a brand-new indefinite ('Một quyển sách, tôi mua') sounds odd; use it for items the listener can already identify.

examples.vi: Việc đó thì tôi đã làm xong từ lâu rồi.
examples.en: That task — I finished it long ago.

examples.vi: Tiền bạc, nó coi nhẹ; danh dự, nó coi trọng.
examples.en: Money, he holds lightly; honour, he holds dear.

examples.vi: Cái áo này thì để tôi giặt cho.
examples.en: This shirt — let me wash it for you.

examples.vi: Những lời ấy, tôi không bao giờ quên được.
examples.en: Those words, I can never forget.

units.title: Topic-comment chaining (zero-anaphora chains)
units.explanation: Literary Vietnamese strings together a sequence of topic-comment clauses in which the topic, once established, is dropped (zero anaphora) in following clauses. The result is a flowing 'chain' where each comment adds a new layer about the same topic without grammatical re-linking, producing a compact, cumulative rhythm typical of descriptive prose and reportage. The relationship between clauses is inferred, not spelled out by conjunctions.
units.note: The chain holds together only while the topic stays constant. The instant the referent changes you must re-establish a new topic explicitly, otherwise the reader will wrongly carry the old one forward — the most common comprehension trap in this style.

examples.vi: Làng tôi nghèo, đất cằn, người thưa, quanh năm bám lấy mấy sào ruộng.
examples.en: My village is poor — the soil barren, the people few, year-round clinging to a few plots of paddy.

examples.vi: Nó ngồi đó, mắt nhìn xa xăm, tay run run, chẳng nói một lời.
examples.en: He sat there, eyes gazing into the distance, hands trembling, not saying a word.

examples.vi: Con sông quê hương, nước trong veo, đôi bờ tre rủ bóng.
examples.en: The river of my homeland — its water crystal clear, both banks draped in bamboo shade.

examples.vi: Hà Nội mùa thu, cây cơm nguội vàng, cây bàng lá đỏ.
examples.en: Hanoi in autumn — the cơm nguội trees golden, the almond trees with leaves gone red.

units.title: Subject ellipsis across narrative action chains
units.explanation: Once a subject is established, narrative prose can omit it across a whole run of clauses or even short sentences, presenting bare predicates in sequence. This 'camera' technique foregrounds the actions and quickens the pace, giving an effect of immediacy or breathlessness. It is a marked, deliberate device, distinct from ordinary conversational subject-drop, and is sustained over longer stretches.
units.note: This is safe only with a single, unambiguous agent. If a second participant could perform any of the verbs, the chain becomes ambiguous and you must reinsert the subject. Vietnamese has no agreement to disambiguate, so the burden falls entirely on context.

examples.vi: Mở cửa. Bước ra. Đứng lặng một hồi lâu.
examples.en: Opened the door. Stepped out. Stood still for a long while.

examples.vi: Lặng lẽ thu dọn hành lý, khoá cửa, rồi đi thẳng ra ga.
examples.en: Quietly packed the luggage, locked the door, then walked straight to the station.

examples.vi: Cúi đầu, lau vội nước mắt, gượng cười.
examples.en: Bowed her head, hastily wiped away the tears, forced a smile.

examples.vi: Chạy. Vấp ngã. Lồm cồm bò dậy. Lại chạy.
examples.en: Ran. Tripped and fell. Scrambled up on all fours. Ran again.

units.title: Ellipsis of copula and connectors in compressed style
units.explanation: Elevated and aphoristic Vietnamese routinely omits the copula 'là' between two nominals and drops coordinating or contrastive connectors ('và', 'nhưng', 'thì'), leaving the relationship to be inferred from juxtaposition. The result is terse, balanced, often parallel structures characteristic of proverbs, headlines, slogans, and gnomic prose, where compression itself carries rhetorical weight.
units.note: Dropping 'là' is natural before a nominal predicate in maxims ('Thời gian là vàng bạc' compressed to 'Thời gian, vàng bạc') but ungrammatical in ordinary identifying sentences — you cannot say '*Tôi sinh viên' in normal speech for 'I am a student'. Restrict copula-ellipsis to genuinely aphoristic or telegraphic registers.

examples.vi: Thời gian là vàng bạc → Thời gian, vàng bạc.
examples.en: Time is gold and silver → Time — gold and silver.

examples.vi: Nói ít, làm nhiều.
examples.en: Say little, do much.

examples.vi: Đời cha ăn mặn, đời con khát nước.
examples.en: The father's life eats salty, the children's life goes thirsty (the parents' sins fall on the children).

examples.vi: Trẻ cậy cha, già cậy con.
examples.en: Young, one leans on the father; old, one leans on the child.

modules.title: Register & Style Shifting
modules.description: Teaches how to re-encode the same propositional content across colloquial, formal, journalistic and literary registers of Vietnamese—choosing vocabulary, connectives, pronouns and syntax appropriate to audience and medium. Used whenever a C2 learner must move fluidly between speech and writing, or rewrite a message to fit a different communicative situation.
modules.mainPattern: [same idea] → colloquial (Sino-Vietnamese minimized, particles ↑) ⇄ formal/journalistic (Hán-Việt ↑, nominalization: việc/sự/cuộc + verb) ⇄ literary (figurative, marked word order)

faqs.question: How do I know whether to use a native Vietnamese word or its Sino-Vietnamese (Hán-Việt) equivalent?
faqs.answer: Match the word to the social situation, not to a 'hard vs. easy' scale. Use native (thuần Việt) words in everyday speech, warmth and intimacy; reach for Hán-Việt in official, ceremonial, technical or written-formal contexts. For death you say mất or chết with family/friends, but qua đời or từ trần in an obituary or to show respect. For a wife you say vợ casually but phu nhân about a dignitary's spouse. The danger runs both ways: piling Hán-Việt into casual talk (e.g. Tôi xin phép thực hiện việc ăn cơm) sounds absurdly pompous, while using blunt native words at a funeral or in a press release sounds disrespectful or unprofessional. When unsure, ask: would this appear in a newspaper headline (Hán-Việt) or in a text to a friend (native)?

faqs.question: Is Vietnamese passive (bị/được) the main way to sound formal or journalistic, like the English passive?
faqs.answer: Partly, but agent-demotion in Vietnamese is broader than a single passive construction. News and official prose do use bị (for unfavourable events) and được (for favourable ones)—Đối tượng đã bị bắt giữ ('the suspect has been apprehended')—to remove the actor and sound objective. But formal Vietnamese just as often achieves impersonality through abstract collective subjects (dư luận 'public opinion', các cơ quan chức năng 'the relevant authorities') or the impersonal người ta. So to shift a sentence like Cảnh sát bắt nó ('the police caught him') into news register, you can demote the agent with bị (Nó đã bị bắt) or recast the subject entirely (Vụ bắt giữ đã được tiến hành). Note bị/được carry an evaluative tone—bị implies something bad happened to the subject—so they are not the neutral, purely grammatical passive English speakers expect.

units.title: Native vs. Sino-Vietnamese lexical pairs (the register dial)
units.pattern: colloquial từ thuần Việt ⇄ formal từ Hán-Việt (e.g. chết ⇄ từ trần / qua đời; nhà ⇄ gia đình)
units.explanation: The single most powerful register lever in Vietnamese is swapping a native (thuần Việt) word for its Sino-Vietnamese (Hán-Việt) synonym. Native words feel plain, warm and everyday; Hán-Việt words feel formal, abstract, official or solemn. The same proposition keeps its meaning but moves up or down the formality scale purely through this lexical choice. Mastery means knowing which member of a pair fits a given situation, since using the wrong one sounds either pompous or disrespectful.
units.note: Hán-Việt is not automatically 'better'. Over-using it in casual speech sounds stilted or sarcastic; using a blunt native word (chết, vợ) where decorum is expected (từ trần, phu nhân) can sound rude. Match the word to the situation, not to a difficulty ranking.

examples.vi: Ông cụ mất rồi. → Cụ ông đã từ trần.
examples.en: The old man has died. (colloquial → formal/obituary)

examples.vi: Vợ ông giám đốc cũng tới. → Phu nhân giám đốc cũng có mặt.
examples.en: The director's wife came too. → The director's wife was also present. (everyday → formal)

examples.vi: Họ cãi nhau to lắm. → Hai bên đã xảy ra tranh chấp gay gắt.
examples.en: They had a big argument. → A heated dispute arose between the two sides. (spoken → journalistic)

examples.vi: Nó giúp tao nhiều. → Anh ấy đã hỗ trợ tôi rất nhiều.
examples.en: He helped me a lot. (intimate → polite/formal)

units.title: Nominalization with việc / sự / cuộc / quá trình
units.pattern: colloquial [clause with finite verb] → formal việc/sự/cuộc/quá trình + V (turning the action into a noun phrase)
units.explanation: Formal, academic and journalistic Vietnamese favours nominalization: an event or action expressed as a verb in speech is repackaged as a noun phrase headed by a classifier-like noun—việc (a matter/the -ing of), sự (an abstract state/occurrence), cuộc (an organized event), or quá trình (a process). This lets the writer make the action a subject or object, attach formal modifiers, and achieve the dense, impersonal texture of official prose. Choosing the right head noun is idiomatic: sự + stative/abstract verb (sự phát triển), cuộc + bounded social event (cuộc họp, cuộc đàm phán), việc + concrete task or fact (việc tăng giá).
units.note: The heads are not interchangeable. *sự họp and *cuộc phát triển are wrong; you say cuộc họp and sự phát triển. Spoken Vietnamese resists heavy nominalization—stacking these in conversation sounds bureaucratic.

examples.vi: Giá xăng tăng làm mọi người lo lắng. → Việc giá xăng tăng khiến dư luận lo ngại.
examples.en: Petrol prices rising worries everyone. → The rise in petrol prices causes public concern. (spoken → press)

examples.vi: Kinh tế phát triển nhanh. → Sự phát triển nhanh chóng của nền kinh tế...
examples.en: The economy is developing fast. → The rapid development of the economy... (clause → noun phrase)

examples.vi: Hai nước họp lại để bàn. → Cuộc đàm phán giữa hai nước nhằm...
examples.en: The two countries met to discuss. → The negotiations between the two countries aimed to... (plain → diplomatic)

examples.vi: Người ta đô thị hóa rất nhanh. → Quá trình đô thị hóa diễn ra nhanh chóng.
examples.en: People are urbanizing very fast. → The process of urbanization is unfolding rapidly. (colloquial → academic)

units.title: Connectives across registers: từ "nên" to "do đó / vì vậy / chính vì lẽ đó"
units.pattern: spoken: ... nên ... / cho nên ... → written-formal: do đó, vì vậy, vì thế, bởi vậy → literary/rhetorical: chính vì lẽ đó, ấy thế mà, song
units.explanation: Logical relations (cause, contrast, addition) are signalled by different connectives at different register levels. In conversation, speakers lean on light particles and clause-final/clause-initial words: nên, cho nên (so), nhưng (but), với lại (and besides). Formal writing replaces these with disyllabic, often Hán-Việt connectives placed at the head of a sentence: do đó, vì vậy, tuy nhiên, hơn nữa, đồng thời. Literary and oratorical prose reaches for marked, emphatic or archaic forms: song (but), ấy thế mà (and yet), chính vì lẽ đó (it is for this very reason that). Shifting register therefore means re-selecting the whole connective inventory, not just translating one word.
units.note: tuy nhiên and nhưng both mean 'but', but tuy nhiên begins a new sentence in writing, whereas nhưng joins clauses within a sentence; song is literary/formal and never used casually. Mixing levels (e.g. song with slangy vocabulary) clashes badly.

examples.vi: Trời mưa to nên tụi mình ở nhà. → Do trời mưa lớn, chúng tôi quyết định ở nhà.
examples.en: It rained hard so we stayed home. → Owing to heavy rain, we decided to stay home. (chat → formal)

examples.vi: Nó cố gắng nhưng vẫn trượt. → Anh đã rất nỗ lực; tuy nhiên, kết quả vẫn không như ý.
examples.en: He tried but still failed. → He made great efforts; however, the result was still not as desired.

examples.vi: Khó lắm nhưng vẫn làm được. → Khó khăn chồng chất, song chúng ta vẫn vượt qua.
examples.en: It was hard but we managed. → Difficulties piled up, yet we still overcame them. (spoken → literary)

examples.vi: Chính vì lẽ đó, chúng ta không thể chần chừ thêm nữa.
examples.en: It is for this very reason that we can no longer hesitate. (oratorical cause connective)

units.title: Pronoun and self-reference shift: from kin-terms to institutional voice
units.pattern: intimate tao/mày, tớ/cậu → polite tôi/anh/chị → formal-written chúng tôi, quý vị, ông/bà → journalistic agentless: được + V / người ta / dư luận
units.explanation: Vietnamese has no neutral 'I/you'; every pronoun encodes the relationship and thus the register. To shift style for the same idea you must re-set the deixis: blunt tao/mày among intimates, neutral tôi in polite or professional contexts, the collective-modest chúng tôi and the deferential quý vị / quý độc giả in formal address. Crucially, journalistic and official Vietnamese often deletes the agent entirely, using the passive được/bị + verb, the impersonal người ta, or abstract collective subjects (dư luận, các cơ quan chức năng) to sound objective and authoritative. Re-voicing the same sentence across these is a core C2 skill.
units.note: chúng tôi (exclusive 'we', not including the listener) vs chúng ta (inclusive 'we, including you') is a register and meaning trap: a speech that should rally the audience needs chúng ta, while a company statement distancing itself uses chúng tôi. Choosing wrong reverses the intended stance.

examples.vi: Tao thấy mày sai rồi. → Tôi cho rằng anh đã nhầm.
examples.en: I think you're wrong. (intimate → polite)

examples.vi: Bọn tao quyết định hủy. → Chúng tôi xin trân trọng thông báo việc hủy chương trình.
examples.en: We decided to cancel. → We respectfully announce the cancellation of the programme. (casual → official)

examples.vi: Cảnh sát bắt nó rồi. → Đối tượng đã bị bắt giữ.
examples.en: The police arrested him. → The suspect has been apprehended. (spoken → news, agent demoted)

examples.vi: Mọi người đang bàn tán chuyện này. → Vụ việc đang gây xôn xao dư luận.
examples.en: Everyone's talking about this. → The affair is stirring up public opinion. (colloquial → journalistic)

units.title: Literary marked syntax: fronting, inversion and figurative re-encoding
units.pattern: neutral S–V–O → literary: [fronted complement/adverbial] + (đảo ngữ) V + S; reduplication & metaphor for the same idea
units.explanation: Literary Vietnamese distinguishes itself less by vocabulary than by marked word order, rhythm and figuration. Writers front a complement, adverbial or object for emphasis and emotional weight, sometimes inverting subject and verb (đảo ngữ): e.g. placing a predicate adjective or verb before the subject (Lác đác bên sông chợ mấy nhà). They exploit reduplicatives (từ láy) and balanced four-syllable expressions for musicality, and recast a plain statement as imagery. The propositional content is identical to the colloquial version, but the form foregrounds aesthetic effect—so style-shifting upward into literary register means restructuring the clause, not merely swapping words.
units.note: Inversion is a deliberate literary device; using đảo ngữ in ordinary prose or speech sounds affected or like a mistake. Reserve it for poetry, descriptive writing and high rhetoric, and keep the rhythm balanced—an unbalanced inversion reads as clumsy rather than elevated.

examples.vi: Mấy chiếc lá rơi xuống. → Lặng lẽ rơi xuống, từng chiếc lá vàng chạm đất.
examples.en: A few leaves fell. → Falling silently, each yellow leaf touched the ground. (neutral → fronted/literary)

examples.vi: Trên đồi có một ngôi nhà nhỏ. → Thấp thoáng trên đồi, một ngôi nhà nhỏ đơn sơ.
examples.en: On the hill there is a small house. → Faintly visible on the hill, a small, plain house. (fronting + từ láy)

examples.vi: Cô ấy rất buồn. → Lòng cô trĩu nặng một nỗi buồn không tên.
examples.en: She was very sad. → Her heart was weighed down by a nameless sorrow. (plain → figurative)

examples.vi: Gió thổi mạnh và sóng dâng cao. → Gió gào, sóng thét, cả mặt biển cuộn lên dữ dội.
examples.en: The wind blew hard and the waves rose. → The wind howled, the waves screamed, the whole sea churned violently. (factual → literary balanced)
